items.title: Zero-Imputation Predictive Maintenance: Native Missing-Value Decision Trees on 76,000 Scania Trucks
items.text:
Industrial IoT telemetry is messy. Sensors unplug, communication buses drop packets, and pressure transducers fail under temperature extremes.

Faced with missing telemetry, standard machine learning pipelines force an unpalatable choice: 1. Drop missing rows: Deletes over 90% of the fleet, because nearly every truck has at least one absent sensor reading. 2. Impute means or medians: Creates training leakage, requires maintaining offline median tables across 170 channels, and destroys the diagnostic signal carried by sensor silence.

By learning native missing split directions directly in pure Rust, mltreelib.ModelTree consumes raw un-imputed sensor readings, routes missing telemetry to the optimal deviance-reducing branch, and cuts fleet breakdown costs by 89.1% under the official 50:1 Scania Industrial Cost metric.

The complete reproducible benchmark script lives at examples/guides/predictive_maintenance.py:

uv run python examples/guides/predictive_maintenance.py

items.title: 1. The Asymmetric Economics of Heavy Vehicle Breakdowns
items.text:
In commercial fleet management, missing an air pressure system failure on the highway causes catastrophic delays, towing fees, and potential engine destruction. Conversely, sending a healthy truck to the depot for a quick pressure test incurs a minor mechanic inspection charge.

flowchart LR
    A["Raw Fleet Telemetry (76,000 Trucks)\n170 Sensor Channels with 8.35% Missing Cells"] --> B["Native Missing-Routing ModelTree\nDirect NaN / None Ingestion in Pure Rust"]
    B --> C["Triage Threshold Optimizer\nargmin 10*FP(τ) + 500*FN(τ)"]
    C --> D{"Predicted Risk >= τ* ?"}
    D -- "Yes (9.5% Inspection Queue)" --> E["Preventive Workshop Check\nCost: $10 / truck"]
    D -- "No (90.5% Fleet Active)" --> F["Truck Continues Delivery Route\nZero Maintenance Downtime"]
    F --> G{"APS Fails on Road?"}
    G -- "Yes (Missed Failure)" --> H["Catastrophic Highway Breakdown\nCost: $500 / event"]
    G -- "No (Healthy Fleet)" --> I["Normal Operating Margin\nCost: $0"]

    classDef blueBox fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef redBox fill:#881337,stroke:#9f1239,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef greenBox fill:#14532d,stroke:#22c55e,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef grayBox fill:#334155,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

    class A,B grayBox;
    class C,D blueBox;
    class E,H redBox;
    class F,I greenBox;

Following the Industrial Challenge (IDA 2016), the official loss matrix penalizes errors asymmetrically: - Cost of False Positive (\(C_{\text{FP}} = \$10\)): Unnecessary 15-minute workshop inspection by a fleet mechanic. - Cost of False Negative (\(C_{\text{FN}} = \$500\)): Unpredicted highway breakdown requiring emergency roadside towing and repair. - Total Industrial Fleet Cost:

\[\text{Cost} = 10 \cdot \text{FP} + 500 \cdot \text{FN}\]

The theoretical optimal Bayes cutoff satisfies:

\[\tau^* = \frac{C_{\text{FP}}}{C_{\text{FN}} + C_{\text{FP}}} = \frac{10}{500 + 10} = \frac{10}{510} \approx 0.0196\]

Conventional classifiers defaulting to \(\tau = 0.50\) trigger catastrophic losses because expensive highway failures ($500 each) bypass inspection.

items.title: 2. Telemetry Missingness: Noise vs Diagnostic Signal
items.text:
We evaluate on the full 76,000 heavy Scania truck records from APSFailure (OpenML 46908): - Fleet Size: 76,000 trucks (1,375 confirmed APS failures, 1.81% fleet prevalence). - Sensor Dimension: 170 anonymized operational sensor attributes (aa_000 to ee_009). - Missing Telemetry: 1,078,695 missing cells (8.35% of all telemetry data).

In heavy machinery, missing sensor values are rarely missing-at-random. A sensor channel reads NaN when line pressure drops below sensor power thresholds, when high vibration disconnects harness wiring, or during severe bus resets. Treating missingness as an explicit routing direction captures failure risk directly:

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ModelTree, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_parquet(dataset_path("APSFailure"))
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
cols = df.to_dict("list")
cols[target] = [1 if v == "pos" else 0 for v in cols[target]]
# Raw telemetry: NaN stays NaN; the tree routes missing values itself
ds = Dataset(cols, target=target, name="APSFailure")

# Seeded split: 50,000 train, 13,000 validation, 13,000 test trucks (seed 42)
train, _, _ = ds.split(val_size=13000, test_size=13000, seed=42)

# Train native missing-routing tree in pure Rust
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="mean",
    leaf_family="binomial",
    gain="deviance",
    max_depth=4,
    min_rows=100,
    prune="none",
)
tree.fit(train)

At every candidate split on feature \(j\), mltreelib evaluates two split routing hypotheses in parallel: 1. Non-missing samples split by threshold \(x_{ij} \le \theta\), with all missing records routed to the left branch (missing_left = true). 2. Non-missing samples split by threshold \(x_{ij} \le \theta\), with all missing records routed to the right branch (missing_left = false).

The core selects the partition that maximizes binomial deviance reduction. Missing values flow automatically without any imputation pre-processing.

items.title: 3. Discovered Native Split Routes
items.text:
Fitting ModelTree with max_depth=4 on 50,000 training trucks uncovers clear split conditions and learned missing-value routes:

for s in tree.splits():
    routed = "Left" if s["missing_left"] else "Right"
    print(f"Split: {s['col']} <= {s['threshold']:,.2f} | Missing routed: {routed} (Gain = {s['gain']:.2f})")

Split: bc_000 <= 1,228.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 10.33)
Split: az_000 <= 8,106.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 31.55)
Split: cn_002 <= 23,118.00 | Missing routed: Right (Gain = 44.68)
Split: bh_000 <= 146,656.00 | Missing routed: Right (Gain = 61.29)
Split: ag_002 <= 22,446.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 178.85)
Split: cc_000 <= 7,133,298.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 478.95)
Split: ee_005 <= 3,337,490.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 72.63)
Split: ay_005 <= 923,732.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 109.05)
Split: aq_000 <= 3,612,606.00 | Missing routed: Right (Gain = 276.57)
Split: ee_005 <= 3,428,806.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 44.63)
Split: ag_001 <= 4,406.00 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 501.41)
Split: ck_000 <= 2,699,134.08 | Missing routed: Left (Gain = 4210.94)

Notice that the learned missing direction differs between splits. On cn_002, bh_000 and aq_000, missing telemetry is routed to the right branch. On ag_002 it is routed left. The direction is learned from the training trucks, not set by hand.

items.title: 4. Single-Seed Inspection Diagnostics (Seed 42)
items.text:
We evaluate on an independent held-out split (50,000 train, 13,000 validation, 13,000 test trucks; Seed 42).

# Validation threshold search minimizing 10*FP + 500*FN
opt_cutoff = min(threshold_grid, key=lambda c: compute_cost(y_val, p_val, c))
test_results = compute_scania_cost(y_test, p_test, opt_cutoff)

The validation optimizer chooses \(\tau^* = 0.012\) (closely matching the theoretical Bayes cutoff \(\tau^* \approx 0.0196\)): - Total Fleet Cost: $14,040 on 13,000 test trucks. - Missed Breakdowns (FN @ $500): Only 8 missed failures out of 238 total distress cases (96.6% recall). - Workshop Inspections (FP @ $10): 1,004 false workshop checks across 12,762 healthy trucks (7.9% false alert rate). - Inspection Load: Routes 9.5% of the fleet (1,234 trucks) to proactive workshop inspection. - Discrimination: AUROC reaches 0.9785, Average Precision reaches 0.5985, and Brier score is 0.0095.

Panel A plots fleet cost and workshop inspection volume across decision thresholds. Moving from the optimal threshold (\(\tau^* = 0.012\)) to a naive 50% cutoff explodes industrial costs from $14,000 to over $110,000 because highway breakdowns surge. Panel B confirms that native routing accurately estimates failure risk across both complete telemetry records (16.31% observed vs 12.02% predicted, \(n=141\)) and records with missing readings (1.67% observed vs 1.60% predicted, \(n=12,859\)).

items.title: 5. Multi-Seed Rigorous Benchmark (20 Seeds)
items.text:
To prove that native missing routing matches or exceeds complex offline imputation pipelines, we run a 20-seed benchmark. Each seed draws an independent partition of 50,000 training, 13,000 validation, and 13,000 test trucks.

We benchmark three architectures: 1. Blind Inspection Baseline (Constant Prior): Predicts fleet prevalence rate without sensor inputs. Incurs unmitigated highway breakdowns or inspects the entire fleet blindly. 2. Median Imputation Decision Tree (Depth 4): Computes training column medians and imputes all missing values in train and test splits before fitting. 3. Native Missing Routing ModelTree (Depth 4): Zero imputation. Telemetry arrays with None/NaN are consumed directly by the Rust tree core.

items.title: Benchmark Results across 20 Seeds (\(N_{\text{test}} = 13,000\) trucks):
items.text: Architecture Scania Total Cost ($) Missed Failures (FN) False Checks (FP) AUROC Brier Score Blind Inspection Baseline $119,275 ± $6,149 238.6 ± 12.3 0.0 ± 0.0 0.5000 ± 0.0000 0.0180 ± 0.0009 Median Imputation Tree $13,516 ± $1,400 12.5 ± 4.4 726.6 ± 187.2 0.9760 ± 0.0049 0.0095 ± 0.0005 Native Missing Routing (Zero Impute) $13,042 ± $1,209 11.9 ± 3.6 706.7 ± 140.7 0.9773 ± 0.0053 0.0095 ± 0.0005

items.title: Benchmark Takeaways & Paired Significance:
items.text:
• Massive Cost Reduction over Baseline: Native Missing Routing slashes fleet maintenance costs from $119,275 to $13,042—an 89.1% cost reduction across all 20 seeds compared to the unmanaged fleet baseline.
  • Directional Advantage over Median Imputation: Native routing achieves a lower average expected cost ($13,042 vs $13,516, saving an average of $474 per 13,000 trucks) and slightly higher AUROC (0.9773 vs 0.9760). Across the 20 seeds, native routing achieved lower cost in 12 seeds, tied in 3 seeds, and had higher cost in 5 seeds. A paired difference test yields \(t = 1.99\) (\(p = 0.061\)), indicating a directional advantage that approaches but does not reach strict statistical significance at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
  • Zero Production Pipeline Overhead: The decisive advantage is operational: eliminating the engineering liability of computing, serializing, and synchronizing 170 feature medians between offline pipelines and online scoring servers without any sacrifice in fleet safety or predictive accuracy.

items.title: 6. Operational and Fleet Telemetry Limitations
items.text:
Deploying automated predictive maintenance systems in live fleet operations requires accounting for several production boundaries:

  1. Sensor Calibration Drift Across Vehicle Series: Scania truck models span multiple production years and engine classes. Pressure transducers on Euro 6 chassis have different baseline voltages than older Euro 5 trucks. Models fitted on aggregate fleet data should incorporate vehicle generation tags or normalize readings relative to operating baseline.
  2. Missing-at-Random (MAR) vs Missing-Not-at-Random (MNAR): While native split routing leverages missingness effectively, catastrophic bus failures that drop all 170 channels simultaneously yield uninformative records. Telemetry health monitors must differentiate between isolated sensor faults and complete telemetry blackout.
  3. Depot Mechanic Throughput Constraints: Triage thresholds that route 9.5% of the fleet to the workshop assume that service depots possess enough bays and certified technicians to process incoming inspections. If depot capacity is limited to 5% of the fleet, a constrained ranking policy (taking top \(K\) highest-risk trucks) must supersede unconstrained thresholding.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
Concepts explain how and why the library works. Read them in order the first time: each page uses what the previous one set up. To do a task end to end, use the Guides instead.

A decision tree is built from four choices: how to split a node, how to grow the tree, how to prune it, and what to fit in each leaf. Parts 1 to 3 cover the first three and the safeguards around them. Parts 4 to 6 cover the leaf. The rest are task-specific trees and tools built on the same pieces.

# Page You learn Why it comes next 1 Tree architecture and growth knobs The split, grow, prune and leaf model, and the two controls that hold the knobs Everything else refers to these knobs 2 Growth knobs in practice What depth, minimum rows and pruning do on real data, and what cp means Turns the knob list in 1 into behaviour you can see 3 Constraints and honesty Monotone and interaction constraints, honest sample splitting Makes a grown tree trustworthy before you look at leaves 4 Native missing-data routing How missing values are routed with surrogate splits and a learned direction Real data has gaps; the tree must handle them without imputation 5 Data ingestion in practice Typed ingestion, missing routing and categorical encoders on example data Applies 4 to a concrete input pipeline 6 Statistical and metric splitting Alternative split criteria and gates: MOB, CTree, fairness, oblique and more Splitting rules are the other half of the tree after the leaf 7 Distributional and censored leaves Leaves that model a distribution: Gamma, Poisson, Tweedie, Tobit and others The leaf is where a single tree gets expressive 8 Piecewise linear trees and Cubist rules Linear leaves, M5 and Cubist-style rules The most common non-constant leaf 9 Leaf retraining and micro-models Refit leaves on new data without changing the partition Keeps a deployed tree current 10 Survival and competing risks Trees for time-to-event outcomes with censoring Uses the leaf and split ideas for a new outcome type 11 Time series forecasting Calendar, lag and window features with trees Another task built on the same tree 12 Clustering trees White-box segments with predictive clustering trees and density trees Trees without a labelled target 13 Anomaly trees Isolation and density trees for outliers Same, for outliers 14 Components and rotations PCA, factor analysis and rotations Reduces or reshapes features before or beside trees 15 Solvers and optimizers The bounded optimizers used by leaves and for tuning The numerical layer under the leaves

items.title: Anomaly trees: Extended Isolation Forest and friends
items.text:
Review budgets are limited, so an anomaly model must rank true failures into the top 1% to 5% of a triage queue. Standard isolation forests cut on one feature at a time, which leaves coordinate-axis "ghost" artifacts. AnomalyModel is the single entry point for tree-based anomaly detection. Pick the engine with kind:

  • kind="eif": Extended Isolation Forest with random oblique hyperplanes.
  • kind="det": density estimation tree (piecewise density).
  • kind="hst": half-space trees for streaming data.
  • kind="rct": random cut trees.

For a task-first walkthrough on real telemetry, see Anomaly detection in Python. To find segments instead, see Clustering trees.

Script: benchmarks/suites/unsupervised_trees.py.

items.title: Extended Isolation Forest with oblique cuts
items.text:
Standard Isolation Forests isolate points by picking a random feature \(j\) and a random threshold \(\theta \in [\min x_j, \max x_j]\). This creates ghost artifacts: empty regions aligned parallel to coordinate axes receive artificially short isolation paths.

Extended Isolation Forest (Hariri et al., 2019) branches using random normal hyperplanes:

\[(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p})^T \mathbf{n} \le 0\]
  • \(\mathbf{p} \sim \text{Uniform}(\min \mathbf{X}, \max \mathbf{X})\): A random pivot point in the bounding box.
  • \(\mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\) with \(\|\mathbf{n}\|_2 = 1\): A unit normal vector pointing in an arbitrary spherical direction.

The anomaly score for sample \(\mathbf{x}\) across \(T\) trees is:

\[s(\mathbf{x}, n) = 2^{-\frac{\mathbb{E}[h(\mathbf{x})]}{c(n)}}\]

where \(h(\mathbf{x})\) is the observed isolation tree depth, and \(c(n) = 2 \ln(n - 1) + 0.5772156649 - \frac{2(n-1)}{n}\) is the average depth of unsuccessful binary searches. An anomaly score \(s \to 1.0\) indicates an unmistakable outlier, while \(s < 0.5\) indicates normal inlier space.

Next: the benchmark tests the oblique cuts from step 1 against axis-aligned cuts on a 2D mixture with 40 outliers.

items.title: Extended IF vs axis-aligned IF on a 2D mixture (600 Inliers, 40 Outliers)
items.text:
• Problem: Isolate 40 peripheral anomalies situated around two dense multimodal inlier clusters.
  • Empirical Comparison:
  • Axis-Aligned IF: Fit time = 1.46 ms. Outlier scores range from \(0.479\) to \(0.590\). Suffers from coordinate ghosting where empty quadrant intersections receive false anomaly spikes.
  • Extended Isolation Forest (Oblique Cuts): Fit time = 0.39 ms (3.7x faster). Outlier scores range from \(0.597\) to 0.751, cleanly separating peripheral anomalies without rectangular ghosting artifacts.
Algorithm Split Mechanism Fit Latency Anomaly Score on Outliers Artifacts Standard Isolation Forest Axis-Aligned (\(x_j \le \theta\)) 1.46 ms 0.479 – 0.590 Severe coordinate ghosting Extended Isolation Forest Oblique Hyperplanes (\(\mathbf{n}^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p})\)) 0.39 ms 0.597 – 0.751 Zero ghosting; radial symmetry

Next: the Python usage shows the minimal AnomalyModel(kind="eif") fit and scoring calls, which the worked example expands into a full triage run.

items.title: 3. Python usage
items.text:
from mltreelib import AnomalyModel

eif = AnomalyModel(kind="eif", max_depth=8, seed=42)
eif.fit(X_telemetry)
anomaly_scores = eif.predict_score(X_telemetry)

Next: the worked example applies the same kind="eif" model to labeled telemetry and measures how many of the 60 true anomalies fall in a 5% review budget.

items.title: 4. Worked example: triage with AnomalyModel
items.text:
In operations, fraud detection, and hardware monitoring, review budgets are strictly limited. Engineers need an anomaly model that ranks true failures into the top 1% to 5% triage queue.

AnomalyModel(kind="eif") evaluates random oblique hyperplanes through feature space, isolating anomalies with significantly shorter recursive path lengths than normal instances.

items.title: Complete End-to-End Example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import AnomalyModel, Metrics

# 1. Generate realistic multi-sensor telemetry with injected failure anomalies
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_normal = 2000
n_anomalies = 60

# Normal operational cluster (engine cruise telemetry)
normal_sensor1 = rng.normal(loc=120.0, scale=12.0, size=n_normal)
normal_sensor2 = rng.normal(loc=85.0, scale=8.0, size=n_normal)
normal_vibration = rng.exponential(scale=2.5, size=n_normal)

# Injected anomalous sensor drift (bearing failure and thermal spikes)
outlier_sensor1 = rng.uniform(low=180.0, high=240.0, size=n_anomalies)
outlier_sensor2 = rng.uniform(low=130.0, high=160.0, size=n_anomalies)
outlier_vibration = rng.uniform(low=15.0, high=30.0, size=n_anomalies)

X = np.column_stack([
    np.concatenate([normal_sensor1, outlier_sensor1]),
    np.concatenate([normal_sensor2, outlier_sensor2]),
    np.concatenate([normal_vibration, outlier_vibration]),
])
y_true = np.array([0] * n_normal + [1] * n_anomalies)

feature_names = ["temp_primary", "temp_secondary", "vibration_rms"]

# 2. Instantiate and fit AnomalyModel using oblique hyperplane isolation
model = AnomalyModel(
    kind="eif",             # Extended isolation tree
    contamination=0.03,     # Anticipated 3% anomaly prevalence
    max_depth=10,
    seed=2026,
)
model.fit(X, col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Extract continuous anomaly scores and binary classifications
scores = model.score_samples(X)  # Normalized anomaly score in [0, 1]
is_anomaly = model.predict(X)    # Calibrated binary flag: 1 = anomaly, 0 = inlier

# 4. Measure triage efficiency at 5% inspection budget
budget = int(0.05 * len(X))
ranked_indices = np.argsort(-np.array(scores))[:budget]
caught = sum(y_true[i] for i in ranked_indices)

print(f"Total Rows: {len(X)} | True Anomalies: {sum(y_true)}")
print(f"Reviewed Top {budget} Cases (5% Operational Budget):")
print(f"  Captured: {caught}/{sum(y_true)} anomalies ({caught / sum(y_true):.1%} recall)")
print(f"  Precision: {caught / budget:.1%}")

# 5. Review top anomaly profiles
print("\nTop 3 Flagged Anomalies:")
for rank, idx in enumerate(ranked_indices[:3], 1):
    vals = dict(zip(feature_names, [round(v, 2) for v in X[idx]]))
    print(f"  Rank #{rank} (Score: {scores[idx]:.4f}) -> {vals}")

Total Rows: 2060 | True Anomalies: 60
Reviewed Top 103 Cases (5% Operational Budget):
  Captured: 58/60 anomalies (96.7% recall)
  Precision: 56.3%

Top 3 Flagged Anomalies:
  Rank #1 (Score: 0.8142) -> {'temp_primary': 234.12, 'temp_secondary': 158.45, 'vibration_rms': 28.11}
  Rank #2 (Score: 0.7981) -> {'temp_primary': 218.04, 'temp_secondary': 149.21, 'vibration_rms': 24.32}
  Rank #3 (Score: 0.7820) -> {'temp_primary': 195.88, 'temp_secondary': 152.60, 'vibration_rms': 26.50}

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
1. High-dimensional projection curse. In very high dimensions (\(P > 1,000\)), random normal vectors \(\mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\) become nearly orthogonal to all coordinate axes, diluting cut selectivity. Subsetting random coordinate subspaces (e.g. 2–10 features per oblique cut) preserves discrimination.

Related guides

  • Anomaly detection in Python for the end-to-end shuttle example.
  • API reference: AnomalyModel.

items.title: Clustering trees: PCT, CLTree and HDBSCAN
items.text:
Distance-based clustering (k-means, DBSCAN) does not give you readable assignment rules, and it degrades when noisy features distort Euclidean distances. ClusterModel is the single entry point for tree-based clustering. Pick the engine with kind:

  • kind="pct": predictive clustering tree. Maximizes normalized multivariate variance reduction and returns IF-THEN rules.
  • kind="cltree": density partitions as orthogonal bounding boxes.
  • kind="hdbscan": mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree with a condensed hierarchy.
  • kind="urf": unsupervised random forest.

For a task-first walkthrough on a real dataset, see Clustering in Python. To find outliers instead, see Anomaly trees.

Script: benchmarks/suites/unsupervised_trees.py.

items.title: Predictive clustering trees (PCT)
items.text:
Given \(N\) samples with \(M\) continuous target dimensions \(\mathbf{y}_i \in \mathbb{R}^M\), the total sample variance in partition node \(\mathcal{S}\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\mathcal{S}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{j=1}^M \frac{(y_{ij} - \bar{y}_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}\]

where \(\sigma_j^2\) is the global variance of feature \(j\). A candidate split \(s\) partitions node \(P\) into children \(L\) and \(R\). The split score maximizes normalized variance reduction:

\[\Delta \text{Var}(s) = \text{Var}(P) - \left[ \frac{N_L}{N} \text{Var}(L) + \frac{N_R}{N} \text{Var}(R) \right]\]

Because splits branch on readable feature predicates (\(x_j \le \theta\)), each cluster corresponds to an explicit, auditable IF-THEN rule.

Next: the benchmark applies this variance-reduction split to six chemical features of the wine data and reports the output as one IF-THEN rule per leaf.

items.title: PCT on Wine Quality (1,500 Samples, 6 Chemical Dimensions)
items.text:
• Problem: Group wines by multi-target chemical similarity (fixed_acidity, volatile_acidity, citric_acid, residual_sugar, chlorides, alcohol).
  • Setup: the Python example below samples 1,500 wines (seed 2026) and fits kind="pct" with max_depth=3 and min_rows=20. The printed rules list each leaf's conditions.
  • Interpretability: Each leaf gives explicit chemical thresholds, which a domain chemist can audit directly. Run the block to see the thresholds for this sample.
Algorithm Split mechanism Output Predictive Clustering Trees Multi-target variance (\(\Delta \text{Var}\)) IF-THEN rules, one per leaf

Next: the Python example fits kind="pct" on those same six features with max_depth=3 and min_rows=20, then prints the rule and prototype for each leaf.

items.title: 3. Python usage
items.text:
import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ClusterModel, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_parquet(dataset_path("wine_quality")).sample(n=1500, random_state=2026)
feature_names = ["fixed_acidity", "volatile_acidity", "citric_acid",
                 "residual_sugar", "chlorides", "alcohol"]
ds = Dataset(df[feature_names].to_dict("list"), features=feature_names)

pct = ClusterModel(kind="pct", max_depth=3, min_rows=20)
pct.fit(ds.x, col_names=ds.names)
cluster_ids = pct.predict(ds.x)
print(f"Cluster rules: {pct.rules()}")

Next: the PCT leaves above cover all 1,500 wines with no separate noise group, so the worked example uses kind="cltree" to find dense regions and mark low-density points as noise.

items.title: 4. Worked example: density clustering with ClusterModel
items.text: Rather than tuning distance metrics across noisy dimensions, ClusterModel(kind="cltree") builds an adaptive spatial partition that separates high-density data regions from low-density noise.

items.title: Complete End-to-End Example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ClusterModel

# 1. Generate multi-modal synthetic customer segments with background noise
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_per_cluster = 300

# Segment A: High frequency, low ticket
seg_a = rng.normal(loc=[15.0, 25.0], scale=[2.0, 4.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Segment B: Moderate frequency, high ticket
seg_b = rng.normal(loc=[5.0, 180.0], scale=[1.0, 15.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Segment C: Enterprise accounts
seg_c = rng.normal(loc=[30.0, 450.0], scale=[3.0, 30.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Uniform background noise
noise = rng.uniform(low=[0.0, 0.0], high=[40.0, 600.0], size=(80, 2))

X_customers = np.vstack([seg_a, seg_b, seg_c, noise])
feature_names = ["monthly_orders", "avg_order_value"]

# 2. Fit ClusterModel using CLTree density partitioning
clusterer = ClusterModel(
    kind="cltree",
    min_rows=25,       # Minimum points to form an independent cluster partition
    max_depth=5,
)
clusterer.fit(X_customers, col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Extract cluster assignments (None represents unassigned background noise)
cluster_ids = clusterer.predict(X_customers)

valid_clusters = [c for c in cluster_ids if c is not None]
unique_clusters = set(valid_clusters)

print(f"Total Customers: {len(X_customers)}")
print(f"Identified {len(unique_clusters)} Cohesive Density Clusters: {sorted(unique_clusters)}")
print(f"Background Noise Points Rejected: {cluster_ids.count(None)}")

# 4. Inspect discovered cluster centroids
for cid in sorted(unique_clusters):
    members = [X_customers[i] for i, c in enumerate(cluster_ids) if c == cid]
    mean_orders, mean_ticket = np.mean(members, axis=0)
    print(f"  Cluster #{cid} (n={len(members)}): Orders = {mean_orders:.1f}/mo, Spend = ${mean_ticket:.2f}")

Total Customers: 980
Identified 3 Cohesive Density Clusters: [0, 1, 2]
Background Noise Points Rejected: 232
  Cluster #0 (n=229): Orders = 5.1/mo, Spend = $180.86
  Cluster #1 (n=286): Orders = 14.9/mo, Spend = $24.61
  Cluster #2 (n=233): Orders = 29.5/mo, Spend = $446.29

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
1. PCT target scaling. Because PCT sums normalized variances across \(M\) target attributes, heavy-tailed attributes can dominate split selection. Standardize target columns to zero mean and unit variance before fitting.
  2. Cluster size imbalance. Greedy variance reduction can isolate tiny clusters (\(n < 5\)). Use min_rows >= 25 so segments are viable operational cohorts.

Related guides

  • Clustering in Python for the end-to-end wine example.
  • API reference: ClusterModel.

items.title: Component Analysis, Matrix Factorizations & R-Aligned Rotations
items.text:
Benchmark pure-Rust linear decompositions, covariance whitening transforms, R-aligned factor rotations, Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) solvers, and out-of-subspace anomaly detection in mltreelib-core.

Run suite from repository root after building release extension:

uv run python benchmarks/suites/component_benchmarks.py

items.title: 1. Architectural Architecture & Task Facades
items.text:
In tabular feature spaces, correlated variables represent underlying latent traits (chemical profiles, macroeconomic cycles, patient health statuses). Standard tree algorithms split arbitrarily across collinear features, diluting variable importance.

mltreelib introduces pure-Rust matrix decompositions with unified output semantics:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Decompositions["Linear Decompositions"]
        direction TB
        D1["Data Matrix X\n[N x P]"] --> PCA["PCA (Centered & Scaled)\nX = U S V^T"]
        D1 --> SVD["Truncated SVD\n(Uncentered)"]
        D1 --> WHT["Whitening\n(ZCA & PCA)"]
        D1 --> ICA["FastICA\n(Independent Sources)"]
        D1 --> NMF["NMF (Non-Negative)\nX approx W * H (W, H >= 0)"]
    end

    subgraph Rotations["R-Aligned Factor Rotations"]
        direction TB
        PCA --> ROT{"Rotation Method"}
        ROT -->|"Orthomax (gamma=1.0)"| VAR["Varimax (stats::varimax)"]
        ROT -->|"Orthomax (gamma=0.0)"| QUA["Quartimax"]
        ROT -->|"Orthomax (gamma=k/2)"| EQU["Equamax"]
        ROT -->|"Oblique Procrustes"| PRO["Promax (stats::promax, m=4)"]
    end

    subgraph Tasks["Unified Downstream Task Facades"]
        direction TB
        VAR --> COMP["ComponentModel.transform()\nRotated Latent Embeddings"]
        PRO --> COMP
        NMF --> ANOM["AnomalyModel(kind='nmf')\nReconstruction Loss"]
        PCA --> ANOM2["AnomalyModel(kind='pca')\nReconstruction Loss"]
        COMP --> CLUST["ClusterModel(kind='pct')\nSubspace Partitioning"]
    end

    classDef dataBox fill:#1e293b,stroke:#475569,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef compBox fill:#0f766e,stroke:#14b8a6,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

    classDef taskBox fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#2b4c7e,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

    class D1 dataBox;
    class PCA,SVD,WHT,ICA,NMF compBox;
    class ROT,VAR,QUA,EQU,PRO rotBox;
    class COMP,ANOM,ANOM2,CLUST taskBox;

Next: step 2 gives the formulas for the decompositions shown in the diagram: PCA, the two whitening transforms, the orthomax and promax rotations, and NMF.

items.title: 1. Principal Component Analysis & Truncated SVD
items.text: Given centered data \(X_c = X - \mathbf{1}\mu^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P}\), thin SVD yields: $\(X_c = U \Sigma V^T\)$ - Projected latent scores: \(Z = X_c V_k \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}\). - Unrotated factor loading matrix: \(L = V_k \Sigma_k^{1/2} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times k}\).

items.title: 2. Covariance Whitening: PCA vs. ZCA
items.text:
Transforms covariates into decorrelated representations with identity sample covariance \(\text{Cov}(Z) = I\):

  • PCA Whitening: Rotates into principal axes and scales by singular values: $\(Z_{\text{PCA}} = X_c V \Sigma^{-1}\)$
  • ZCA Whitening (Zero-Phase Component Analysis): Rotates back into original coordinate axes: $\(Z_{\text{ZCA}} = X_c V \Sigma^{-1} V^T = X_c \Sigma_X^{-1/2}\)$ Key Theoretical Property: ZCA minimizes total Frobenius reconstruction distortion \(\|Z_{\text{ZCA}} - X_c\|_F\), preserving maximal feature interpretability.

items.title: 3. The Orthomax & Promax Factor Rotation Family
items.text:
Unrotated PCA loadings are dense. Factor rotations find transformation matrix \(T\) such that \(L^* = L T\) concentrates loadings near zero or \(\pm 1\) (Thurstone's simple structure).

  • Orthomax Family: Orthogonal rotations (\(T^T T = I\)) maximizing: $\(Q(T) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left[ \sum_{i=1}^P (l^*_{ij})^4 - \frac{\gamma}{P} \left( \sum_{i=1}^P (l^*_{ij})^2 \right)^2 \right]\)$
  • \(\gamma = 1.0\): Varimax (aligned with R stats::varimax). Maximizes loading variance within factors.
  • \(\gamma = 0.0\): Quartimax. Maximizes loading variance across rows.
  • \(\gamma = k/2\): Equamax. Balances row and column simplification.
  • \(\gamma = \frac{P(k-1)}{P+k-2}\): Parsimax. Penalizes complex factor assignments.

  • \(\gamma = \frac{k}{2P}\): Biquartimax.

  • Promax Rotation: Oblique rotation (\(T^T T \ne I\)) allowing correlated latent factors:

  • Compute orthogonal Varimax loadings \(L_{\text{varimax}}\).
  • Construct target simple-structure matrix \(B\) by element-wise exponentiation: $\(B = (L_{\text{varimax}})^{\circ m} \oslash |L_{\text{varimax}}|, \quad m = 4\)$
  • Solve Procrustes least-squares problem: \(T = (L^T L)^{-1} L^T B\), followed by column normalization.

items.title: 4. Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
items.text:
Approximates non-negative data \(X \ge 0\) as \(X \approx W H\) where \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}_{\ge 0}\) (basis) and \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times P}_{\ge 0}\) (encodings): $\(\min_{W \ge 0, \, H \ge 0} \frac{1}{2} \|X - WH\|_F^2 + \lambda_1 \|H\|_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|H\|_F^2\)$

mltreelib-core implements three distinct solver engines: - Multiplicative Updates (MU): $\(H \leftarrow H \odot \frac{W^T X}{W^T W H + \epsilon}, \qquad W \leftarrow W \odot \frac{X H^T}{W H H^T + \epsilon}\)$ - Alternating Least Squares (ALS): Solves Ridge normal equations for \(H\) and \(W\), projecting solutions onto non-negative orthant \(\max(0, \cdot)\). - Hierarchical Alternating Least Squares (HALS): Sequential exact single-coordinate Non-Negative Least Squares (NNLS) update: $\(H_{k, \cdot} \leftarrow \max\left(0, \, \frac{W_{\cdot, k}^T \left(X - \sum_{j \ne k} W_{\cdot, j} H_{j, \cdot}\right) - \lambda_1}{W_{\cdot, k}^T W_{\cdot, k} + \lambda_2}\right)\)$ Guarantees monotonic loss reduction with true \(L_1\) sparsity without numerical instability.

Next: step 3 applies the rotations, the whitening transforms and the NMF solvers from step 2 to the Wine Quality features.

items.title: 3. Empirical Benchmark on Real Data
items.text:
We evaluate the full component analysis suite on the Wine Quality dataset (1,000 samples, 12 continuous chemical features).

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ComponentModel, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_parquet(dataset_path("wine_quality")).sample(n=1000, random_state=2026)
ds = Dataset(
    df.to_dict("list"),
    target="median_wine_quality",
    exclude=["wine_color"],
)
X = ds.x

items.title: 1. PCA & R-Aligned Factor Rotations
items.text:
# Fit ComponentModel with Varimax and Promax rotations
comp_varimax = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=3, rotation="varimax")
comp_varimax.fit(X)

comp_promax = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=3, rotation="promax", promax_m=4.0)
comp_promax.fit(X)
Method Variance Retained Rotation Matrix Loading Sparsity NONE (Raw PCA) 60.68% No 25.0% VARIMAX 60.68% Yes (orthogonal) 27.8% QUARTIMAX 60.68% Yes (orthogonal) 25.0% EQUAMAX 60.68% Yes (orthogonal) 27.8% PARSIMAX 60.68% Yes (orthogonal) 25.0% BIQUARTIMAX 60.68% Yes (orthogonal) 27.8% PROMAX 60.68% Yes (oblique) 36.1%

Key Finding: Rotated factor loadings preserve 100% of subspace variance (60.68%) while concentrating variance into high-magnitude features, increasing loading sparsity from 25.0% to 36.1% under Promax.

items.title: 2. Covariance Whitening: ZCA vs. PCA
items.text:
comp_zca = ComponentModel(kind="whitening", whitening_kind="zca")
Z_zca = comp_zca.fit_transform(X)

comp_pca_white = ComponentModel(kind="whitening", whitening_kind="pca")
Z_pca_white = comp_pca_white.fit_transform(X)
Method Mean Covariance Error \(\|\text{Cov}(Z) - I\|_{\text{mean}}\) Key Property ZCA 0.006972 Minimizes \(\|Z - X\|_F\); keeps whitened features closest to raw inputs. PCA Whitening 0.006704 Aligns coordinates along principal variance axes.

items.title: 3. NMF Solver Face-Off
items.text:
# Compare NMF solvers on strictly non-negative chemical features
nmf_mu = ComponentModel(kind="nmf", n_components=3, solver="mu")
nmf_als = ComponentModel(kind="nmf", n_components=3, solver="als", l2_reg=0.01)
nmf_hals = ComponentModel(kind="nmf", n_components=3, solver="hals")
nmf_sparse = ComponentModel(kind="nmf", n_components=3, solver="hals", l1_reg=0.01, l2_reg=0.005)
Solver Reconstruction Error \(\|X - WH\|_F\) \(H\) Sparsity (% zeros) MU (Multiplicative Updates) 233.0816 0.0% ALS (\(L_1=0, L_2=0.01\)) 172.5155 0.0% HALS 142.3001 8.3% HALS (\(L_1=0.01, L_2=0.005\)) 256.4853 36.1% HALS (\(L_1=0.01, L_2=0.05\)) 256.4980 36.1%

Key Finding: HALS coordinate descent achieves superior loss convergence (142.30 vs. 233.08 for MU) and enables true \(L_1\) zero-coefficient sparsity (36.1%) without division-by-zero numerical collapse.

items.title: 4. Subspace Reconstruction Anomaly Detection
items.text:
Out-of-subspace anomalies project poorly onto low-rank basis components, producing large reconstruction residuals: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{anom}}(x) = \|x - \hat{x}\|_2^2 = \|x - W h(x)\|_2^2\)$

[!NOTE] API gap (not yet runnable): subspace reconstruction error as an anomaly score is not yet exposed on AnomalyModel (its kinds are eif, det, hst, rct, active, context) and ComponentModel does not yet expose inverse_transform. The block below illustrates the intended formula only; output values are illustrative. 

# Detect anomalies via subspace reconstruction error
detector = AnomalyModel(method="pca", n_components=3)
detector.fit(X)

inlier_loss = detector.score_samples([X[0]])[0]
outlier_point = list(X[0])
outlier_point[0] += 50.0  # Synthetic feature injection
outlier_loss = detector.score_samples([outlier_point])[0]

print(f"Normal Inlier Loss:  {inlier_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Outlier Spike Loss:  {outlier_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Separation Ratio:    {outlier_loss / inlier_loss:.1f}x")


Normal Inlier Point   -> Reconstruction Loss: 437.4652 | Label: NORMAL
Outlier Spike (+50.0) -> Reconstruction Loss: 1535844674.9892 | Label: ANOMALY
Ratio (Outlier/Inlier Loss): 3510781.2x separation

Next: the worked example is a separate, self-contained case: it generates a synthetic aptitude battery, not the wine data, to show why rotation makes loadings easier to read.

items.title: 4. Worked example: PCA rotations
items.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) decomposes high-dimensional feature spaces into orthogonal axes that maximize explained variance. However, raw principal component loadings are dense, unaligned with natural domain concepts, and hard to interpret.

mltreelib.ComponentModel provides a pure Rust implementation of factor and PCA rotations mirroring the classic R statistical foundations (stats::varimax, stats::promax, and the Orthomax family), resolving rotational indeterminacy to discover Thurstone's simple structure.

Run the educational example and benchmark suite directly:

uv run python examples/guides/pca_rotations_educational.py
uv run python benchmarks/suites/component_benchmarks.py

Executable Reference Scripts: - examples/guides/pca_rotations_educational.py — Cognitive aptitude battery case study, Thurstone's simple structure criteria, and loading matrix comparisons. - benchmarks/suites/component_benchmarks.py — Quantitative benchmark across PCA rotations, ZCA/PCA whitening, and NMF solvers (MU, ALS, HALS).

items.title: Why PCA Rotations Were Built (The Interpretability Problem)
items.text:
Standard PCA computes eigenvectors \(\mathbf{V} = [\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k]\) of the empirical covariance matrix \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\) corresponding to the largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_k\):

\[\max_{\mathbf{v}_j} \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{v}_j \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_j = 1, \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_l = 0 \; (l \ne j)\]

This mathematical criterion produces severe interpretability issues in real-world data:

  1. Dense Global Loadings: The first principal component (PC1) maximizes global variance. Consequently, almost all variables exhibit non-zero loadings of similar magnitude (the classic "general factor", such as general intelligence \(g\), general company size, or overall user activity).
  2. Artificial Bipolarity: Higher components (PC2, PC3, ...) are constrained to be globally orthogonal to PC1. This forces negative and positive loadings across unrelated features that are mathematical artifacts of orthogonality rather than genuine domain phenomena.
  3. Rotational Indeterminacy: The subspace spanned by \(k\) components is invariant under any invertible rotation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\): $\(\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}^T = (\mathbf{Z} \mathbf{T}) (\mathbf{V} \mathbf{T})^{-T} = \mathbf{Z}^* (\mathbf{V}^*)^T\)$ When \(\mathbf{T}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\)), the reconstructed subspace and the total variance explained remain 100% identical. The rotation simply chooses new coordinate axes within the same subspace to make the factor loadings human-interpretable.

items.title: Thurstone's Simple Structure Criteria (1947)
items.text:
In Multiple-Factor Analysis (1947), Louis Leon Thurstone formalized five criteria for an interpretable coordinate system:

  1. Each variable (row of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)) must have at least one loading close to zero.
  2. For each factor (column of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)), there should be at least \(k\) variables with near-zero loadings.
  3. For every pair of factors, several variables must load heavily on one factor and near zero on the other.
  4. For every pair of factors, a large fraction of variables must have near-zero loadings on both factors (when \(k \ge 4\)).
  5. Only a small fraction of variables should have high loadings on both factors.

PCA rotations mathematically maximize these criteria.

items.title: 1. Orthomax Family: Orthogonal Rotations (\(\gamma \in [0, 1]\))
items.text:
The Orthomax family defines a general criterion parameterized by \(\gamma\):

\[Q(\mathbf{\Lambda}) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^4 - \frac{\gamma}{p} \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^2 \right)^2 \right)\]

where \(\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{V}^* = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{T}\) is the rotated loading matrix, and \(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\). mltreelib solves this via Kaiser's (1958) planar Jacobi rotations until convergence (\(\Delta < 10^{-6}\)).

items.title: Supported Orthomax Variants:
items.text:
• Varimax (\(\gamma = 1.0\)): The gold standard in applied statistics and R's default (stats::varimax). Maximizes the variance of squared loadings within each column. Forces each factor to have either high or near-zero loadings on each variable.
  • Quartimax (\(\gamma = 0.0\)): Simplifies rows (variables) rather than columns (factors). Maximizes the kurtosis of squared loadings across variables.
  • Equamax (\(\gamma = k / 2\)): Balanced compromise between column simplicity (Varimax) and row simplicity (Quartimax).
  • Parsimax (\(\gamma = \frac{p (k - 1)}{p + k - 2}\)): Weight adjusted for the variable-to-factor ratio, maximizing overall factor parsimony.
  • Biquartimax (\(\gamma = 0.5\)): Fixed equal weighting between row and column simplicity criteria.
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ComponentModel

# 1. Generate correlated multi-test aptitude battery
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_students = 500

# Latent ability factors: Verbal (v) and Quantitative/Spatial (m)
v = rng.normal(0, 1, n_students)
m = 0.45 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.89, n_students)  # Correlated latent abilities

# Observed test battery scores with noise
read = 0.85 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
vocab = 0.80 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
gram = 0.75 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
geom = 0.85 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
arith = 0.80 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
algeb = 0.88 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_students)

X = np.column_stack([read, vocab, gram, geom, arith, algeb])
feature_names = ["Reading", "Vocab", "Grammar", "Geometry", "Arithmetic", "Algebra"]

# 2. Fit ComponentModel with Varimax orthogonal rotation
pca_vari = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="varimax")
pca_vari.fit(X)

# 3. Transform to factor scores and inspect rotated loadings
Z_scores = pca_vari.transform(X)
loadings = np.array(pca_vari.components_)

print("Varimax Rotated Factor Loadings (Simple Structure):")
print(f"{'Test':12} | {'Factor 1 (Verbal)':18} | {'Factor 2 (Math)':18}")
print("-" * 54)
for name, row in zip(feature_names, loadings):
    print(f"{name:12} | {row[0]:+18.3f} | {row[1]:+18.3f}")

Varimax Rotated Factor Loadings (Simple Structure):
Test         | Factor 1 (Verbal)  | Factor 2 (Math)   
------------------------------------------------------
Reading      |             +0.172 |             +0.170
Vocab        |             +0.571 |             +0.563

items.title: 2. Promax Rotation: Oblique Simple Structure (Hendrickson & White, 1964)
items.text:
Real-world latent dimensions often correlate (for example, verbal aptitude correlates with mathematical aptitude). Forcing factor axes to remain strictly perpendicular (\(90^\circ\), orthogonal) introduces artificial distortion and cross-loadings.

Promax relaxes orthogonality through an efficient oblique Procrustes solve:

  1. Compute the orthogonal Varimax rotated loadings \(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}\).
  2. Construct a non-linear target matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) by raising loadings to a power \(m\) (default \(m = 4\)): $\(H_{ij} = \text{sgn}(\lambda_{ij}) |\lambda_{ij}|^m\)$ Because small loadings shrink dramatically (\(0.2^4 = 0.0016\)) while large loadings stay substantial (\(0.8^4 = 0.4096\)), \(\mathbf{H}\) acts as an idealized simple structure template.
  3. Solve the unconstrained Procrustes least-squares rotation towards \(\mathbf{H}\): $\(\mathbf{L} = (\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}})^{-1} \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{H}\)$
  4. Normalize the columns of \(\mathbf{L}\) to unit length, yielding the oblique transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\).
  5. Calculate the factor correlation matrix: $\(\mathbf{\Phi} = (\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T})^{-1}\)$
# Fit PCA with Promax oblique rotation (power m=4.0)
pca_promax = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="promax", promax_m=4.0)
pca_promax.fit(X)

# Loadings and inter-factor correlation
loadings = pca_promax.components_
phi = pca_promax.factor_correlations_

items.title: 3. Cognitive Aptitude Battery Case Study
items.text: To illustrate how rotation transforms uninterpretable mathematical eigenvectors into distinct psychological concepts, consider an 8-variable cognitive aptitude battery (1,200 individuals): - Verbal Tests: ReadingComp, Vocabulary, GrammarUsage - Quantitative & Spatial Tests: GeometryProof, ArithmeticSpeed, Algebra, BlockDesign, ObjectAssembly

items.title: Interpretation of Results:
items.text:
1. Raw PCA: PC1 places roughly equal weight (\(0.33 - 0.38\)) on all 8 tests. It represents a general factor ("g"), but cannot distinguish verbal aptitude from spatial reasoning. PC2 contrasts verbal against spatial purely to satisfy mathematical orthogonality.
  2. Varimax: Rotates axes to maximize column variance. Factor 1 isolates Verbal Ability (0.84 to 0.89 on verbal tests, \(< 0.12\) on math/spatial). Factor 2 isolates Quantitative/Spatial Ability (0.75 to 0.88 on math/spatial, \(< 0.10\) on verbal). Sparsity improves from 0.0% to 50.0%.
  3. Promax: Discovers the true oblique structure and reveals that Verbal and Quantitative/Spatial abilities share an empirical correlation of \(\rho = 0.428\), consistent with psychometric literature.

items.title: 4. Decision Guide: Which Rotation When?
items.text: Method Type Property Best Use Case R Equivalent Raw PCA (None) Orthogonal Max variance along decreasing eigenvalues Dimension reduction, compression, pre-whitening stats::prcomp "varimax" Orthogonal Maximizes squared column loading variance General exploratory factor analysis, independent features stats::varimax "quartimax" Orthogonal Maximizes row kurtosis (simplifies variables) Eliminating cross-loadings for dominant variables psych::quartimax "equamax" Orthogonal Balanced column and row criteria (\(k/2\)) Moderately correlated batteries with moderate factor count psych::equamax "parsimax" Orthogonal Adjusted for variable-to-factor ratio High-dimensional data with small target factor count psych::parsimax "promax" Oblique Procrustes target power (\(m=4\)) rotation Natural domains where latent constructs correlate stats::promax

items.title: Configuration Parameters
items.text:
ComponentModel(
    kind="pca",               # "pca", "svd", "whitening", "ica", "nmf", "fa"
    n_components=2,           # Subspace rank
    rotation="varimax",       # "none", "varimax", "quartimax", "equamax", "parsimax", "biquartimax", "promax"
    promax_m=4.0,             # Promax target exponent (default 4.0)
    max_iter=200,             # Max iterations for iterative algorithms
    tol=1e-4,                 # Convergence tolerance for iterative algorithms
    seed=42,                  # Random seed
)

items.title: Fitted Attributes
items.text:
• components_: Rotated factor loadings \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) (shape \(p \times k\)).
  • rotation_matrix_: Transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) (shape \(k \times k\)).
  • factor_correlations_: Inter-factor correlation matrix \(\mathbf{\Phi}\) (shape \(k \times k\), identity for orthogonal rotations).
  • explained_variance_ratio_: Realized variance share per factor.
  • report(): Unified ModelReport containing condition number, reconstruction error, and sparsity statistics.

items.title: Operational Limitations & Failure Modes
items.text:
1. Strict Non-Negativity Violation in NMF: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization requires \(X_{i, j} \ge 0\) for all entries. Supplying standardized, centered, or negative covariates causes immediate mathematical domain errors. Shift or scale features to the interval \([0, 1]\) before fitting NMF.
  2. Non-Convexity & Local Minima: The NMF objective \(\min_{W, H \ge 0} \|X - WH\|_F^2\) is non-convex in \((W, H)\) jointly. Convergence to a global minimum is not guaranteed. mltreelib-core uses deterministic SVD/NNDSVD initialization to ensure reproducible, high-quality basis convergence.
  3. Rotational Indeterminacy Under Degenerate Eigenvalues: When principal components share identical singular values (\(\sigma_i \approx \sigma_j\)), orthogonal and oblique factor rotations encounter spherical indeterminacy, causing convergence oscillation in iterative Orthomax sweeps.
  4. Whitening High-Frequency Noise Amplification: Covariance whitening inverses singular values (\(\Sigma^{-1}\)). For ill-conditioned datasets with near-zero trailing eigenvalues, unregularized PCA and ZCA whitening amplify numerical noise. Always apply a regularization floor \(\epsilon > 0\) when singular values approach machine precision.

items.title: References
items.text:
• Kaiser, H. F. (1958). "The varimax criterion for analytic rotation in factor analysis." Psychometrika, 23(3), 187-200.
  • Hendrickson, A. E., & White, P. O. (1964). "PROMAX: A quick method for rotation to oblique simple structure." British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 17(1), 65-70.
  • Cichocki, A., & Phan, A. H. (2009). "Fast local algorithms for large scale nonnegative matrix and tensor factorizations." IEICE Transactions on Fundamentals of Electronics, Communications and Computer Sciences, 92(3), 708-721.
  • Bell, A. J., & Sejnowski, T. J. (1995). "An information-maximization approach to blind separation and blind deconvolution." Neural Computation, 7(6), 1129-1159.

items.title: Structural Constraints & Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
This guide details domain-informed structural constraints—dual monotonicity and variable interaction group isolation—coupled with Generalized Random Forest (GRF)-style honest sample-split estimation.

Script: benchmarks/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py (uv run python benchmarks/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Regulatory Rationale
items.text:
Unconstrained tree algorithms greedily optimize in-sample loss functions. This frequently violates foundational physical, economic, or regulatory laws:

  1. Monotonicity Violations: In insurance underwriting and credit scoring, physical or actuarial reality dictates that medical expenses strictly increase with age, and credit default risk strictly increases with debt-to-income. An unconstrained decision tree can create spurious dips where a 45-year-old is predicted to have lower healthcare costs than a 44-year-old due to local sampling noise.
  2. Uncontrolled Interaction Leakage: Regulatory compliance (such as FCRA and ECOA) often prohibits model decision paths from interacting sensitive attributes with commercial covariates.
  3. Estimation Bias & Overfitting (Data Snooping): When the exact same sample observations are used to both choose split points and calculate leaf estimates, the resulting leaf parameter estimates are systematically biased away from the true population parameters.

mltreelib addresses these requirements through native Rust-level structural constraints and sample-split honesty: - Dual Monotonicity: Enforces directional ordering across tree splits (\((\bar{y}_R - \bar{y}_L) \cdot m_j \ge 0\)) and directional sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\)). - Interaction Groups: Guarantees that no root-to-leaf path mixes features across forbidden variable groups. - Honest Sample Splitting: Partitions the training data into two disjoint subsamples: a structure sample (\(S^{\text{tr}}\)) used exclusively to evaluate split criteria, and an estimation sample (\(S^{\text{est}}\)) used exclusively to fit terminal leaf models.

flowchart LR

        Raw["Training Sample (X, y)"] --> Split{"Bernoulli Subsample\n(honesty_fraction=0.5)"}

Next: section 2 states each mechanism as a formula (split and leaf monotonicity, interaction groups, honest splitting), and each one addresses a risk listed in section 1.

items.title: A. Split-Level Monotonicity (tree_monotone)
items.text:
For a feature \(j\) with assigned monotone direction \(m_j \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\): - \(m_j = +1\) (Strictly non-decreasing): Any split on feature \(j\) must satisfy \(\bar{y}_R \ge \bar{y}_L\). - \(m_j = -1\) (Strictly non-increasing): Any split on feature \(j\) must satisfy \(\bar{y}_R \le \bar{y}_L\). - \(m_j = 0\) (Unconstrained): Normal split evaluation.

Candidate splits violating the directional inequality \(m_j \cdot (\bar{y}_R - \bar{y}_L) \ge 0\) are assigned \(-\infty\) gain and discarded immediately in pure Rust.

items.title: B. Leaf Slope Monotonicity (leaf_monotone)
items.text:
When fitting linear model leaves \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\beta}\), local slopes must respect global physical signs:

\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \beta_0 - \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta})^2 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad m_j \cdot \beta_j \ge 0 \quad \forall j\]

The Rust core solves this quadratic program via projected coordinate descent, truncating violations to the boundary \(\beta_j = 0\).

items.title: C. Interaction Group Isolation (interaction_groups)
items.text:
Let the total feature set \(\mathcal{F}\) be partitioned into \(K\) mutually exclusive governance groups \(\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_2, \dots, \mathcal{G}_K\).

For any root-to-leaf decision route \(\mathcal{P} = \{f_1, f_2, \dots, f_d\}\), features along the path must belong to at most one interaction silo:

\[\forall f_a, f_b \in \mathcal{P}, \quad \exists k \text{ such that } f_a, f_b \in \mathcal{G}_k\]

If a split path has already branched on a feature in \(\mathcal{G}_1\), all features in \(\mathcal{G}_2, \dots, \mathcal{G}_K\) are masked out from subsequent split evaluations.

items.title: D. Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
Standard decision trees use full training sample \(\mathcal{D}\) for both tree discovery \(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{D})\) and leaf estimation \(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{D})\). This induces adaptive selection bias:

\[\mathbb{E}\left[ \hat{\theta}_{\text{leaf}}(\mathcal{D}) - \theta^* \mid X \in \text{leaf} \right] \neq 0\]

Under honest estimation, \(\mathcal{D}\) is partitioned into disjoint sets \(S^{\text{tr}}\) and \(S^{\text{est}}\): 1. \(\mathcal{T} = \text{TreeBuild}(S^{\text{tr}})\) optimizes split criteria purely on \(S^{\text{tr}}\). 2. Observations from \(S^{\text{est}}\) are routed down the frozen topology \(\mathcal{T}\) to compute parameter estimates:

\[\hat{\theta}_{\text{leaf}} = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{i \in S^{\text{est}} \cap \text{leaf}} \mathcal{L}(y_i, f(x_i; \theta))\]

Honest estimates are asymptotically unbiased, Gaussian, and provide valid coverage intervals.

Next: section 3 runs the healthcare insurance data through an unconstrained baseline and three trees that each use one of these mechanisms, then compares their test RMSE.

items.title: 3. Benchmark Study: Healthcare Insurance Expenses
items.text:
We evaluate on the standard actuarial dataset: Healthcare Insurance Expenses (1,338 policyholders, continuous medical charges).

from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

# 1. Load domain benchmark dataset
features = ["age", "bmi", "children"]
ds = Dataset.load(
    "healthcare_insurance_expenses", target="charges", features=features
)

# 80/20 split with no shuffling: first 80% of rows train, last 20% test
train, test = ds.split(test_size=0.2, time=True)

# 2. Fit unconstrained baseline
tree_uncon = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=20, leaf="mean")
tree_uncon.fit(train)

# 3. Fit monotone-constrained tree (+1 on age: charges must not decrease with age)
tree_mono = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    leaf="mean",
    tree_monotone=[1, 0, 0],
)
tree_mono.fit(train)

# 4. Fit interaction-constrained tree (isolate 'children' from ['age', 'bmi'])
tree_inter = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    interaction_groups=[["age", "bmi"], ["children"]],
)
tree_inter.fit(train)

# 5. Fit honest sample-split tree (50% structure, 50% estimation)
tree_honest = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    honesty=True,
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=42,
)
tree_honest.fit(train)

for name, fitted in [("unconstrained", tree_uncon), ("monotone (age)", tree_mono),
                     ("interaction groups", tree_inter), ("honest", tree_honest)]:
    rmse = MetricsReport("regression", y_true=test.y, y_pred=fitted.predict(test))["rmse"]
    print(f"{name:18s} test RMSE = {rmse:.2f}")

unconstrained      test RMSE = 11867.81
monotone (age)     test RMSE = 11867.81
interaction groups test RMSE = 11934.83
honest             test RMSE = 11864.07

Next: section 4 reads the printed RMSE values from that run and states what they do and do not show.

items.title: 4. Empirical Benchmark Output & Quantitative Findings
items.text:
The block in section 3 fits the four trees on the first 80% of the rows (1,070) and prints test RMSE on the last 20% (268). The output is the only source for the numbers on this page:

The image was drawn from an earlier run and is not regenerated by the block above, so it may not match these numbers.

Reading the printed results:

  • The printed RMSE values show the cost or benefit of each constraint on this split. A constraint can raise error, and it can leave it unchanged.
  • Monotonicity, interaction isolation and honesty are properties of how the trees are built. The block does not print checks for them. Verify each property on your own data before relying on it.
  • Honest splitting uses half the training rows to choose structure and the other half to estimate leaves, so it gives up some data for leaf estimates.

items.title: Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Monotone Infeasibility under Strong Feature Correlation: When two highly correlated features possess opposing empirical trends, enforcing strict monotonicity on one feature can force the tree to pick suboptimal split thresholds on the other, increasing training error.
  2. Honesty Sample-Size Sensitivity: On small sample sets (\(N < 500\)), splitting observations between \(S^{\text{tr}}\) and \(S^{\text{est}}\) halves effective node sample sizes, increasing leaf coefficient variance. Honesty is recommended for \(N \ge 1,000\).
  3. Clique Interaction Overhead: Enforcing fine-grained interaction groups restricts the tree's search space. If forbidden interactions reflect genuine synergistic non-linearities, predictive accuracy drops.

items.title: Core Tree Architecture, Two-Control Decoupling & Growth Knobs
items.text:
This benchmark unifies the architectural mechanics of mltreelib: decoupling between greedy tree topology growth and terminal leaf models, 0D distributional profiles across partitioned leaves, and hypothesis-driven structural break gating via the Chow test.

Companion executable script: - benchmarks/suites/core_tree_architecture.py (uv run python benchmarks/suites/core_tree_architecture.py)

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Mathematical Formulation
items.text:
Classical decision tree libraries (such as scikit-learn or rpart) couple recursive partitioning directly to scalar leaf statistics (mean, median, or class frequency). This introduces two severe structural limitations:

  1. Parameter Explosion and Inflexible Solvers: Fitting linear models at every candidate split threshold across all features scales as \(O(K \cdot N \cdot P^2)\), creating an unacceptable computational bottleneck.
  2. The Step-Function Distortion: Constant-leaf trees partition continuous functional relationships into rigid step functions, requiring excessive depth to approximate simple linear gradients.

mltreelib decouples global topology search from local terminal leaf parameter optimization:

\[\min_{\mathcal{T}, \, \{\theta_m\}_{m=1}^M} \sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{i \in R_m} \ell(y_i, f(x_i; \theta_m)) + \alpha \cdot |\mathcal{T}| + \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{R}(\theta_m)\]

where: - \(\mathcal{T} = \{R_1, \dots, R_M\}\) denotes the orthogonal partition of the feature space into \(M\) disjoint terminal regions. - \(\alpha \cdot |\mathcal{T}|\) governs tree complexity regularization (cost-complexity pruning). - \(\theta_m\) represents the local parameter vector (e.g. Ridge regression slopes \(\beta_m\), Huber parameters, or GLM coefficients) fitted inside leaf \(m\). - \(\mathcal{R}(\theta_m) = \lambda_1 \|\theta_m\|_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\theta_m\|_2^2\) enforces local regularization.

Next: section 2 applies this decoupling to real data, setting LeafControl apart from the tree's max_depth and min_rows.

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength
items.text:
We evaluate the architecture on the standard civil engineering benchmark: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength (1,030 industrial concrete mixtures, 8 continuous ingredients; 80% train / 20% test).

from mltreelib import LeafControl, MetricsReport, ModelTree
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

# 1. Load benchmark dataset and split 80/20 without shuffling
ds = Dataset.load(
    "concrete_compressive_strength", target="ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
)
train, test = ds.split(test_size=0.2, time=True)

# 2. Configure LeafControl independently of tree topology
leaf_ctrl = LeafControl(
    leaf="linear",
    l1=0.0,
    l2=1e-3,
    leaf_family="gaussian",
)

# 3. Configure ModelTree and inject leaf controls
model = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    prune="none",
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
model.fit(train)

# 4. Measure holdout performance
preds = model.predict(test)
rep = MetricsReport("regression", y_true=test.y, y_pred=preds)
print(f"ModelTree Linear Leaves: RMSE = {rep['rmse']:.2f} MPa, R2 = {rep['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {rep['mae']:.2f} MPa")

ModelTree Linear Leaves: RMSE = 7.28 MPa, R2 = 0.813, MAE = 5.07 MPa

items.text:
1. Immediate Accuracy Lift at Depth 1: A 1-split stump with linear leaves achieves 7.63 MPa RMSE, against 10.16 MPa for a depth-4 CART tree and 15.24 MPa for a depth-1 CART stump.
  2. Variance Reduction: At depth 3, ModelTree achieves 7.28 MPa RMSE and \(R^2 = 0.813\), capturing 81.3% of the variance compared to CART's 56.6%.
  3. Parity Alignment: In Panel 4, ModelTree predictions cluster symmetrically along the 1:1 diagonal without the horizontal striations characteristic of step-function leaves.

Next: section 4 inspects the leaves of the depth-3 model fitted in section 2, because each leaf profile describes one terminal partition of that tree.

items.title: 4. 0D Descriptive Leaf Statistics
items.text:
Every terminal leaf in ModelTree computes a comprehensive 0D statistical profile over its assigned partition samples without extra passes. Access these profiles directly via leaf["stats"] or tree.leaf_stats():

leaves = model.leaves()
for idx, leaf in enumerate(leaves[:2]):
    stats = leaf["stats"]
    print(f"Leaf {idx} (support n={leaf['n']}):")
    print(f"  Center : mean={stats['mean']:.2f}, median={stats['median']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Spread : variance={stats['var']:.2f}, MAD={stats['mad']:.2f}, IQR={stats['iqr']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Shape  : skewness={stats['skew']:.2f}, kurtosis={stats['kurtosis']:.2f}")

Leaf 0 (support n=143):
  Center : mean=15.44, median=14.37
  Spread : variance=45.41, MAD=4.15, IQR=8.96
  Shape  : skewness=1.10, kurtosis=1.79
Leaf 1 (support n=47):
  Center : mean=27.67, median=25.69
  Spread : variance=48.11, MAD=4.43, IQR=10.67
  Shape  : skewness=0.41, kurtosis=-0.51

You can predict these 0D moments row-wise at test time using predict(X, kind="median"|"var"|"stats").

Next: section 5 adds a Chow test gate that decides whether a split is kept, using the same leaf_ctrl and training data from section 2.

items.title: 5. Chow Structural Break Test Hypothesis Gating
items.text: Standard trees rely purely on empirical gain thresholds (min_gain) or post-pruning to prevent overfitting. ModelTree implements the econometric Chow structural break test (split_test="chow") as a statistical significance gate.

items.title: Hypothesis Test Formulation
items.text:
• Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): Regression coefficients are invariant across child partitions: $\(\beta_L = \beta_R = \beta_P\)$
  • Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): Significant parameter instability exists across the candidate split: $\(\beta_L \ne \beta_R\)$

The test statistic follows an exact Snedecor's \(F\)-distribution under \(H_0\): $\(F_{\text{Chow}} = \frac{(\text{RSS}_P - (\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R)) / k}{(\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R) / (N - 2k)} \sim F(k, \, N - 2k)\)$ where \(k = P + 1\) is the number of estimated parameters (features plus intercept).

If the \(p\)-value exceeds split_alpha (e.g. \(\alpha = 0.01\)), the null hypothesis of structural stability is retained, and subtree branching is automatically terminated:

tree_chow = ModelTree(
    max_depth=5,
    min_rows=25,
    split_test="chow",
    split_alpha=0.01,
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
tree_chow.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

This prevents the tree from creating spurious subtrees where local regressions show no statistically significant parameter shift.

items.title: Operational Limitations & Failure Modes
items.text:
1. High-Dimensional Parameter Degeneracy (\(P > N_{\text{leaf}}\)): Fitting multivariate linear leaves requires sufficient sample support per terminal node. If \(N_{\text{leaf}} \le P + 1\), unregularized least-squares matrices become singular. Set l2 > 0 (e.g. l2=0.01) or enforce min_rows >= 2 * (P + 1) in ModelTree.
  2. Chow Test Sample Size Floors: The denominator degrees of freedom in the Chow test is \(N - 2k\). If a partition contains fewer than \(2k\) samples, the \(F\)-statistic is undefined. mltreelib-core automatically suppresses splits with insufficient degrees of freedom.
  3. Boundary Discontinuity: While linear leaves provide continuous predictions within each partitioned hyper-rectangle, predictions across split boundaries are discontinuous step transitions. For smooth global transitions across boundaries, combine with hierarchical retrain or ensemble bagging.

items.title: Data Matrix Ingestion, Missing Routing & Categorical Encoders
items.text:
Machine learning algorithms live or die on how they handle dirty tabular real-world inputs: high-cardinality categoricals, mixed numeric types, and widespread unrecorded values.

mltreelib builds its data ingest and split evaluation on a zero-copy Rust columnar engine (mltreelib-core::frame) that treats missingness as a first-class branch direction rather than a flaw to be masked with heuristic imputations.

    C -- "No" --> E["Zero-Copy Column Slices"]

    B --> F{"Categorical Features?"}
    F -- "Low-Cardinality" --> G["Native Integer Indexing\nBitset Subset Partitions"]
    F -- "High-Cardinality" --> H["Empirical Bayes Target Encoding\nShrinkage toward Global Prior"]

items.title: 1. Native Missing Value Routing (Surrogate Splits)
items.text:
Standard decision trees force users to impute missing entries (mean, median, mode) or drop rows entirely. Mean imputation distorts correlation structures and destroys predictive signal in missingness itself.

mltreelib.ModelTree handles missing values natively during tree growth: 1. Learned Missing Direction (missing_left on each split): Evaluates whether routing missing rows to the left child or the right child minimizes post-split deviance, picking the optimal direction. Reported per split by tree.splits(). 2. Surrogate Splits (maxsurrogate=N): When a primary split feature is missing at prediction time, the tree evaluates an ordered ranking of backup surrogate features that best mimic the primary split partition.

items.title: Complete End-to-End Missing Routing Example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ModelTree, Metrics

# 1. Generate multi-sensor telemetry with correlated features and sensor dropouts
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_samples = 1500

# Primary sensor reading and redundant backup sensor
primary = rng.normal(loc=50.0, scale=10.0, size=n_samples)
backup = 0.85 * primary + rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=3.0, size=n_samples)
temperature = rng.uniform(low=20.0, high=90.0, size=n_samples)

# Physical failure response depending strongly on primary sensor threshold (> 58.0)
y = ((primary > 58.0) & (temperature > 50.0)).astype(float) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, n_samples)

# Inject 30% realistic sensor dropouts (represented by None / NaN)
primary_with_missing = [None if rng.uniform() < 0.30 else round(val, 2) for val in primary]
backup_clean = [round(val, 2) for val in backup]
temp_clean = [round(val, 2) for val in temperature]

X = [[p, b, t] for p, b, t in zip(primary_with_missing, backup_clean, temp_clean)]
feature_names = ["sensor_primary", "sensor_backup", "temperature"]

# 2. Train ModelTree with native learned missing routing
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    maxsurrogate=2,  # Backup splits for rows whose primary feature is missing
)
tree.fit(X, y.tolist(), col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Inspect splits and assigned missing directions
print("Fitted Tree Splits & Native Missing Direction:")
for i, s in enumerate(tree.splits()[:3], 1):
    direction = "LEFT" if s.get("missing_left", True) else "RIGHT"
    print(f"  Split #{i}: Feature '{s['col']}' <= {s['threshold']:.2f} | Missing Rows Route -> {direction}")

# 4. Predict on new record with missing primary sensor
test_sample = [[None, 62.5, 75.0]]
predicted_risk = tree.predict(test_sample)[0]
print(f"\nPrediction for Missing Primary Reading (Backup=62.5, Temp=75.0): {predicted_risk:.3f}")

Fitted Tree Splits & Native Missing Direction:
  Split #1: Feature 'temperature' <= 49.77 | Missing Rows Route -> LEFT
  Split #2: Feature 'sensor_primary' <= 57.93 | Missing Rows Route -> LEFT
  Split #3: Feature 'temperature' <= 49.97 | Missing Rows Route -> LEFT

Prediction for Missing Primary Reading (Backup=62.5, Temp=75.0): 0.885

Next: encode the categorical features, because the ingest diagram sends high-cardinality categories through an encoder before they reach the split engine.

items.title: 2. Categorical Encoders: Empirical Bayes & Ordered Target Encoding
items.text:
Tabular data features categorical variables ranging from low-cardinality ordinal levels (e.g. Education: High School, Bachelor, Graduate) to high-cardinality entities (ZIP codes, merchant IDs, product SKUs).

Method Flavour Mechanism Overfitting Guard TargetEncoder Smoothed Mean \(w \cdot \bar{y}_c + (1 - w) \cdot \bar{y}_\text{global}, \quad w = \frac{n_c}{n_c + m}\) Empirical Bayes \(m\)-smoothing toward global prior CatBoostEncoder Ordered Target Running target mean accumulated over random permutations Dynamic permutation eliminates in-sample leakage OneHotEncoder Sparse Dummies Boolean bitsets for low-cardinality variables (\(K \le 16\)) Tree branch regularization 
from mltreelib import TargetEncoder, CatBoostEncoder

# High-cardinality merchant categories and chargeback labels
merchants = ["electronics", "apparel", "electronics", "travel", "apparel", "electronics"]
labels = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

# 1. Smoothed Empirical Bayes Target Encoding
target_enc = TargetEncoder(smoothing=5.0)
target_enc.fit(merchants, labels)
encoded_features = target_enc.transform(merchants)
print("Smoothed Target Encodings:", [round(v, 3) for v in encoded_features])

# 2. Ordered Target Encoding (Leakage-Free Training)
cb_enc = CatBoostEncoder(prior=0.5, permutations=4, seed=2026)  # prior multiplies the global mean; keep it <= 1 for a 0/1 target
ordered_features = cb_enc.fit_transform(merchants, labels)
print("Ordered CatBoost Encodings:", [round(v, 3) for v in ordered_features])

Smoothed Target Encodings: [0.792, 0.619, 0.792, 0.556, 0.619, 0.792]
Ordered CatBoost Encodings: [0.528, 0.583, 0.639, 0.333, 0.292, 0.611]

Next: summarize each column's type, missing count and spread, because the engine checks these same properties before tree growth and isolates constant features.

items.title: 3. The Typed Ingestion Frame & Variance Decomposition
items.text:
At the Rust core level, datasets are ingested into a typed frame. The engine automatically tracks column data types, computes realized variance shares, and isolates zero-variance or constant features before tree growth.

from mltreelib import summarize

columns = {
    "cement": [540.0, 540.0, 332.5],
    "water": [162.0, 162.0, 228.0],
    "age": [28, 28, 270],
}

for name, values in columns.items():
    s = summarize(values)
    print(f"{name:10} | missing: {s['n_missing']} | mean: {s['mean']:.2f} | std: {s['std']:.2f}")

cement     | missing: 0 | mean: 470.83 | std: 97.82
water      | missing: 0 | mean: 184.00 | std: 31.11

items.title: Distributional & Censored Leaf Families
items.text:
Standard regression trees assume homoscedastic Gaussian errors: \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with identity link. This assumption breaks down on insurance claims (multiplicative skew), defect arrivals (discrete non-negative counts), credit defaults (latent utility thresholds), and corner-solution labor data (censoring at zero).

mltreelib implements native Rust-level Generalized Linear Model (GLM) and maximum likelihood leaves: Probit, Gamma, Poisson, Tweedie, and Tobit (Censored Normal).

Script: benchmarks/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py (uv run python benchmarks/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py).

items.title: 1. Mathematical Formulation of Distributional Families

    Support -- "Non-Negative Discrete Counts [0, 1, 2, ...]" --> Poisson["Poisson Leaf\ng(mu) = log(mu)\nNo Negative Predictions"]
