Next: step 5 scores the fitted trees on the test rows with discrimination and calibration metrics, using the CIF and survival predictions that step 4 returns.

items.title: 5. Model Evaluation with Modern Calibration Metrics
items.text:
Evaluate models with classical IPCW concordance and frontier calibration metrics:

from mltreelib import (
    MetricsReport,
    d_calibration,
    integrated_calibration_index,
    one_calibration,
    competing_risks_calibration,
)

# 1. Classical Discrimination & Calibration
cif_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=1)
cif_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=2)
risk_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=1)
risk_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=2)

cr_summary = MetricsReport(
    "competing_risks",
    durations=dur_test,
    events=ev_test,
    cif_curves={1: cif_all_c1, 2: cif_all_c2},
    risk_scores={1: risk_all_c1, 2: risk_all_c2},
    times=time_horizons,
)

print(f"Cause 1 Harrell C:  {cr_summary['cause_1_c_index']:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 Uno IPCW C: {cr_summary['cause_1_uno_c']:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 IBS:        {cr_summary['cause_1_ibs']:.4f}")
print(cr_summary)

# 2. D-Calibration (Haider et al. 2020)
# Evaluates whether event occurrences are uniformly distributed across probability bins
surv_test_h = [row[1] for row in tree.predict(X_test, kind="survival", times=time_horizons)] # at t=2.0 yr
d_rep = d_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, n_bins=10)
print(f"D-Calibration: Chi2 = {d_rep['chi2_stat']:.3f}, p-value = {d_rep['p_value']:.4f}, Calibrated = {d_rep['is_calibrated']}")

# 3. Integrated Calibration Index (ICI) (Austin et al. 2020)
# IPCW-weighted mean absolute calibration error at horizon t_0
ici_rep = integrated_calibration_index(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"ICI: {ici_rep['ici']:.4f}, E50: {ici_rep['e50']:.4f}, E90: {ici_rep['e90']:.4f}, Emax: {ici_rep['emax']:.4f}")

# 4. 1-Calibration Slope & Intercept
one_rep = one_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"1-Calibration: Intercept = {one_rep['intercept']:.3f}, Slope = {one_rep['slope']:.3f}")

# 5. Competing Risks Multi-Cause Calibration (Alberge et al. 2026)
cr_rep = competing_risks_calibration(
    dur_test,
    ev_test,
    {1: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c1], 2: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c2]},

)

items.title: Assumptions & Limitations
items.text:
1. Conditionally Independent Censoring: \(T_i^* \perp C_i \mid X_i\). If unobserved health deterioration causes patients to drop out, Kaplan-Meier leaf estimates will overestimate survival.
  2. Competing Risks vs. Censoring: Do not treat competing events (e.g., organ transplant, accidental death) as right-censoring. Doing so overestimates the cumulative incidence of the primary event. Use gain="gray" and kind="cif".
  3. Cumulative Hazard vs. Instantaneous Hazard Rate: predict(kind="hazard") computes \(\hat{\Lambda}(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(u) du\) (dimensionless accumulated expected event count). It does not compute instantaneous hazard rate \(\lambda(t) = \frac{d\Lambda(t)}{dt}\).
  4. Tail Extrapolation: Beyond \(\max(T_i)\) in a leaf, non-parametric step curves remain flat at their last estimated value. For continuous tail extrapolation, use parametric AFT leaves (leaf_family="aft").

items.title: Research Foundations & Benchmark Reproductions
items.text:
The implementation reproduces eleven key findings from classical (1988–2014) and frontier (2020–2026) survival analysis literature:

Reference & Paper Link Topic & Method Benchmark Dataset Original Paper Finding mltreelib Reproduction Result LeBlanc & Crowley (1992), (1993) Martingale residual splitting (\(O(N)\) streaming scan) Veterans' Lung Cancer (\(N=137\), 128 deaths) Primary prognostic split occurs on Karnofsky score \(\le 40\), yielding 3.1x mortality hazard jump. ModelTree(gain="martingale", max_depth=2) isolates primary cut at karno <= 40. Yields median survival of 30 days vs 111 days. items.title: Time Series Feature Engineering & Additive Forecasting
items.text:
In enterprise demand planning and energy load forecasting, models face secular growth trends, intra-week cycles, and calendar shocks.

Standard flat decision trees fail out-of-sample on trending series because constant-leaf partitions cannot extrapolate beyond the maximum target value seen during training.

mltreelib implements a zero-allocation, pure Rust feature engineering engine—providing ISO calendar extraction, entity-grouped calendar day lags, windowed rolling statistics, and additive trend decomposition—coupled with piecewise-linear model trees that extrapolate trends out-of-time.

Script: benchmarks/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py (uv run python benchmarks/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py).

items.title: Why Flat Trees Fail on Time Series:
items.text:
1. The Step-Function Ceiling: Standard regression trees predict leaf sample means \(\bar{y}_{\text{leaf}}\). In a growing business where future sales exceed historical peaks, a constant-leaf tree predicts the historical maximum for all future dates.
  2. Calendar Offset Misalignment: Naive array row shifts (df['sales'].shift(7)) fail when store closures or holiday gaps omit records. Real forecasting requires shifting by elapsed wall-clock calendar days (\(t - 7 \text{ days}\)) grouped by entity.
  3. Imputation Distortion: Shifting introduces unobserved initial histories (None). Forcing median imputation erases autoregressive relationships.

Next: define the calendar-aware lag, decomposition and trend transforms, because each answers a failure listed above: shifts by calendar day, missing lags kept as None, and a trend term that lets leaves extrapolate.

items.title: 2. Mathematical Formulation of Pure Rust Transforms
A. Entity-Grouped Calendar Day Lags (lag_by_days)
items.text:
Given entity keys \(\mathbf{k}\), date timestamps \(\mathbf{t}\), and values \(\mathbf{y}\), the Rust engine computes:

\[L_k(t, \Delta d) = y(t') \quad \text{where } t' = t - \Delta d \text{ days, with } \text{entity}(t') = \text{entity}(t)\]

If no transaction occurred on exact calendar date \(t'\), the cell is assigned None and routed via ModelTree's native missing handler without distorting observed lags.

items.title: B. Additive Classical Time Series Decomposition (decomposed_transform)
items.text:
For periodic series with period \(m\) (e.g. \(m = 7\) for weekly retail cycles):

\[y_t = T_t + S_t + I_t\]
  1. Trend (\(T_t\)): Computed via two-sided moving average filter: $\(T_t = \frac{1}{m} \left( \frac{1}{2} y_{t - m/2} + \sum_{k = -m/2 + 1}^{m/2 - 1} y_{t+k} + \frac{1}{2} y_{t + m/2} \right)\)$
  2. Seasonality (\(S_t\)): Detrended averages normalized to sum to zero over the cycle: $\(\tilde{S}_k = \text{mean}(y_t - T_t \mid t \equiv k \pmod m), \quad S_k = \tilde{S}_k - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^m \tilde{S}_j\)$
  3. Residual Irregularity (\(I_t\)): \(I_t = y_t - T_t - S_t\).

items.title: C. Continuous Trend Extrapolation via Linear Leaves
items.text:
In terminal leaf \(\mathcal{R}_m\), ModelTree fits local ridge regression:

\[\hat{y}(t, \mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{trend}} \cdot t + \sum_{k=1}^P \beta_k \cdot L_k(t)\]

Because time \(t\) enters as an explicit continuous predictor with non-zero slope \(\beta_{\text{trend}}\), predictions continue along the secular trajectory beyond the training horizon.

Next: run these transforms on a simulated panel and compare a linear-leaf tree with a mean-leaf baseline, because the formulas show that a trend term exists but not that it extrapolates out of time.

items.title: 3. Benchmark Study: Multi-Store Retail Demand Panel
items.text:
We evaluate on a simulated multi-store retail panel (240 records across 2 stores over 120 days from 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-30) exhibiting weekly seasonality and strong upward secular growth. - Training Period: First 90 days (2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, 180 records). - Out-of-Time Test Period: Final 30 days (2025-04-01 to 2025-04-30, 60 records).

import datetime as dt
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ModelTree
from mltreelib import calendar_features, decomposed_transform, lag_by_days, windowed_transform

# 0. Seeded synthetic panel: 2 stores x 120 days, weekend lift, upward trend
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
start = dt.date(2025, 1, 1)
dates, stores, sales = [], [], []
for day in range(120):
    d = start + dt.timedelta(days=day)
    for store in (0, 1):
        dates.append(d.isoformat())
        stores.append(f"store_{store}")
        sales.append(100 + 0.8 * day + 15.0 * (d.weekday() >= 5) + 10.0 * store + rng.normal(0, 5))

# 1. Transform features (pure Rust)
cal = calendar_features(dates)
lag_1 = lag_by_days(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, lag_days=1)
lag_7 = lag_by_days(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, lag_days=7)
win_7 = windowed_transform(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, window_days=7, kind="mean", include_current=False)
# Note: the decomposition uses the whole panel, so it is not a strictly out-of-time feature.
decomp = decomposed_transform(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, season_granularity="weekday", trend_window=7)

# 2. Build feature matrix and split out-of-time (first 180 rows = first 90 days)
X = [list(row) for row in zip(cal["weekday"], cal["month"], lag_1, lag_7, win_7, decomp["detrended"])]
X_train, y_train = X[:180], sales[:180]
X_test, y_test = X[180:], sales[180:]

# 3. Fit standard CART step-function baseline
tree_cart = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=15, leaf="mean")
tree_cart.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_cart = tree_cart.predict(X_test)

# 4. Fit ModelTree piecewise linear model tree
tree_linear = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=15, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3)
tree_linear.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_linear = tree_linear.predict(X_test)

rmse = lambda pred: (sum((p - t) ** 2 for p, t in zip(pred, y_test)) / len(y_test)) ** 0.5
print(f"Out-of-time RMSE  CART: {rmse(pred_cart):.2f}  linear leaves: {rmse(pred_linear):.2f}")
print(f"Test sales range: {min(y_test):.1f} to {max(y_test):.1f}")

Out-of-time RMSE  CART: 15.13  linear leaves: 2.66
Test sales range: 171.1 to 225.2

Next: read the RMSE output and its scope, because the run above is one simulated panel with one seed, and the page notes it is not a general forecasting benchmark.

items.title: 4. Empirical Benchmark Output & Quantitative Findings
items.text:
The block in section 3 builds the features on the seeded panel, trains a CART-style baseline (leaf="mean") and a linear-leaf tree on the first 180 rows, and scores the last 60 rows. It prints:

  • Out-of-time RMSE 15.13 for the mean-leaf baseline.
  • Out-of-time RMSE 2.66 for the linear-leaf tree.

On this synthetic panel the linear leaves give the lower error. Mean leaves predict piecewise-constant values, so they cannot follow the upward trend beyond the training range. These are results for one simulated panel with one seed, not a general forecasting benchmark. The decomposed feature uses the whole panel, so this example is not a strictly out-of-time feature set.

items.title: Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Multi-Step Recursive Error Compounding: In multi-step autoregressive rollouts, errors in \(\hat{y}_{t+1}\) feed into lagged inputs for \(\hat{y}_{t+2}\). For horizons exceeding 30 days, direct forecasting or periodic re-anchoring is required.
  2. Trend Over-Extrapolation Risk: Linear leaves fit unconstrained local slopes. If historical growth was parabolic or transient, linear extrapolation will over-predict over long horizons. Setting l2 >= 1.0 or clipping leaf slopes bounds long-term drift.
  3. Irregular Calendar Gaps: When telemetry ceases for extended periods (e.g., store shutdown for 3 months), all day-lags up to \(\Delta d = 90\) become missing, routing records through the missing path.

items.title: Tree Architecture, Growth Knobs & Structural Constraints
items.text:
Decision trees are notorious for high variance and unconstrained overfitting when grown without structural bounds. Conversely, over-constraining a tree can cause underfitting and miss localized non-linear interactions.

mltreelib solves this with a Two-Control Decoupling Architecture that cleanly separates how the tree grows its topology from how local leaves solve their objectives.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Growth [GrowthControl: Tree Topology & Search]
        G1[max_depth: Maximum recursive height]
        G2[min_rows: Minimum node partition support]
        G3[min_gain: Minimal deviance improvement]
        G4[max_leaves: Best-first leaf budget]
        G5[criterion: SSE, Deviance, Tweedie, etc.]
    end

    subgraph Structural [StructuralControl: Domain & Legal Constraints]
        S1[monotone_constraints: Directional sign enforcement]
        S2[interaction_groups: Restricted split pairs]
        S3[honesty: Independent sample splitting]
        S4[pruning: Cost-complexity CCP validation]
    end

    Growth --> T["Fitted ModelTree Topology\nValid White-Box Partitions"]
    Structural --> T
    T --> L["Leaf Solvers: 0D Mean / 1D OLS / Huber / Quantile"]

items.title: 1. The Growth Knob Grid (Depth, Min Rows, and Pruning)
items.text:
The balance between model bias and variance is tuned via recursive growth controls:

Parameter Type Default Operational Effect max_depth int 6 Hard ceiling on recursive partitioning depth. min_rows int 15 Minimum rows on each side of a split. min_gain float 1e-9 Minimum reduction in split deviance required to accept a partition. prune str "cp" Post-pruning: "cp" (cost-complexity), "bic", "mdl" or "none". cp_alpha float 5.0 Absolute per-leaf penalty in target units (squared-error units for a Gaussian leaf). Depends on the target's scale. cp float None Scale-free penalty as a fraction of the root cost, as in rpart. When set it overrides cp_alpha.

The defaults above come from the live constructor. Pruning is bottom-up with one penalty: a split survives only when its error reduction exceeds the per-leaf penalty. There is no cross-validated choice of the penalty.

from mltreelib import ModelTree
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

ds = Dataset.load(
    "concrete_compressive_strength", target="ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
)

for cp in (None, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf="mean", max_depth=6, min_rows=15, prune="cp", cp=cp)
    tree.fit(ds)
    print(f"cp={cp}: {tree.n_leaves()} leaves")

cp=None: 36 leaves
cp=0.001: 30 leaves
cp=0.01: 13 leaves
cp=0.05: 5 leaves

Next: section 2 adds monotone and interaction constraints, which are set alongside the depth and min_rows bounds from section 1; its example sets max_depth=3 and min_rows=30.

items.title: 2. Monotone & Interaction Constraints
items.text:
In regulated domains such as insurance rating and credit underwriting, legal and physical rules dictate that increasing risk indicators (e.g. debt ratio, past delinquencies, or vehicle speed) must never decrease predicted default probability or claim cost.

mltreelib enforces strict monotonicity along split paths: - +1: Monotonically non-decreasing (\(\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial x_j} \ge 0\)). - -1: Monotonically non-increasing (\(\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial x_j} \le 0\)). - 0: Unconstrained split behavior.

import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ModelTree, Metrics

# 1. Generate credit applicant data with natural risk relationships
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_applicants = 1200

# Predictors: Revolving Utilization (%), Borrower Age (Years), Monthly Income ($k)
utilization = rng.uniform(0.05, 1.20, n_applicants)
age = rng.uniform(21.0, 75.0, n_applicants)
income = rng.uniform(2.0, 20.0, n_applicants)

# Default risk increases with utilization, decreases with age and income
risk_score = 0.45 * utilization - 0.005 * age - 0.02 * income + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n_applicants)

X = np.column_stack([utilization, age, income])
feature_names = ["revolving_utilization", "borrower_age", "monthly_income"]

# 2. Enforce domain monotonicity: +1 (increasing), -1 (decreasing)
# Utilization must increase risk (+1), Age must decrease risk (-1), Income must decrease risk (-1)
monotone_spec = [1, -1, -1]

tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    monotone=monotone_spec,     # Enforces sign constraints along every split path
    honesty=True,               # Disjoint sample splitting for structure vs leaf estimation
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=2026,
)
tree.fit(X, risk_score.tolist(), col_names=feature_names)

print("Monotone & Honest Tree Fit Successfully.")
print(f"Total Leaves: {len(tree.leaves())}")
for s in tree.splits():
    print(f"  Split: Feature '{s['col']}' <= {s['threshold']:.3f}")

Monotone & Honest Tree Fit Successfully.
Total Leaves: 2
  Split: Feature 'revolving_utilization' <= 0.577

Related guides

  • Structural Constraints & Honesty for mathematical proofs of monotone projection.
  • Core Tree Architecture for allocator-free growth benchmarks.

items.title: How to use the documentation
items.text:
1. Run one pathway. Get its dataset and follow the analysis from split through evaluation.
  2. Change one part. The example library covers missing routing, alternative leaves, calibration diagnostics, retraining and other focused variations.
  3. Review the decision. Use the evaluation guide, visualization catalog and serving contract.

The dataset setup page lists the downloads. Synthetic checks sit after the practical workflows. They make known effects and missing-data behavior easier to test.

items.title: Reading order
items.text:
Each guide stands alone, but this order builds on itself: prepare data, fit for your outcome type, then evaluate, inspect and ship.

  1. Prepare data: inspect missing values and choose the preparation before fitting.
  2. Regression: fit and compare trees for a numeric target.
  3. Classification: the same workflow for a binary or multiclass target, with a decision threshold.
  4. Survival: time-to-event outcomes with censoring and competing risks.
  5. Uplift: randomized experiments and who to treat.
  6. Clustering: find segments without a target.
  7. Anomaly detection: rank rows for review without a target.
  8. Evaluate and monitor: held-out evaluation and calibration for a finished model.
  9. Metrics, diagnostics and calibration: the diagnostic plots and metrics in detail.
  10. Inspect a model: rules and stumps: read a model as rules.
  11. Visualization: draw the tree and explain one row.
  12. Serving contract: record the prediction contract, save, load and check before release.
  13. Extend a model tree: censored outcomes, constraints, leaf retraining and tuning.
  14. Get the real datasets: where the example data comes from.

items.title: Extend a model tree
items.text:
Start with a regression or classification pathway. Then choose the change that matches the modeling problem. These options are different decisions, not a checklist to enable together.

Need Technique Read next Outcome is censored at a known bound Tobit leaves Tobit example Domain limits on direction or combinations Monotone or interaction constraints Constraint example Preserve segments while updating leaf models Leaf retraining Retraining examples Control fit complexity and flexibility Growth and leaf settings Growth knob tour Different outcome distributions Distributional families Distributional leaves Predict only from approved input columns Feature and interaction controls Parameters

items.title: 1. Censored outcomes: Tobit
items.text:
Tobit is a model for a latent response observed only above a censoring boundary. Structural zeros, truncation and missing outcomes are different problems. Its interpretation depends on the assumed latent model and censoring mechanism.

from random import Random
from mltreelib import ModelTree

rng = Random(12)
x = [[rng.uniform(-2, 2)] for _ in range(160)]
y = [max(0.0, 0.5 + 2 * row[0] + rng.gauss(0, 1)) for row in x]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=0, min_rows=10, leaf="linear",
                  leaf_family="tobit", tobit_threshold=0.0)
model.fit(x[:120], y[:120], col_names=["signal"])
print("Latent predictions:", model.predict(x[120:])[:3])

Latent predictions: [2.1580410607837752, -1.7836864164002812, -1.2136598847652085]

The response above is the fitted latent expectation, so negative values are possible even though observations are censored at zero. Evaluate the desired observed outcome separately. Correct censoring assumptions do not guarantee an unbiased result on every dataset. See Tobin (1958).

items.title: 2. Constrain shape and interactions
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=5, leaf="mean", monotone=[1])
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
print("Predictions:", model.predict([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]]))

Predictions: [0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5]

A positive constraint encodes a domain requirement. Check predictions on meaningful grids and held-out data. A check on the healthcare example found two decreases with linear leaves when age increased. The same check found no decreases with mean leaves. This is a tracked behavior gap; a finite grid does not prove monotonicity elsewhere. Do not assume local coefficient signs guarantee global monotonicity. Interaction constraints restrict paths and should also be checked with split_paths().

items.title: 3. Retrain leaves with fixed partitions
items.text:
from mltreelib import LeafControl, ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=5, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
before = model.splits()
model.retrain(x, [v + 1 for v in y], control=LeafControl(leaf="mean"))
print("Splits preserved:", before == model.splits())
print("Updated prediction:", model.predict([[5.0]]))

Splits preserved: True
Updated prediction: [1.5]

This example mutates the model. Use appropriate independent data for evaluation and check that each leaf has sufficient new observations. Fixed partitions can become stale when the population changes. See the hierarchical retraining guide for alternative feature sets and routing.

Next: section 4 covers tuning on validation data, the independent data that section 3 says a retrained model needs for evaluation.

items.title: 4. Tune deliberately
items.text: Start with max_depth and min_rows to control partition size. Compare mean and linear leaves only when their assumptions and interpretation fit the outcome. Tune on a validation set and keep a final test set untouched. The knob tour is a parameter reference, not a recommended sequence or a substitute for evaluation.

items.title: Anomaly detection in Python: operational triage review queues
items.text:
Use a fixed review budget to surface unusual operating states without synthetic imputation. The goal is a prioritized list of suspicious records an analyst can inspect within operational constraints.

items.title: 1. Domain Context & The Ghost Anomaly Problem
items.text:
Standard Isolation Forests construct trees by sampling orthogonal, axis-aligned cuts. On correlated or multi-modal feature distributions, axis-aligned splits produce artificial rectangular bands of low average path length, creating false-positive "ghost" anomalies in empty spaces between normal clusters.

AnomalyModel(kind="eif") implements Extended Isolation Forest (EIF), sampling random oblique hyperplanes with uniformly distributed normal vectors. This achieves rotationally invariant scoring contours that isolate true anomalies without axis-aligned artifacts.

Next: fit AnomalyModel(kind="eif") on the normal training rows and score held-out telemetry, which applies the oblique-cut model described above.

items.title: 2. Fit the Reference Model and Score New Rows
items.text:
You can evaluate on industrial telemetry using load_dataset("APSFailure") or the UCI Statlog Shuttle benchmark:

This snippet loads the first 10,000 rows of APSFailure into a Dataset, splits them in row order into 7,000 training and 3,000 test rows, fits an AnomalyModel (kind="eif", max_depth=10) on the normal training rows, and evaluates the top 5% review budget and ROC-AUC with MetricsReport.

from mltreelib import AnomalyModel, MetricsReport
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

# 1. Load industrial sensor telemetry (first 10,000 rows in file order)
features = ["aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000"]
ds_full = Dataset.load(
    "APSFailure", target="AirPressureSystemFailure", features=features
)
n_sample = 10000
ds, _ = ds_full.split(test_size=ds_full.n_rows - n_sample, time=True)
train, test = ds.split(test_size=3000, time=True)

y_train = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in train.y]
y_test = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in test.y]
X_train = [x for x, label in zip(train.x, y_train) if label == 0]  # Fit reference on normal operating states
X_test = test.x

# 2. Fit Extended Isolation Forest (oblique cuts, depth=10)
tree = AnomalyModel(kind="eif", max_depth=10, extension_level=1, seed=42)
tree.fit(X_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Score held-out telemetry
scores = tree.predict(X_test, kind="score")

# 4. Allocate fixed 5% operational review budget
budget = round(0.05 * len(scores))
order = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))

hits = sum(y_test[i] for i in order[:budget])
total_anomalies = sum(y_test)
print(f"Review Budget Size : {budget} records (Top 5%)")
print(f"Precision at Budget: {hits / budget:.4f}")
print(f"Recall at Budget   : {hits / max(1, total_anomalies):.4f}")

cutoff = scores[order[budget - 1]]
y_pred = [1 if s >= cutoff else 0 for s in scores]
probs = [1.0 / (1.0 + 2.718281828 ** (-s)) for s in scores]
rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=y_test, y_pred=y_pred, proba=probs)
print(f"ROC-AUC            : {rep['auc']:.4f}")

Review Budget Size : 150 records (Top 5%)
Precision at Budget: 0.1867
Recall at Budget   : 0.4590
ROC-AUC            : 0.8154

What to read in the output: precision and recall at the top-5% review budget measure how many true failures land in the 150 highest-scoring rows, and ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across all 3,000 test rows.

kind="binary" returns labels from the fitted threshold, and kind="score" returns the same scores as score_samples(). The extended isolation tree and its aliases also expose kind="path_length".

For a fitted EIF, tree.save("anomalies.json") stores the model and fitted threshold. Use AnomalyModel.load("anomalies.json") to restore scoring and labels. The API reference lists the JSON and byte methods.

Next: the engine table lists the other kind values, to check whether a different engine suits your data better than the EIF used above.

items.title: 3. Understand the Anomaly Engine Family
items.text:
AnomalyModel provides a unified interface across multiple tree-based anomaly engines:

Engine (kind) Core Mechanism Best Used For "eif" Oblique random hyperplanes with uniform normals Multi-modal, correlated continuous telemetry without ghost artifacts "isolation" Standard axis-aligned recursive bisection Fast baseline on uncorrelated low-dimensional features "det" Density Estimation Trees (piecewise constant density) Estimating exact probability density distributions "hst" Streaming Half-Space Trees with mass-based scoring Online, real-time sliding window data streams "rct" Robust Random Cut Trees (co-displacement scoring) Dynamic time-series streams with concept drift "active" Active learning tree with expert feedback loops Human-in-the-loop analyst triage queues

items.text:

  • For missing sensor routing under telemetry dropouts, review Native Missing Data.
  • See the full Anomaly API Reference.

items.title: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress
items.text: Use the Give Me Some Credit dataset to estimate financial distress within two years. The tutorial fits a decision tree classifier, then uses validation data to decide which scores enter a review queue.

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the decision
items.text:
Download OpenML 46929 to datasets/GiveMeSomeCredit.parquet. The target is FinancialDistressNextTwoYears. The published table has 150,000 labeled rows. This example uses a seeded 12,000-row subset, split into 8,000 training, 2,000 validation and 2,000 test rows. The test rows are held back for the final report.

Use observed values as supplied. In the sample, monthly income and number of dependents can be missing. Pass them through to the tree. The input schema is numeric and needs no encoder.

Next: fit the tree on the 8,000 training rows, use the 2,000 validation rows to choose a threshold, and score the 2,000 test rows for the final report.

items.title: 2. Fit and choose a threshold
items.text:
This snippet loads a seeded 12,000-row sample of GiveMeSomeCredit into a Dataset, splits it into 8,000 training, 2,000 validation, and 2,000 test rows, fits a binomial-logit tree, picks a cost-minimizing threshold on validation probabilities, and scores the test set with MetricsReport.

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_parquet(dataset_path("GiveMeSomeCredit"))
target = "FinancialDistressNextTwoYears"
cols = df.to_dict("list")
cols[target] = [1 if v == "Yes" else 0 for v in cols[target]]

ds = Dataset(cols, target=target, name="GiveMeSomeCredit")
sub, _ = ds.split(test_size=ds.n_rows - 12000, seed=2026)
train, val, test = sub.split(val_size=2000, test_size=2000, seed=2026)

tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
    max_depth=3, min_rows=100, prune="none",
)
tree.fit(train)

val_scores = tree.predict_proba(val)
def cost(threshold):
    return sum(
        5 if y and p < threshold else 1 if not y and p >= threshold else 0
        for y, p in zip(val.y, val_scores)
    )

threshold = min([.02, .05, .10, .20, .40, 1.01], key=cost)
scores = tree.predict_proba(test)
alerts = [int(score >= threshold) for score in scores]

rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=test.y, y_pred=alerts, proba=scores)
base = MetricsReport(
    "classification",
    y_true=test.y,
    y_pred=[0] * test.n_rows,
    proba=[sum(train.y) / train.n_rows] * test.n_rows,
)
prevalence = sum(test.y) / test.n_rows
print(f"Validation threshold: {threshold:.2f}; flagged test rows: {sum(alerts)} of {len(alerts)}")
print(rep.tables["confusion"])
print(f"Average precision: {rep['average_precision']:.4f} (test prevalence {prevalence:.4f})")
print(f"Brier score: {rep['brier']:.4f} (constant training rate {base['brier']:.4f})")
print(f"Root split: {tree.root_split()['col']}; split columns: {[s['col'] for s in tree.splits()]}")
miss = train.missing()["per_column"]
print(f"Training missing: MonthlyIncome {miss['MonthlyIncome']['n_missing']}, NumberOfDependents {miss['NumberOfDependents']['n_missing']}")

Validation threshold: 0.10; flagged test rows: 200 of 2000
[{'actual': 0, 'pred 0': 1727, 'pred 1': 138}, {'actual': 1, 'pred 0': 73, 'pred 1': 62}]
Average precision: 0.2647 (test prevalence 0.0675)
Brier score: 0.0542 (constant training rate 0.0629)
Root split: RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines; split columns: ['RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines', 'NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse', 'NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse', 'RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines', 'NumberOfTimes90DaysLate', 'RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines']
Training missing: MonthlyIncome 1578, NumberOfDependents 205

What to read in the output: check the validation-chosen threshold, the confusion matrix at that cutoff, average precision against the test prevalence baseline, and Brier score against the constant training-rate baseline. Missing values in MonthlyIncome and NumberOfDependents stay intact and are routed natively by the tree.

The costs are illustrative. A missed event costs five units and a false alert costs one. A threshold above 1 represents no alerts. The full script also compares probability error with the training event rate.

uv run python examples/guides/real_tree_studies.py credit

Next: read the test confusion matrix from step 2 at the validation threshold of 0.10, and compare the tree's average precision and Brier score with the reference values.

items.title: 3. Read the result
items.text:
The validation threshold was 0.10. It flagged 200 of 2,000 test rows. Of the 135 observed distress events, 62 were flagged and 73 were missed. The remaining 138 alerts were false positives.

Test metric Tree Reference Average precision 0.2647 0.0675 event prevalence Brier score 0.0542 0.0629 constant training rate

The root uses revolving utilization. A later split uses the count of payments 60 to 89 days past due. The training sample contains 1,578 missing income values and 205 missing dependent counts.

Average precision measures how well the scores rank the positive cases. Compare it with test prevalence as a reference. Brier score measures squared probability error. Compare it with the constant training-rate model. The probability plot is a diagnostic. Review bin counts and treat sparsely populated bins with care.

Next: review the splits and leaf support behind these alerts, because the metrics in step 3 come from one random historical split.

items.title: 4. Review the model before acting
items.text:
Use tree.splits() to see the original feature names and tree.leaves() to check support. Evaluate calibration, decision cost and review volume on realistic future records. This random historical split demonstrates a workflow. An underwriting decision needs time-based validation, group analysis, documented data provenance and governance.

Read the credit article for a deeper walkthrough of explanation and threshold choice. Use the evaluation guide for the differences between probability, ranking and decision metrics.

items.title: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry
items.text: Use a predictive clustering tree to group wines by measurements a lab can inspect. The output is a leaf ID, a rule and a profile. A lab could investigate an unexpected shift in the size of a segment across production batches.

items.title: 1. Get the data and choose the features
items.text:
Save OpenML Wine Quality 46964 to datasets/wine_quality.parquet. The 6,497 records come from the UCI Wine Quality collection. Use four numeric measurements. Keep median_wine_quality and wine_color out of fitting. Those columns can help interpret groups later.

PCT splits to reduce the variation of numeric features inside its leaves. The measurements have different units, so give them comparable scales using training means and standard deviations. Keep the original units for the report. Scaling is an explicit choice for this similarity objective.

Next: fit the PCT model on the scaled training wines from step 1, then assign the held-out review wines to segments.

items.title: 2. Fit, assign and profile
items.text:
Run this from the repository root. The second split supports a refit check. Assign the review records with both models before comparing them.

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ClusterModel, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_parquet(dataset_path("wine_quality"))
features = ["residual_sugar", "volatile_acidity", "alcohol", "chlorides"]
ds = Dataset(df[features].to_dict("list"), features=features, name="wine_quality")
# Seeded split: 2,500 train, 2,500 refit check (middle split), remaining rows review
train_ds, val_ds, review_ds = ds.split(
    val_size=2500, test_size=ds.n_rows - 5000, seed=2026
)
train_df = pd.DataFrame({f: train_ds.columns[f] for f in features})
val_df = pd.DataFrame({f: val_ds.columns[f] for f in features})
review = pd.DataFrame({f: review_ds.columns[f] for f in features})
center = train_df.mean()
scale = train_df.std()

def design(frame):
    return ((frame[features] - center) / scale).to_numpy().tolist()

tree = ClusterModel(kind="pct", max_depth=2, min_rows=150)
tree.fit(design(train_df), col_names=features)
review["segment"] = tree.predict(design(review), kind="cluster")
print(review.groupby("segment")[features].median().round(3))
print(review["segment"].value_counts().sort_index())

# Refit at depth 2 on the middle split, then compare the review assignments by pairwise Jaccard
refit = ClusterModel(kind="pct", max_depth=2, min_rows=150)
refit.fit(design(val_df), col_names=features)
first = review["segment"].tolist()
second = refit.predict(design(review), kind="cluster")
both = either = 0
for i in range(len(first)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(first)):
        same_first, same_second = first[i] == first[j], second[i] == second[j]
        both += same_first and same_second
        either += same_first or same_second
print(f"Pairwise Jaccard after refit: {both / either:.3f}")
print(tree.rules())

uv run python examples/guides/real_tree_studies.py wine

Next: read the segment profiles from step 2 in lab units and check whether the segments hold when the model is refit on another training sample.

items.title: 3. Read the profiles and check stability
items.text:
Leaf Review rows Median residual sugar (g/L) Median volatile acidity (g/L) Median alcohol (%) 0 671 2.0 0.26 11.0 1 376 2.2 0.49 9.8 2 339 12.0 0.26 9.3 3 111 9.2 0.29 11.0

The two lower-sugar groups differ on acidity. The higher-sugar groups differ on alcohol. Pairwise Jaccard agreement on the 1,497 review wines was 0.858 after refitting at depth two on the second training sample. This is one check with a shared training scale.

A scatter plot only shows two of the four input features. Use the profile panel to see how the segments differ across the full feature list. It displays each segment's median in units of the training standard deviation. For a rule review, convert a standardized threshold back to lab units using threshold * scale + center.

Report pairwise Jaccard agreement after refitting. It counts pairs assigned together in both fits as a fraction of pairs assigned together in either fit. It avoids matching arbitrary leaf IDs and excludes the usually large number of pairs separated by both fits. This tests the stability of one partition with fixed scaling. Before using the groups operationally, repeat with independent batches and compare against a simpler lab rule.

Next: compare the other engines behind ClusterModel, because the profiles and stability check in step 3 describe only the PCT segmentation.

items.title: 4. Choose an engine through ClusterModel
items.text:
The following observations are from a small numeric, two-group synthetic check. They establish the interface paths exercised, not comparative model quality.

kind Training and prediction output checked rules() in that check pct Training labels and new-row labels Conditions, prototypes and support cltree Labels can include None for unassigned rows Bounding boxes and support hdbscan Training and new-row labels Empty list urf Training and new-row labels Empty list

The sample check returned 8 PCT leaves, 3 CLTree groups plus unassigned points, 2 HDBSCAN groups, and a highly imbalanced URF assignment. These results depend on the data and settings. They do not rank the engines. Check whether a segment is stable and useful before assigning an action to it.

For URF, tree.predict(x, kind="distances") returns one row per query and one column per training row in fit order. Each distance is the square root of one minus the fraction of trees in which the two rows share a leaf.

For a fitted PCT, tree.save("clusters.json") stores the model, training assignments, and rules. Use ClusterModel.load("clusters.json") to restore the fitted tree. The API reference lists the JSON and byte methods.

items.title: Missing values and categories: product gaps
items.text:
The wrapper currently converts None to 0.0 for cltree, hdbscan and urf during fitting and prediction. This is implicit imputation and conflicts with the package's missing-data goal. Track it as a product gap. Do not assume those engines distinguish missing from a real zero. They also reject raw strings in the checked inputs.

PCT accepted raw categorical labels and missing numeric entries in a separate check. Its returned rules displayed category codes rather than the original labels. In that check, an unseen category and a missing category went to different leaves. Category-label rendering and unseen-category routing need further investigation before those rules become a business handoff.

For density and proximity methods, check scaling, distance choice and the meaning of an unassigned or noise label. For all kinds, test the actual new-row behavior and input schema that your workflow uses.

Next: run a synthetic example with known generating groups, which shows how a tree can split one true group into several leaves, something the wine segments cannot show.

items.title: 5. Run the controlled stability example
items.text:
The synthetic clustering workflow lets you change the overlap between known generating groups. It uses 1,000 independent review rows and illustrates how a tree can split a single generating group into several leaves.

See Blockeel et al. on predictive clustering and the engine comparison.

items.title: Prepare data for modeling
items.text:
Path: Define the prediction time → Describe the columns → Check missingness → Run quality checks → Measure associations → Split rows → Bin and transform on training rows → Hand the frame to the model → Apply the same schema to new data.

This guide follows one real dataset from raw columns to a model input. It covers the data helpers in mltreelib.data. It does not cover categorical encoders or time-series features; see the links in step 8.

Decision Check Split Keep future observations, customers or groups out of training when they define the deployment setting. Numeric Check units, impossible values, missingness and whether scaling is appropriate for the chosen model. Categorical Preserve the distinction between labels and ordered numeric measurements. Fit any mapping on training data. Target Exclude the outcome and features that become available only after the prediction time. New data Preserve column order, names, types and the fitted mapping. Test unknown levels and missing values.

The example is the Give Me Some Credit table (GiveMeSomeCredit, 150,000 rows). The target FinancialDistressNextTwoYears says whether a borrower was in financial distress within two years. Each feature is assumed to be known when the lending decision is made; confirm that with the data owner before a real deployment. Two columns, MonthlyIncome and NumberOfDependents, have missing values. Every helper below keeps them as they are.

items.title: 1. Describe each column
items.text:
describe gives one row per column: its kind, how much is missing, the summary statistics, and outlier counts. Its statistics skip missing and infinite values and never fill them.

from mltreelib import load_dataset
from mltreelib.data import describe, infer_types

d = load_dataset("GiveMeSomeCredit")
cols = d["columns"]
target = "FinancialDistressNextTwoYears"
cols[target] = [1 if v == "Yes" else 0 for v in cols[target]]  # hand recode: helpers never recode

print(infer_types(cols)[target])
rows = describe(cols, kinds={target: "categorical"})
print(f"{'column':<40}{'kind':<14}{'missing':>8}{'mean':>12}{'trim_mean':>12}{'mad':>10}{'iqr_out':>9}")
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['name']:<40}{r['kind']:<14}{r['n_missing']:>8}{r['mean']:>12.3f}"
          f"{r['trimmed_mean']:>12.3f}{r['mad']:>10.3f}{r['n_outliers_iqr']:>9}")

{'kind': 'ordinal_candidate', 'n_levels': 2, 'ordinal_candidate': True}
column                                  kind           missing        mean   trim_mean       mad  iqr_out
FinancialDistressNextTwoYears           categorical          0       0.067       0.000     0.000    10026
RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines    numeric              0       6.048       0.274     0.148      763
age                                     numeric              0      52.295      51.969    11.000       46
NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse    categorical          0       0.421       0.075     0.000    23982
DebtRatio                               numeric              0     353.005      51.655     0.246    31311
MonthlyIncome                           numeric          29731    6670.221    5787.565  2317.000     4879
NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans         numeric              0       8.453       7.963     3.000     3980
NumberOfTimes90DaysLate                 categorical          0       0.266       0.000     0.000     8338
NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines            numeric              0       1.018       0.877     1.000      793
NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse    categorical          0       0.240       0.000     0.000     7604
NumberOfDependents                      categorical       3924       0.757       0.538     0.000    13336

Read the table this way:

  • kind is a hint, not a type check. An integer column with fewer than six distinct values is ordinal_candidate: a category code or a 1-to-5 rating. The first line of the output shows the target with that hint, because its two codes are integers. Passing kinds={target: "categorical"} overrides the hint, and the table row then reports kind_source="user". Ordered levels suit monotone constraints, so decide which columns are ordinal on purpose.
  • trimmed_mean removes the top and bottom 10% by default (trim=0.1), so it is less affected by extreme values than mean. The gap is large here: RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines has a mean of 6.048 but a trimmed mean of 0.274, and MonthlyIncome has 6,670 against 5,788.
  • mad (median absolute deviation from the median, unscaled) is a robust spread. Compare it with the standard deviation to see whether a column is heavy-tailed.
  • n_outliers_iqr counts values outside the Tukey fences. It describes them; nothing is removed. Read it with care for sparse columns: when the middle half is constant, the IQR is zero and every non-zero value counts as an outlier. The target (10,026 ones) and the delinquency counts show this, so their counts carry no meaning.
  • Pass inf_as_missing=True to count infinite values as missing in n_missing and pct_missing. The statistics ignore infinities either way.

Next: the missingness step counts where the missing values are and checks whether they relate to the target, because a column with many gaps may carry a signal of its own.

items.title: 2. Check missingness
items.text:
missing_profile counts missing values per column and per row, groups rows by which columns they miss together, and gives a co-missing matrix. missing_vs_target compares the mean of the target when a column is missing with its mean when the column is observed.

from mltreelib.data import missing_profile, missing_vs_target

mp = missing_profile(cols)
print("complete rows:", mp["n_complete_rows"], "of", mp["n_rows"])
for p in mp["patterns"]:
    if p["columns"]:
        print("missing together:", p["columns"], p["count"])
names = mp["co_missing"]["names"]
i, j = names.index("MonthlyIncome"), names.index("NumberOfDependents")
print("rows missing both:", mp["co_missing"]["matrix"][i][j])

mv = missing_vs_target(cols, cols[target])
for name in ["MonthlyIncome", "NumberOfDependents"]:
    r = mv[name]
    print(name, r["n_missing"], r["y_mean_when_missing"], r["y_mean_when_observed"])

complete rows: 120269 of 150000
missing together: ('MonthlyIncome',) 25807
missing together: ('MonthlyIncome', 'NumberOfDependents') 3924
rows missing both: 3924
MonthlyIncome 29731 0.05613669234132723 0.06948590243537403
NumberOfDependents 3924 0.04561671763506626 0.0674101152824557

Two findings. First, the gaps overlap. 25,807 rows miss only MonthlyIncome, and 3,924 rows miss both columns. No row misses NumberOfDependents alone, so every missing dependents count also lacks income. The two gaps probably come from one source. 120,269 of the 150,000 rows are complete.

Second, the gaps relate to the target. The mean target is 0.0561 where income is missing and 0.0695 where it is observed; for dependents, 0.0456 against 0.0674. The rate differs, so the gap carries information, and the question for the data owner is why the field is blank.

Neither helper imputes or drops a row. The missing rows stay in every later step of this guide: the tree routes them natively in step 8, and any other model needs its own explicit choice. Check the same pattern by source, group and time when those fields exist.

Next: the quality checks look for columns and rows that add no information or that will break a later step, such as constant columns, duplicates and a target with too few cases of one class.

items.title: 3. Run quality checks
items.text:
These checks flag problems and change nothing. class_balance reports the target's share of each class. constant_columns and near_zero_variance find columns that barely vary. duplicate_rows groups identical rows. outlier_flags marks values outside the IQR fences for one column. schema_capture records each column's kind, range and levels, and schema_validate checks a later batch against that record.

from mltreelib.data import (class_balance, constant_columns, duplicate_rows,
                            near_zero_variance, outlier_flags, schema_capture,
                            schema_validate, take)

print("constant:", constant_columns(cols))
print("near zero variance:", [r["name"] for r in near_zero_variance(cols)])
groups = duplicate_rows(cols)
print("duplicate groups:", len(groups), "rows in groups:", sum(len(g) for g in groups))
print("target balance:", class_balance(cols[target]))
flags = outlier_flags(cols["MonthlyIncome"])
print("MonthlyIncome flagged:", sum(f is True for f in flags), "missing:", sum(f is None for f in flags))

schema = schema_capture(cols)
batch = take(cols, range(1000))  # a copy: the original columns are not changed
batch["age"][0] = 200
print("schema problems:", schema_validate(batch, schema))

Read the results with the data in mind:

  • near_zero_variance flags NumberOfTimes90DaysLate and NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse because most of their values are 0. Both are among the strongest columns in step 6, so the flag marks a sparse column, not a useless one. Do not drop a column on this flag alone.
  • 351 duplicate groups hold 960 rows. Two borrowers can share every recorded value. Decide with the data owner whether a duplicate is a repeated record or a real match, and only then remove rows.
  • The target has 139,974 zeros and 10,026 ones, an imbalance ratio of 13.96. A model that always predicts 0 would be right 93.3% of the time, so judge models on the rare class. Step 8 reports AUC for that reason.
  • 4,879 incomes lie outside the IQR fences. Each flag is a value to inspect, not to delete: some high incomes are real and some are entry errors. The 29,731 missing incomes are not flagged; they stay None.
  • schema_validate reports the one changed age as out_of_range: 200.0 is outside the captured range [0.0, 109.0]. Missing values pass unless allow_missing=False. Run it on every new batch before scoring.

Next: the association step looks at pairs of columns. Strong correlation or association between features costs accuracy and interpretability, and a feature that is almost the target can be a leak.

items.title: 4. Measure associations
items.text:
correlation_matrix gives pairwise correlation, using only the rows where both values are observed, and correlation_filter applies the greedy rule that drops columns until no remaining pair is above a cutoff. cramers_v_matrix gives the same kind of pairwise table for categorical columns. vif gives the variance inflation factor of each numeric column on complete rows. leakage_hints scores each feature alone against the target and flags high scores; it removes nothing.

from mltreelib.data import correlation_filter, correlation_matrix, cramers_v_matrix, leakage_hints, vif

features = {k: v for k, v in cols.items() if k != target}
corr = correlation_matrix(features, method="spearman")
flt = correlation_filter(corr, cutoff=0.9)
print("correlation drop:", flt["drop"])
names = corr["names"]
pairs = [(abs(corr["matrix"][i][j]), names[i], names[j])
         for i in range(len(names)) for j in range(i + 1, len(names))
         if corr["matrix"][i][j] is not None]
top = max(pairs)
print("largest pair:", round(top[0], 3), top[1], top[2])

cv = cramers_v_matrix(cols)
print("categorical columns:", cv["names"])
for name, row in zip(cv["names"], cv["matrix"]):
    print(f"{name:<40}", [None if x is None else round(x, 3) for x in row])

out = vif(features)
print("VIF rows used:", out["n_used"], "excluded:", out["n_excluded"])
print({k: (None if v is None else round(v, 2)) for k, v in out["vif"].items()})

hints = leakage_hints(features, cols[target])
print([(h["name"], None if h["score"] is None else round(h["score"], 3), h["flagged"]) for h in hints])

NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse     [0.289, 1.0, 0.372, 0.42, 0.021]

{'RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines': 1.0, 'age': 1.09, 'NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse': 26.77, 'DebtRatio': 1.0, 'MonthlyIncome': 1.02, 'NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans': 1.28, 'NumberOfTimes90DaysLate': 49.21, 'NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines': 1.25, 'NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse': 60.64, 'NumberOfDependents': 1.07}

What to read here:

  • correlation_matrix uses Spearman ranks here, which are robust to the long right tails of the income and debt columns. It skips non-numeric columns and reports the rows used for each pair in n_pairs.
  • correlation_filter drops the column with the larger mean absolute correlation to the others, and ties drop the later column. At cutoff 0.9 it drops nothing: the largest pair is open credit lines against real-estate loans, at 0.473. A pairwise rule can miss collinearity among several columns, which VIF catches.
  • cramers_v_matrix treats integer columns with at most 20 distinct values as categorical, and it reports a bias-corrected V and a chi-square p-value for each pair. The target has V of 0.289 with the 30-59 day count, 0.356 with the 90-day count and 0.289 with the 60-89 day count, and 0.047 with dependents. The three delinquency counts also associate with each other at 0.37 to 0.42.
  • VIF uses 120,269 complete rows and excludes the 29,731 rows with missing income. The three delinquency counts have VIF of 26.77, 49.21 and 60.64; every other numeric column is between 1.0 and 1.3. Those three move together, so decide which of them to keep before reading any coefficient that uses all three. VIF is also expensive: each numeric column needs its own regression on all the others, so the cost grows quickly as columns are added. Screen the columns first, then compute VIF on the shortlist.
  • leakage_hints scores each feature alone against the target and flags scores at or above the threshold (0.95 here). Nothing is flagged; the highest score is 0.778 for RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines. A flag is a question for the data owner: does this column exist at the prediction time? It is not a verdict.

Next: the split step fixes which rows train the model and which evaluate it. Every association and screening result above used all rows for description; from here on, only training rows should inform choices that the model will use.

items.title: 5. Split rows
items.text:
train_test_split returns index lists. Pass stratify to keep the class share the same in both sides, groups to keep all rows of a group on one side, or time_order to put the latest rows in the test set. kfold does the same for cross-validation. take subsets a dict of columns and select_rows subsets an xy result, both by row index and neither changes a missing value.

from mltreelib.data import kfold, select_rows, take, train_test_split, xy

n = len(cols[target])
train_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(n, test_size=0.2, seed=2026, stratify=cols[target])
train_cols, test_cols = take(cols, train_idx), take(cols, test_idx)
print("stratified sizes:", len(train_idx), len(test_idx))
print("target share train:", round(class_balance(train_cols[target])["proportions"][1], 4),
      "test:", round(class_balance(test_cols[target])["proportions"][1], 4))

# Grouped: the dataset has no household id, so NumberOfDependents stands in to show the mode.
g_train, g_test = train_test_split(n, test_size=0.2, seed=2026, groups=cols["NumberOfDependents"])
shared = {cols["NumberOfDependents"][i] for i in g_train} & {cols["NumberOfDependents"][i] for i in g_test}
print("groups shared between sides:", len(shared))

# Time-ordered: the dataset has no date column, so row order stands in for time.
t_train, t_test = train_test_split(n, test_size=0.2, time_order=list(range(n)))
print("time-ordered test starts at row:", min(t_test), "of", n)

folds = kfold(n, k=5, seed=2026, stratify=cols[target])
print("fold test sizes:", [len(test) for _, test in folds])

frame = xy(cols, target)
tr, te = select_rows(frame, train_idx), select_rows(frame, test_idx)

def missing_cells(f):
    return sum(v is None for row in f["x"] for v in row)

print("missing feature cells, whole table:", missing_cells(frame))
print("missing feature cells, train plus test:", missing_cells(tr) + missing_cells(te))
print("train rows:", len(tr["y"]), "test rows:", len(te["y"]), "names:", tr["names"][:3])

Notes on the split:

  • The stratified split gives each class its exact share, within one row. Both sides show a target share of 0.0668, the share of the whole table.
  • A group is never split across the two sides: no group is shared here. Missing group labels form their own group. This dataset has no household or customer id, so NumberOfDependents is used only to show the mode. Use a real id in practice.
  • time_order makes the test set the last rows, with no shuffling. Use a real event date in practice; the row order here is not a claim about when the rows were recorded.
  • kfold with stratify gives five test folds of 30,000 rows each. kfold with time_order instead expands the training window fold by fold.
  • No split drops a row, and take and select_rows do not change a value. Both sides together hold 33,655 missing feature cells, the same as the whole table. The split moved the gaps and changed none.

Next: the binning step measures how strongly each numeric column separates the two outcomes. It must use training rows only, because a bin edge or an information value fitted on the test rows would leak the answer into the model.

items.title: 6. Bin a numeric column and measure information value
items.text:
iv_bins cuts a numeric column into ordered bins, merges them to respect a monotone trend, and reports the information value (IV). binner gives the bin assignment for each row. iv_levels does the same for a categorical column, and information_value_table runs the screen over every column.

from mltreelib.data import binner, information_value_table, iv_bins, iv_levels

y_tr = train_cols[target]
util = train_cols["RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines"]
r = iv_bins(util, y_tr, n_bins=10, monotone="increasing")
print("IV:", round(r["iv"], 4), "trend:", r["trend"], "ordered bins:", len(r["bins"]))
b = binner(util, n_bins=10)
print("bin counts:", b["counts"], "missing:", b["n_missing"])
print("levels IV:", round(iv_levels(train_cols["NumberOfDependents"], y_tr)["iv"], 4))
features_tr = {k: v for k, v in train_cols.items() if k != target}
for row in information_value_table(features_tr, y_tr, n_bins=10):
    print(f"{row['name']:<40}{round(row['iv'], 4):>8}  {row['strength']}")

bin counts: [12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000, 12000] missing: 0

The greedy merge above is fast but not guaranteed optimal. optimize="dp" finds the best set of cut points under the same constraints with an exact dynamic programme over fine pre-bins. It also takes a trend ("increasing", "decreasing", "peak", "valley" or "auto"), a minimum bin share, a maximum number of bins, and special_values that get their own bins outside the trend.

exact = iv_bins(util, y_tr, optimize="dp", trend="auto", max_bins=8, min_bin_frac=0.05)
print("greedy IV:", round(r["iv"], 4), "| dp IV:", round(exact["iv"], 4))
print("dp trend:", exact["trend"], "bins:", len(exact["bins"]), "relaxed:", exact["constraint_relaxed"])
for b_ in exact["bins"]:
    print(f"({b_['lo']:.3f}, {b_['hi']:.3f}]  n={b_['n']:>6}  event rate={b_['event_rate']:.3f}  woe={b_['woe']:+.3f}")

What to read here:

  • iv_bins with monotone="increasing" cuts the 120,000 training rows into ten quantile bins of 12,000 rows each, merges them to eight ordered bins, and reports an IV of 1.0998. The event rate is forced to rise with the bin order. Without the argument the table below gives 1.1212 for the same column, because it applies no trend.
  • The exact mode reaches an IV of 1.114 against 1.0998 for the greedy merge on the same column: a small gain, and it is guaranteed to be the best split under these constraints. It keeps eight bins, the event rate rises from 0.017 in the lowest bin to 0.222 in the highest, and constraint_relaxed is False, so every constraint was met.
  • The table reads the strength labels as a rule of thumb: below 0.02 useless, below 0.1 weak, below 0.3 medium, below 0.5 strong, and above that suspicious. Four columns are above 0.5: utilization (1.1212), the 90-day count (0.8271), the 30-59 day count (0.7458) and the 60-89 day count (0.5779). Those are past-delinquency measures. A value this high is a reason to check leakage (step 4) and to confirm with the data owner that the history exists at the prediction time. age is medium at 0.2598, and the other five are weak.
  • NumberOfDependents gives 0.0366 from iv_levels, which treats each value as its own level, and 0.0352 in the table, which bins the numeric column. The two methods differ by design.
  • binner counts every row. Missing values get no bin and are counted in n_missing; they are never merged into a neighbouring bin. This column has no missing values, so its count is 0.
  • Choose bins and trend on training rows. The test rows stay out of this step.

Next: the transform step fits scalings on training rows and applies them to both sides. Scalings and bin edges belong to the training data, so they travel with the model.

items.title: 7. Transform numeric columns
items.text:
FeatureTransformer fits one transform on the observed values of a column and applies it, with an exact inverse. The kinds are log1p, boxcox, yeojohnson, mean_diff and median_diff. A missing value passes through every kind unchanged. log1p needs no fit, so it is also available as a plain function. Box-Cox needs strictly positive values, so the snippet adds 1 to MonthlyIncome first; Yeo-Johnson accepts zero and negative values directly.

from mltreelib.data import FeatureTransformer, log1p

inc = train_cols["MonthlyIncome"]
shifted = [None if v is None else v + 1.0 for v in inc]  # Box-Cox needs x > 0

def round_trip_ok(before, after):
    missing_kept = [a is None for a in before] == [b is None for b in after]
    return missing_kept and max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(before, after) if a is not None) < 1e-6

print("log1p first values:", log1p(inc[:3]))
for kind, values in [("boxcox", shifted), ("yeojohnson", inc), ("mean_diff", inc), ("median_diff", inc)]:
    t = FeatureTransformer(kind).fit(values)
    z = t.transform(values)
    print(f"{kind:<12} params={ {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in t.params_.items()} } "
          f"round trip ok={round_trip_ok(values, t.inverse_transform(z))}")

log1p first values: [9.222466551774023, 8.955577146281511, None]
boxcox       params={'lambda': 0.3407} round trip ok=True
yeojohnson   params={'lambda': 0.3407} round trip ok=True
mean_diff    params={'mean': 6690.3986} round trip ok=True
median_diff  params={'median': 5400.0} round trip ok=True

What to read here:

  • params_ is what the fit learned: a lambda for the power transforms, a centre for the difference transforms. Fit it on the training column and reuse it on new data.
  • log1p keeps the missing value: the first three training incomes give 9.2225, 8.9556 and a missing value.
  • boxcox and yeojohnson both fit a lambda of 0.3407. For non-negative values, Yeo-Johnson equals Box-Cox of x + 1, so the two fits on this column must agree. The match is a consistency check, not a coincidence.
  • The difference transforms centre the column on the training mean (6690.3986) or median (5400.0). They move the centre only, not the shape.
  • Every round trip returns the original values, and the missing values sit in the same places. The check uses a tolerance of 1e-6, not exact equality.
  • Box-Cox and log transforms have a domain. A value outside it raises ValueError and names the first bad row; it is not silently replaced. That is why the snippet shifts the income before Box-Cox.

Next: the hand-off step fits the tree on the untransformed frame from step 5. A tree separates rows by thresholds on the order of values, so a monotone transform such as a log does not change which rows a split separates. The transforms in this step matter for models that use distances or linear coefficients.

items.title: 8. Hand the frame to the model
items.text:
xy turns the columns into the feature rows, the target, the feature names and the dtypes that a model needs. Step 5 already built the training and test frames with select_rows, so this step passes them straight to the tree. Keep dtypes and names with the rows so that the column order at prediction time is the one the tree saw.

from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree

tree = ModelTree(leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
                 max_depth=3, min_rows=100, prune="none")
tree.fit(tr["x"], tr["y"], dtypes=tr["dtypes"], col_names=tr["names"])
scores = tree.predict_proba(te["x"])
rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=te["y"], proba=scores)
print("test AUC:", round(rep["auc"], 4))
print("test log loss:", round(rep["logloss"], 4))

test AUC: 0.8194
test log loss: 0.1887

On the 30,000 test rows the tree reaches an AUC of 0.8194 and a log loss of 0.1887. The fit used the frame as it came out of step 5, with the 33,655 missing feature cells still in place. The tree routes them natively, so no imputation step is needed before this call. If a comparison model needs imputation, that step is a deliberate choice that belongs to that comparison, not to this frame.

items.title: Choose the preparation
items.text:
Models take categorical labels and missing predictors natively. The diagram shows the path from raw rows to the tree; the snippet below uses a categorical column with missing values and no separate encoder.

from mltreelib import ModelTree

x = [["north", 1.0], ["north", None], ["south", 1.0], ["south", None]] * 10
y = [1.0, 2.0, 9.0, 10.0] * 10
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=4, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x, y, dtypes=["categorical", "numeric"],
          col_names=["region", "amount"])
print(model.predict([["north", None], ["south", None]]))
print(model.splits())

[1.5, 9.5]
[{'col': 'region', 'threshold': 0.0, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 640.0}]

Use native categorical inputs for ModelTree. Use a separate encoder only when the downstream estimator or another workflow requires it, and fit it on training data only. Target-based encoders need leakage-safe training representations and an independently fitted evaluation pipeline. Missing-value behavior varies by operation. Test missing predictors, targets and unknown categories for the exact estimator before deployment.

  • Missing routing explains ModelTree routing.
  • Categorical encoders explains training leakage.
  • Data processing shows typed ingestion, summaries and time features.
  • Time series forecasting shows prior-day features and a time split.
  • Data API catalogs builders, encoders, transforms and the mltreelib.data helpers.

items.title: What remains
items.text: The existing references do not yet give a checked missing and unseen-value matrix for every model and encoder. They also need a single end-to-end example that carries a fitted schema through deployment. The schema helpers in step 3 capture and validate a schema, but this guide stops before scoring a new batch with a fitted model. In a checked two-category example, an unseen category routed differently from a missing value. This conflicts with the stated unseen-as-missing contract and is recorded as a product gap for investigation. A checked IndexMapper maps an unseen label to missing. In a separate check, OneHotEncoder mapped missing and unseen labels to all-zero vectors, CountEncoder mapped them to missing and zero respectively, and TargetEncoder mapped them to missing and the fitted prior.

items.title: Evaluate and monitor a model
items.text:
Path: Choose a baseline → Choose the split → Select metrics and costs → Tune on validation data → Report once on test data → Monitor outcomes and drift.

Task Start with Also check Regression MAE and RMSE against a mean or operational baseline Residuals, large errors, segments, time periods Classification Confusion matrix and precision/recall at a chosen threshold Probability calibration, PR curve, costs, subgroup outcomes Clustering Segment sizes, profiles and stability Out-of-sample assignment, usefulness and sensitivity to scaling Anomaly Reviewed precision at a fixed review budget Score drift, alert volume, missed cases when labels are available Survival Censoring-aware discrimination and calibration Risk sets and reliability at the chosen horizon Uplift Randomized held-out policy value Arm counts, uncertainty, cost and overlap

items.title: 1. A complete held-out example
items.text:
The data and metrics example uses the same raw mixed inputs for regression and classification. It generates 4,000 synthetic rows with a fixed seed: 2,000 for training, 1,000 for validation and 1,000 for test. It uses raw category labels and missing numeric values without encoding or imputation.

uv run python examples/guides/data_metrics_pathway.py

items.title: Regression: compare with a baseline
items.text: The script compares test MAE with a constant equal to the training outcome mean. Its numbers describe its own generated sample, so run it to see them. Use residual plots to look for error patterns rather than relying only on an average.

items.title: Classification: ranking, calibration and decisions
items.text:
The script chooses among four thresholds on validation data, using an illustrative cost that assigns three units to a missed event and one unit to a false alert. Run it for its selected threshold and test confusion matrix. The block below checks calibration on seeded synthetic data.

A precision–recall curve shows the tradeoff as the score threshold changes. Compare it with the positive event rate and the capacity of the review team. It does not establish calibration.

Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed event frequencies in bins. Small bins make the plot unstable. The 1,000 test rows come from a synthetic distribution; the plot alone does not establish calibration in production.

Use IsotonicCalibrator to fit a monotone mapping for binary event probabilities. Fit the mapping on validation or out-of-fold probabilities. Compare Brier scores on independent test rows. On this seeded sample the calibrated test Brier score is 0.1933, against 0.1946 for the raw probabilities: a small difference on 1,000 rows.

This snippet simulates a 4,000-row binary dataset, fits a binomial-logit tree on 2,000 rows, fits an IsotonicCalibrator on 1,000 validation rows, and compares raw vs calibrated Brier scores on the 1,000 test rows using MetricsReport.

import numpy as np
from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree
from mltreelib.calibration import IsotonicCalibrator

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
X = rng.normal(size=(4000, 4))
p_true = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.5 * X[:, 0] - X[:, 1])))
y = (rng.uniform(size=4000) < p_true).astype(int).tolist()
X = X.tolist()
X_train, y_train = X[:2000], y[:2000]
X_val, y_val = X[2000:3000], y[2000:3000]
X_test, y_test = X[3000:], y[3000:]

model = ModelTree(leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
                  max_depth=3, min_rows=50, prune="none")
model.fit(X_train, y_train, dtypes=["numeric"] * 4)

calibrator = IsotonicCalibrator.fit(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val))
raw = model.predict_proba(X_test)
calibrated = calibrator.predict(raw)
raw_rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=y_test, proba=raw)
cal_rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=y_test, proba=calibrated)
print(raw_rep["brier"], cal_rep["brier"])

0.19456565411850799 0.1932642638524234

What to read in the output: the two printed numbers are the held-out Brier scores before and after isotonic calibration; lower is better.

The confusion matrix describes decisions at one chosen threshold. Change the cost assumptions or capacity and repeat threshold selection on validation data. Keep the test set independent of that selection.

items.title: Inspect the tree
items.text:
The tree is rendered from ModelTree.to_dot(). Node conditions describe the fitted partitions. Check feature names, missing routing and leaf support before using them in a report. Categorical conditions can display internal codes, so check their meaning before sharing a rule. A prediction path does not establish the effect of an intervention.

Split importance summarizes gain used by the fitted tree. It is not a causal effect and does not measure every source of predictive value. The visualization guide shows how to select and render each view.

items.title: What remains
items.text:
The current metrics guide catalogs many report functions, but it does not provide a complete task-by-task evaluation workflow. Survival, uplift, clustering and anomaly examples still need validated task-specific evaluation and uncertainty examples. Check the API before assuming that a recommended metric is implemented by this package.

Metrics and plots · Metrics reference · Model pathways

items.title: Metrics, Diagnostics & Probability Calibration
items.text:
A model score without diagnostic verification is an operational liability. A high AUC can disguise severe probability miscalibration, and an acceptable test RMSE can hide heteroscedastic residual explosions or catastrophic drift.

mltreelib.Metrics and mltreelib.plots provide an evaluation and visualization engine implemented with pure numeric precision, independent of heavy visualization dependencies (matplotlib is an optional extra: pip install mltreelib[plotting]).

flowchart LR

    B -- "Classification / Risk" --> C["Discrimination\nROC AUC, PR AUC, KS Statistic"]
    B -- "Regression / Amounts" --> D["Loss Surface & Residuals\nRMSE, MAE, MedAE, Pinball Loss"]

    C --> E["Reliability Calibration\nDecile Brier Score & Hosmer-Lemeshow"]
    E --> F["Operational Triage\nCumulative Gain & Lift @ Budget"]
    F --> G["Stability & Drift\nPopulation Stability Index (PSI)"]

    D --> H["Heteroscedasticity\nResidual Variance vs Fitted"]
