items.title: 1. Multi-Panel Diagnostic Surface
items.text:
Every chart in mltreelib.plots operates on native Matplotlib Axes, allowing multi-metric dashboards in a single figure:

uv run python examples/guides/metrics_showcase.py

Next: section 2 lists the classification charts to place on these axes, starting with ROC, PR and calibration.

items.title: 2. Classification Diagnostics & Probability Calibration
items.text:
In credit triage, fraud detection, and medical diagnosis, ranking alone is insufficient. Underwriters make decisions based on expected dollar loss, which demands calibrated probabilities \(P(y=1 \mid \mathbf{x})\).

Diagnostic Chart Core Question Answered Failure Mode Diagnosed plot_roc / plot_pr Can the model rank positive instances ahead of negatives? High ROC with low PR indicates severe false-positive flooding under class imbalance. plot_calibration Does a predicted score of 0.20 correspond to exactly 20% empirical event rate? S-shaped curve indicates over-confidence; inverted curve indicates mis-specified link function. plot_ks What is the maximum separation distance between default and non-default distributions? Identifies the optimal cutoff threshold \(\tau^*\) maximizing operational divergence. plot_double_lift When comparing Model A vs Model B, which model captures more true events across deciles? Reveals regions where a challenger model outperforms a production champion. plot_psi Did the score distribution shift between training (baseline) and inference (current)? PSI \(> 0.25\) signals severe population drift requiring immediate model retraining.

items.title: Visual Examples
items.text:
Reliability Calibration Curve Double-Lift Model Comparison

Next: section 3 covers the regression branch, which swaps the probability charts from section 2 for residual charts drawn on the same Axes.

items.title: 3. Regression & Residual Diagnostics
items.text:
For continuous pricing, demand forecasting, and risk models:

Diagnostic Chart Core Question Answered Failure Mode Diagnosed plot_residuals Are residual errors mean-zero and homoscedastic across all response levels? Funnel-shaped residual spread signals heteroscedasticity, calling for gain="heteroscedastic" or Tweedie. plot_importance Which features drove the split deviance reduction across the tree? Over-reliance on single surrogate features or leakage columns. plot_breakdown Why did this individual loan applicant receive this exact predicted rate? DALE-style waterfall attribution decomposed by tree split paths.

Next: section 4 runs the classification side in one script, computing the ROC, PR, Brier, KS and PSI values from section 2 and plotting calibration and double-lift charts, without the regression charts from section 3.

items.title: 4. Code Example: Computing the Full Metrics Suite
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import Metrics, MetricsReport, plots
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Generate realistic credit default probabilities and observed labels
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_cases = 1000

# True baseline event probability
true_risk = rng.beta(a=0.8, b=4.0, size=n_cases)
y_true = rng.binomial(1, true_risk).tolist()

# Predicted risk probabilities from champion model and noisy challenger
y_prob_champ = np.clip(true_risk + rng.normal(0, 0.08, n_cases), 0.001, 0.999).tolist()
y_prob_chal = np.clip(true_risk + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n_cases), 0.001, 0.999).tolist()

# 2. Compute Discrimination and Calibration Metrics
rep = MetricsReport("classification", y_true=y_true, proba=y_prob_champ)

print("Champion Model Performance:")
print(f"  ROC-AUC: {rep['auc']:.4f}")
print(f"  Average Precision (PR-AUC): {rep['average_precision']:.4f}")
print(f"  Brier Reliability Score: {rep['brier']:.4f}")
print(f"  Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS): {rep['ks']:.4f} (Score @ KS cutoff = {rep['score_at_ks']:.3f})")

# 3. Population Stability Index (PSI) Drift Check against subsequent test cohort
metrics = Metrics()
y_prob_subsequent = np.clip(true_risk * 1.15 + rng.normal(0, 0.08, n_cases), 0.001, 0.999).tolist()
psi_res = metrics.stability_index(y_prob_champ, y_prob_subsequent, 10)
psi_val = psi_res["psi"]
print(f"  Population Stability Index (PSI): {psi_val:.4f} ({'Stable' if psi_val < 0.10 else 'Shift Detected'})")

# 4. Render Calibration and Double Lift Curves Side-by-Side
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
plots.plot_calibration(y_true, y_prob_champ, ax=ax1)
plots.plot_double_lift(y_true, y_prob_chal, y_prob_champ, ax=ax2)
plt.tight_layout()
# In a script or notebook, call plt.show() to display the figure.
plt.close(fig)

Champion Model Performance:
  ROC-AUC: 0.7700
  Average Precision (PR-AUC): 0.4528
  Brier Reliability Score: 0.1196
  Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS): 0.4392 (Score @ KS cutoff = 0.175)
  Population Stability Index (PSI): 0.0273 (Stable)

Related Guides

  • Why Credit Scoring Needs Glass-Box Trees for asymmetric cost optimization using KS cutoffs.
  • Model Inspection & Quinlan Rules for white-box split path audits.

items.title: Model Inspection, Quinlan Rules & Explainable Stumps
items.text:
In regulated lending, healthcare, and safety-critical engineering, deploying black-box models is prohibited or legally risky. Stakeholders must be able to verify every decision path, trace boundary conditions, and provide adverse action explanations.

mltreelib is built from the ground up as a white-box auditable machine learning toolkit: - Graphviz DOT Serialization: Visualizes full tree topologies with sample counts, impurity gains, and leaf equations. - Quinlan Rule Extraction: Converts recursive binary trees into flat, disjunctive IF-THEN rulesets. - Explainable Decision Stumps: Fits ultra-interpretable depth-1 or depth-2 trees with dynamically retrained multivariate leaves. - k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) Leaf Adjustments: Blends global rule boundaries with local neighborhood smoothing.

    B --> C["Graphviz DOT Export\ntree.to_dot()"]

    B --> E["Explainable Stumps\nSingle Split + High-Capacity Leaf"]
    B --> F["Local k-NN Adjustments\ntree.predict_knn_blend(k=5)"]

    C --> G["Auditable SVG Diagram\nExact Node Thresholds & Fallbacks"]
    D --> H["Production Scorecard Rules\nIF Age > 28 THEN y = β*x"]
    E --> I["Maximum Transparency\nZero Black-Box Ensembling"]
    F --> J["Continuous Interpolation\nEliminates Step Artifacts"]

items.title: 1. Graphviz DOT Export and Rule Extraction
items.text:
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# 1. Generate realistic industrial concrete mixture data
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_batches = 600

cement = rng.uniform(200.0, 500.0, n_batches)
water = rng.uniform(140.0, 220.0, n_batches)
age = rng.choice([7, 14, 28, 90], size=n_batches)

# Compressive strength with physical non-linear interaction
y = 0.08 * cement - 0.15 * water + 0.35 * age + rng.normal(0, 3.0, n_batches)

X = np.column_stack([cement, water, age])
feature_names = ["Cement", "Water", "Age"]

# 2. Fit white-box ModelTree with linear leaves
tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", max_depth=2, min_rows=40)
tree.fit(X, y.tolist(), col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Export Graphviz DOT format for visual auditing
dot_str = tree.to_dot()
Path("concrete_tree.dot").write_text(dot_str)
print("Exported Graphviz DOT string (length:", len(dot_str), "chars)")

# 4. Extract Quinlan-style IF-THEN rules
ruleset = tree.extract_rules()
print(f"\nExtracted {len(ruleset.rules)} Global Decision Rules:")
for r in ruleset.rules:
    conditions_str = " AND ".join(r.conditions)
    print(f"  RULE #{r.id} (Cover: {r.cover} samples, Confidence: {r.confidence:.2f}):")
    print(f"    IF {conditions_str}")
    print(f"    THEN Leaf #{r.leaf_id} prediction = {r.prediction:.2f}")

Exported Graphviz DOT string (length: 817 chars)

Extracted 4 Global Decision Rules:
  RULE #1 (Cover: 243 samples, Confidence: 0.95):
    IF Cement > 341.9010 AND Age <= 28.0000
    THEN Leaf #1 prediction = 11.64
  RULE #2 (Cover: 202 samples, Confidence: 0.95):
    IF Cement <= 341.9010 AND Age <= 28.0000
    THEN Leaf #0 prediction = 0.09
  RULE #3 (Cover: 93 samples, Confidence: 0.95):
    IF Cement <= 369.0130 AND Age > 28.0000
    THEN Leaf #2 prediction = 26.86
  RULE #4 (Cover: 62 samples, Confidence: 0.95):
    IF Cement > 369.0130 AND Age > 28.0000
    THEN Leaf #3 prediction = 39.23

items.title: Production Deployment Checklist
items.text:
1. Inputs Contract: Record exact column names, data types, and unit scales.
  2. Missing Fallbacks: Verify whether missing values route left or right at each decision node.
  3. Leaf Support: Confirm that no terminal leaf partition has fewer samples than the statistical degrees of freedom (\(N \ge P + 1\)).
  4. Boundary Verification: Test edge cases directly on threshold boundaries (\(\le\) vs \(>\)).

Next: section 2 fits a single split with retrained linear leaves on the same data, reusing X, y and the feature names from section 1.
path: 10. Inspect a model: rules and stumps

items.title: 2. Explainable Stumps with Dynamic Leaf Retraining
items.text:
Can a single split (a depth-1 decision stump) deliver competitive accuracy when paired with high-capacity leaves?

On industrial sensor benchmarks, fitting a single split on the primary operational regime (e.g. Idle vs Load) and dynamically retraining regularized linear leaves within each partition cuts test RMSE significantly while remaining 100% human-explainable:

# Depth-1 explainable stump with OLS linear leaves
stump = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=1,      # Single split partition
    min_rows=50,
)
stump.fit(X, y.tolist(), col_names=feature_names)

split = stump.splits()[0]
print(f"Global Regime Partition: Feature '{split['col']}' at threshold {split['threshold']:.2f}")

Global Regime Partition: Feature 'Age' at threshold 28.00

Next: section 3 goes back to the full depth-2 tree from section 1, not the stump, because the k-NN smoothing runs on that fitted tree.
path: 10. Inspect a model: rules and stumps

items.title: 3. Cubist-Style k-NN Leaf Neighbor Adjustments
items.text:
When moving across split boundaries, predictions from pure decision trees can exhibit sharp discontinuities. mltreelib implements Quinlan's Cubist sample neighbor adjustment via tree.predict_adjusted(X):

# Predict with Cubist-style k-NN sample neighbor smoothing
y_smooth_pred = tree.predict_adjusted(X[:5])
print("Smoothed k-NN Neighbor Adjusted Predictions:", [round(v, 2) for v in y_smooth_pred])

Smoothed k-NN Neighbor Adjusted Predictions: [19.74, 3.83, 10.12, 6.66, 0.11]

Related Reference Guides

  • Dynamic Leaf Retraining & Stumps.
  • Model Review Checklist for enterprise deployment.

items.title: Get the real datasets
items.text:
Clone the repository and run the examples from its root. The examples use pandas and matplotlib. Use the repository checkout for examples that import a helper from the examples directory. Install Graphviz if you want to regenerate the optional fitted-tree diagrams.

uv sync
uv run python -c "import pandas, matplotlib, mltreelib"

For an OpenML source below, open its dataset page and download the Parquet file. The parquet_url field in the OpenML data description gives its direct location. Save it under the listed path. These files are excluded from Git.

For the full TabArena collection, see the dataset manifest.

items.title: 1. Secondary example: bank churn
items.text:
Use OpenML 46911 at datasets/Bank_Customer_Churn.parquet to compare three interfaces on the same mixed feature schema. The script fits a churn classifier, a cluster tree and an anomaly tree. Only the classifier uses churn labels.

uv run python examples/guides/real_data_workflow.py

This split uses 6,000 training, 2,000 validation and 2,000 test rows. The classifier's test Brier score is 0.1215, compared with 0.1639 for a constant training-rate prediction. The unsupervised outputs describe this customer table. A churn outcome cannot validate an anomaly ranking or determine whether a segment is actionable.

items.title: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices
items.text: Predict the listed price of a diamond from its measurements and grading labels. Compare a simple baseline and two tree configurations. Inspect the largest errors before using the score for a pricing decision.

items.title: 1. Get the data and make the split
items.text:
Dataset.load("diamonds", target="price") reads the OpenML diamonds dataset 46923 (53,940 records) and marks price as the target. The input includes numeric measurements such as carat and raw labels for cut, color and clarity. Keep those labels as strings; the tree routes categories natively.

Take a seeded 8,000-row subset, then split it into 6,000 training rows and 2,000 held-out test rows. A production pricing study needs a split that respects listing date, seller and repeated items where available.

Next: fit mean-leaf and linear-leaf trees at depth 4 on the 6,000 training rows, score the 2,000 test rows with MetricsReport, and print summary() and leaf_summary(0).

items.title: 2. Fit, score and inspect the tree
3. Interpret the errors
items.text:
Prediction Test RMSE Test MAE Global training mean 3,926.26 — Mean leaves (depth 4) 1,248.40 690.52 Linear leaves (depth 4) 1,182.90 598.75

The left panel summarizes error with RMSE. The right panel shows prediction minus observed price. Look for systematic underpricing below the zero line and overpricing above it. Review residuals by cut, price band and support. A shallow linear tree can follow a trend inside a leaf. Check for extrapolation, collinearity and sudden changes at split boundaries before relying on that trend.

Use summary() and leaf_summary(i) to inspect support and coefficients, and splits() to review named feature conditions. Category conditions can display internal codes. Keep that mapping available before showing a rule to a reviewer.

Next: repeat the comparison on synthetic data with raw category labels and 15% missing numeric inputs, because the real training columns used so far had no missing values.

items.title: 4. Repeat the comparison with missing inputs
items.text:
The regression comparison first generates 5,000 records with raw category labels and 15% missing numeric inputs. It fits four ModelTree configurations on 3,000 rows, selects one using 1,000 validation rows, then checks it on 1,000 separate test rows. The test set contains 169 missing numeric values. No imputation or categorical encoder is applied.

uv run python examples/guides/regression_real_and_synthetic.py
Synthetic configuration Validation RMSE Mean leaves, depth 2 3.594 Mean leaves, depth 4 2.704 Linear leaves, depth 2 2.770 Linear leaves, depth 4 2.633

For this seed and simulated data, linear leaves at depth 4 had the lowest validation RMSE. Its test RMSE was 2.933, against 6.385 for a training-mean baseline. This chooses among four settings on one synthetic problem. It does not establish the best model for other datasets.

The same configuration then fits 6,000 rows from the real OpenML diamonds dataset 46923 and predicts 2,000 separate rows. The data has 53,940 total records. Download its parquet file to datasets/diamonds.parquet; see the dataset manifest. The example needs pandas, pyarrow and matplotlib.

On the fixed random split in the block above, test RMSE was 1,576 for linear leaves, 1,613 for mean leaves and 3,926 for the training-mean baseline (the same numbers as the table in section 3). These values use the dataset's price units and describe this split, not a benchmark result. The block reports RMSE only; add MAE in your own run if you need it. The selected real training columns contained no missing values, so the synthetic check supplies the missing-data exercise.

The real tree splits on named size measurements, including x and y, and exposes leaf support and coefficients. Inspect the feature definitions and leaf sample sizes before drawing business conclusions. Category values in fitted structures can appear as internal codes. Coefficients and paths describe the prediction model; they do not establish what happens if a business changes a feature.

For more on local slopes and the fair comparison setup, see the model tree regression reference.

items.title: Prepare a model for prediction
items.text: Record the fitted model's prediction contract, then save the model and check predictions after reloading.

items.title: 1. Record the prediction contract
items.text:
Item Record before handing off the model Decision Outcome, units, prediction horizon and when features are available. Inputs Feature names, order, types, units and allowed values. Missingness Which fields can be missing and how the fitted model routes them. Categories Training vocabulary and how the workflow handles an unseen value. Output Prediction kind, scale, class ordering and any decision threshold. Evidence Training data period, split, baseline, metrics and known model gaps. 
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Ingestion Client / API Gateway
    participant Guard as Schema Guard & Validator
    participant Normalizer as Sentinel Normalizer (None / NaN)
    participant Core as mltreelib-core Tree Route
    participant Leaf as Local Leaf Solver (Linear / GLM)
    participant Decision as Threshold & Policy Post-Processor

    Client->>Guard: Submit Raw Record (JSON Payload)
    Note over Guard: Check required keys, field order, and valid types
    Guard->>Normalizer: Verified Named Features
    Note over Normalizer: Treat unobserved keys, NaNs, and unseen category levels as missing
    Normalizer->>Core: Fast Vector Traversal [x1, x2, ..., xk]
    Note over Core: Traverse internal split nodes using learned missing_left and surrogates
    Core->>Leaf: Deliver to Terminal Leaf Node
    Note over Leaf: Evaluate local linear model: y_hat = b0 + sum(bj * xj)
    Leaf->>Decision: Continuous Raw Score / Probability
    Note over Decision: Apply calibrated threshold (e.g. p >= 0.20 -> Review Queue)
    Decision-->>Client: Final Actionable Prediction & Audit Path

ModelTree accepts raw categorical strings and missing predictor values. Preserve the fitted feature order. A row-based input does not carry column names at prediction time, so your application needs to check the schema before constructing rows.

Next: section 2 applies that contract to a fitted model: it checks the field names against the fitted schema and builds each row in the fitted order.

items.title: 2. Fit and predict with named records
items.text:
The following example checks names before converting a record to the fitted order. It passes category labels and missing values directly to the tree.

from mltreelib import ModelTree

names = ["region", "volume"]
dtypes = ["categorical", "numeric"]
x_train = [["north", 1.0], ["north", None], ["south", 1.0], ["south", None]] * 10
y_train = [1.0, 2.0, 9.0, 10.0] * 10
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=4, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=names, dtypes=dtypes)

record = {"region": "north", "volume": None}
if set(record) != set(names):
    raise ValueError("Input fields do not match the model schema")
row = [record[name] for name in names]
print("Prediction:", model.predict([row])[0])

Prediction: 1.5

Check types, units, ranges and batch sizes at the application boundary as well. The short example checks field names only. It does not provide a complete serving validator.

Next: section 3 saves the fitted model and reloads it, then checks that predictions still match the in-process result from section 2.

items.title: 3. Persist a fitted model
items.text:
ModelTree.save() writes a versioned UTF-8 JSON file. ModelTree.load() restores the fitted tree, including the state used for inference.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

expected = model.predict([row])
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "model.json"
    model.save(path)
    restored = ModelTree.load(path)
    assert restored.predict([row]) == expected

Use model.to_json() and ModelTree.from_json(text) for JSON strings. Use model.to_bytes() and ModelTree.from_bytes(data) when the transport requires bytes. The bytes contain the same JSON encoded in UTF-8. Standard Python pickle uses the same model state.

import pickle

assert ModelTree.from_json(model.to_json()).predict([row]) == expected
assert ModelTree.from_bytes(model.to_bytes()).predict([row]) == expected
assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(model)).predict([row]) == expected

Persistence rejects Python callbacks in the model configuration. Keep the package version with each artifact and check predictions before upgrading the serving environment. Use extract_rules() for rule inspection and load pickle data only from trusted sources.

The artifact contains the training rows and targets retained for neighbor adjustments. Apply the same access controls you use for training data.

Next: section 4 lists the release checks, starting with a comparison of the in-process prediction against the intended serving path, which needs the reloaded model from section 3.

items.title: 4. Checks before release
items.text:
1. Compare a known in-process prediction with the intended serving path.
  2. Check missing values, unseen categories, invalid types and changed column order.
  3. Check the output scale and confirm the decision threshold uses independent validation data.
  4. Record the model and package versions, data period and evaluation results.
  5. Monitor input missingness, category changes, output distributions and observed outcomes.

The following gaps were reproduced in the current worktree and are tracked for investigation:

  • A short or extra-long row was accepted in one test. Do not assume the model rejects a schema mismatch.
  • An unseen category routed differently from a missing category in a tested tree, despite the stated unseen-as-missing rule.
  • break_down rejected a raw string category in a tested row, although predict accepted it.

Do not present the checks above as complete deployment coverage. See the data guide, evaluation guide, and documentation audit for further work.

Next: section 5 checks predictions on either side of a split threshold, which the release checks above do not cover, before a split is turned into an executable rule.

items.title: 5. Check split boundaries
items.text: The DOT export in the checked build labels numeric branches as < and >=. In a one-feature reproduction with a threshold of zero, the fitted tree routed zero with lower values. It routed positive values to the other leaf. Use the fitted model to check predictions below, at, and above a threshold before translating a diagram into executable rules.

items.title: Numerical reproducibility
items.text:
Results are computed in IEEE 754 double precision and are reproducible to about 12 significant digits on the same platform, build, BLAS/LAPACK and thread settings. The test suite checks this at a relative tolerance of 1e-12. We make no guarantee of bit-identical output across operating systems, CPUs, BLAS or LAPACK implementations, thread counts or library versions; differences in the last digits are expected. Randomized procedures are reproducible given the same seed and RNG kind; the seed-to-stream mapping may change across versions.

  • Same inputs, same model file. A saved model (to_json, to_bytes) holds no wall-clock timings, so refitting on identical data and settings on the same machine gives a byte-identical file. Total fit time is a diagnostic and is not part of the saved model.
  • Compare numbers, not printed text. When you check a result against a stored one, use a relative tolerance (for example abs(a - b) <= 1e-12 * max(1.0, abs(b))), not string equality.
  • Missing values are part of the data. Results with missing values follow the same rule; nothing is imputed.

items.title: Survival trees in Python: FLCHAIN mortality follow-up
items.text: Use baseline measurements to estimate survival at one, three and five years. The event is death. If follow-up ends first, the row is right-censored.

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the evaluation
items.text:
The survival package's FLCHAIN cohort contains 7,874 people and right-censored follow-up. futime is follow-up in days and death=1 records a death. We use age, sex, kappa, lambda and creatinine as predictors. We exclude chapter, which describes cause of death and is unavailable at prediction time. Creatinine is missing for 943 of the 5,500 training records and 407 of the 2,374 test records; values enter the tree without imputation.

The snippet below gets the file with dataset_path("flchain_rdatasets"). It downloads the FLCHAIN CSV from Rdatasets on first use, caches it under ~/.cache/mltreelib/datasets/ (or MLTREELIB_DATA_DIR) and checks SHA-256 a96bcc58addb4c127e5012c5974aec8c7daf66123ddb104f309a78f158daa563. Run the shared real-data evaluation script.

uv run python examples/guides/real_survival_uplift.py survival

Next: fit survival trees on the training rows defined in step 1, keeping each follow-up time paired with its death flag.

items.title: 2. Fit leaf survival curves
items.text:
futime is the time to death or last observation. Keep the event flag next to it. For example, someone censored at day 600 survived beyond day 365, but their status at day 1,095 is unknown. Do not replace the censored outcome with an event at day 600.

flowchart TD
    subgraph TimeToEvent["Right-Censored Follow-up Mechanics (T_i, delta_i)"]
        direction LR
        Patient["Patient Baseline\n(Age, Biomarkers)"] --> FollowUp["Follow-up Period\n[0, T_i]"]
        FollowUp --> Event{"Did Event Occur Before\nEnd of Study / Dropout?"}

Run this Python block from the repository root. The evaluation helpers are defined in the block.

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
from collections import Counter

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree, dataset_path
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

def censor_km(times, events):
    """Censoring survival G(t), estimated from training observations."""
    counts = Counter(times)
    censored = Counter(t for t, event in zip(times, events) if not event)
    at_risk, steps, probs, g = len(times), [], [], 1.0
    for t in sorted(counts):
        g *= 1 - censored[t] / at_risk
        steps.append(t); probs.append(g); at_risk -= counts[t]
    def g_at(t, left=False):
        i = (bisect_left if left else bisect_right)(steps, t) - 1
        return 1.0 if i < 0 else probs[i]
    return g_at

def brier(times, events, predictions, horizon, censor):
    """IPCW Brier score at one horizon."""
    g_h = censor(horizon)
    total = 0.0
    for t, e, pred in zip(times, events, predictions):
        if t <= horizon and e:
            total += pred ** 2 / censor(t, left=True)
        elif t > horizon:
            total += (1 - pred) ** 2 / g_h
    return total / len(times)

df = pd.read_csv(dataset_path("flchain_rdatasets"))
features = ["age", "sex", "kappa", "lambda", "creatinine"]
ds = Dataset(
    {k: df[k].tolist() for k in [*features, "futime", "death"]},
    time="futime",
    event="death",
    features=features,
    name="flchain",
)

# Seeded split: 5,500 rows train, the remaining rows test
train, test = ds.split(test_size=ds.n_rows - 5500, seed=2026)
t_train, e_train = train.time, train.event
t_test, e_test = test.time, test.event
grid = [365.0, 1095.0, 1825.0]
censor = censor_km(t_train, e_train)
print(f"Test rows {test.n_rows}: deaths {sum(e_test)}, censored {len(e_test) - sum(e_test)}")
for horizon in grid:
    print(f"Horizon {horizon:.0f}: test at risk {sum(t > horizon for t in t_test)}, censoring survival {censor(horizon):.4f}")
miss_train = train.missing()["per_column"]["creatinine"]["n_missing"]
miss_test = test.missing()["per_column"]["creatinine"]["n_missing"]
print(f"Creatinine missing: {miss_train} training rows, {miss_test} test rows")

for depth in (0, 2):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf_family="survival", max_depth=depth,
                     min_rows=100, prune="none")
    tree.fit(train)
    curves = tree.predict(test, kind="survival", times=grid)
    risk = tree.predict(test, kind="risk")
    rep = MetricsReport(
        "survival", durations=t_test, events=e_test, risk=risk,
        surv_curves=curves, times=grid,
    )
    print("depth", depth, "first survival curve", curves[0], "harrell_c", round(rep["harrell_c"], 4))
    for j, horizon in enumerate(grid):
        print(horizon, brier(t_test, e_test, [curve[j] for curve in curves],
                             horizon, censor))
    print(tree.splits()[:1])

The example uses a seeded random split and estimates the marginal censoring distribution from training data only. A marginal censoring model assumes censoring is independent of the outcome in the relevant population. This observational cohort and one split do not establish clinical usefulness. Check conditional censoring, calibration, discrimination and uncertainty with the intended deployment population before interpreting the comparison.

Next: repeat the Brier comparison on synthetic data where the true survival probability is known, because real individual survival probabilities are not observed.

items.title: 4. Controlled check with synthetic truth
items.text:
The survival and uplift evaluation script simulates 5,000 people. It fits 3,000 and evaluates 2,000 independent records, including 1,391 observed events and 609 censored observations. A global survival model provides the baseline.

uv run python examples/guides/survival_uplift_evaluation.py
Horizon Tree IPCW Brier Global baseline IPCW Brier 10 0.2417 0.2509 20 0.2000 0.2102 30 0.1226 0.1316

The Brier score compares predicted survival probabilities with event outcomes at a fixed horizon. Inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW) account for records censored before that horizon. Lower is better. This simulation uses the known censoring distribution. Real data requires a justified censoring model estimated without using the test outcomes for model selection, adequate follow-up, and positive censoring survival at each evaluated horizon. Conditional censoring requires appropriate conditional weights; a single global curve can be wrong.

The script also compares predictions with the known synthetic survival probability. Real individual survival probabilities are not observed. Check discrimination and horizon-specific calibration on real held-out data, with uncertainty and risk-set sizes. This example implements the evaluation calculation locally; it does not claim an IPCW metric API exists in the package. See Graf et al. (1999).

Next: the last step extends the single-event setup to several causes, because follow-up data often has more than one way for the event to occur and the single-event comparison above does not describe that.

items.title: 5. Competing risks and multi-cause endpoints
items.text:
When subjects can experience mutually exclusive event causes (e.g. disease relapse vs treatment-related mortality), treating competing events as ordinary censoring violates the independent censoring assumption and overestimates cumulative incidence by 20–50%.

mltreelib implements native competing risks trees: - Split Criterion: Gray's subdistribution log-rank test (gain="gray", target_cause=j) maintaining subjects who experienced competing events in the risk set. - Leaf Estimators: Aalen-Johansen multi-state estimator guaranteeing the probability simplex identity: \(\sum_{c=1}^J \hat{F}_c(t) + \hat{S}(t) = 1.0\). - Unified Prediction API: tree.predict(X, kind="cif", times=times, cause=1) and tree.predict(X, kind="risk"). - Validation: MetricsReport("competing_risks", ...) computing cause-specific Harrell's C, Uno's IPCW C-index, and time-dependent Brier scores.

from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree

# Events: 0 = censored, 1 = relapse (primary), 2 = toxicity (competing)
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=25, gain="gray", target_cause=1)
tree.fit(X_train, (durations_train, events_train))

# Evaluate Aalen-Johansen CIF at specified horizons
times = [2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0]
cif_cause1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=times, cause=1)
cif_cause2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=times, cause=2)

# Compute full IPCW competing risks performance report
rep = MetricsReport(
    "competing_risks",
    durations=durations_test,
    events=events_test,
    cif_curves={1: cif_cause1, 2: cif_cause2},
    times=times,
)
print(rep)

items.title: Subject IDs and grouped observations
items.text:
When a clinical dataset carries a subject identifier or clinic group (id_col or group_col), pass it to fit so the tree never splits on an identifier (train_ids=False, train_groups=False by default). You can still pass the full table to leaf_samples(x, id_col=...) to list which subjects fall into each leaf, or set train_ids=True / train_groups=True only when you intend the model to split on them.

items.title: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment
items.text: Decide whether to send a campaign email to everyone, a subset, or nobody. Compare incremental visits on a randomized holdout.

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the evaluation
items.text:
The Hillstrom email experiment randomly assigned 64,000 customers to a men's email, women's email or no email. This example compares women's email versus no email, using a website visit within two weeks as the outcome. It excludes the men's arm and uses only pre-treatment features. A visit is not a purchase or profit.

dataset_path("hillstrom_email") downloads the CSV from the publisher's MineThatData page on first use and caches it under ~/.cache/mltreelib/datasets/ (or MLTREELIB_DATA_DIR). The publisher's HTTPS endpoint fails certificate validation, so the file is fetched over plain HTTP and checked against SHA-256 0e5893329d8b93cefecc571777672028290ab69865718020c78c7284f291aece.

uv run python examples/guides/real_survival_uplift.py uplift

Next: fit a causal tree on the randomized training rows from step 1, and use the validation rows to choose the email threshold while the test outcomes stay sealed.

This snippet loads the Hillstrom CSV, wraps it in a Dataset with outcome="visit" and treatment="treat", and makes a stratified 60% / 20% / 20% split (train, val, test). It fits an honest causal tree at max_depth=4 (min_rows=250, prune="none", honesty=True, seed=42). Note that the causal leaf is always a difference of means (\(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0\)) whatever the leaf setting (leaf="linear" produces the same leaf estimates under gain="causal"). It then calls uplift_threshold on val to pick the score cutoff and prints MetricsReport("uplift", ...) on test.

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import MetricsReport, ModelTree, dataset_path, uplift_threshold
from mltreelib.data import Dataset

df = pd.read_csv(dataset_path("hillstrom_email"))
df = df[df["segment"].isin(["Womens E-Mail", "No E-Mail"])].copy()
df["treat"] = (df["segment"] == "Womens E-Mail").astype(int)
features = ["recency", "history", "mens", "womens", "newbie", "zip_code", "channel"]

ds = Dataset(
    {k: df[k].tolist() for k in [*features, "treat", "visit"]},
    outcome="visit",
    treatment="treat",
    features=features,
    name="hillstrom_women",
)
train, val, test = ds.split(val_size=0.2, test_size=0.2, stratify=True, seed=2026)
print(f"Rows: train {train.n_rows}, validation {val.n_rows}, test {test.n_rows}")

tree = ModelTree(
    gain="causal", leaf="mean", max_depth=4, min_rows=250,
    prune="none", honesty=True, seed=42,
)
tree.fit(train)

val_scores = tree.predict(val, kind="uplift")
threshold = uplift_threshold(val.y, val.treatment, val_scores)
test_scores = tree.predict(test, kind="uplift")
rep = MetricsReport(
    "uplift",
    y_true=test.y,
    treatment=test.treatment,
    tau_pred=test_scores,
    threshold=threshold,
)
print(rep)

items.title: 3. Interpret the held-out results
items.text:
The stratified seeded split contains 25,615 training, 8,539 validation and 8,539 test rows. An honest causal tree at depth 4 ranks customers. uplift_threshold selects the policy threshold (-0.01564) on validation data, and MetricsReport estimates incremental visits on the randomized test set. This example assumes zero treatment cost because campaign costs are not in the data.

Test policy Selected Treated / control Incremental visits per eligible customer Approximate 95% interval Validation-selected policy 8,296 4,158 / 4,138 0.05281 0.03901 to 0.06662 Treat all 8,539 4,278 / 4,261 0.05314 0.03914 to 0.06714 Treat none 0 0 / 0 0 —

The validation-selected policy emails 8,296 of the 8,539 test customers. It yields 0.05281 incremental visits per eligible customer (95% CI 0.03901 to 0.06662), compared with 0.05314 (95% CI 0.03914 to 0.06714) for treat-all. With overlapping confidence intervals and a lower point estimate, this run supplies no evidence that targeting improves on treat-all at zero treatment cost. The interval is a normal approximation conditional on the selected population and excludes model-selection uncertainty. The data is from a historical campaign; repeat evaluation in a new experiment, include costs and use the outcome the business actually values before applying a policy.

Next: check the same kind of policy comparison on a simulated trial, because the Hillstrom data cannot show both potential outcomes for each customer.

items.title: 4. Controlled check with synthetic truth
items.text:
The survival and uplift evaluation script simulates a randomized trial. It uses 3,000 training, 1,000 validation and 2,000 independent test observations. It selects a threshold on validation data and evaluates the fixed policy on test data. The example assigns a treatment cost of 0.5 outcome units per treated person.

uv run python examples/guides/survival_uplift_evaluation.py
Test policy Selected Treated / control among selected Estimated net outcome per person Selected policy 967 471 / 496 0.7072 Treat all 2,000 972 / 1,028 -0.0478 Treat none 0 0 / 0 0

Within the selected subgroup, the script compares observed treated and control outcomes. It subtracts the cost and multiplies by the selected fraction to report value per person in the whole test population. The selected policy's approximate 95% interval is [0.6438, 0.7706]. It uses a normal approximation conditional on the selected fraction; it does not include model-selection uncertainty. Randomized assignment and independent test data support this comparison. Check arm counts and use a suitable uncertainty method for the actual design.

Synthetic truth is available here: the selected policy's true net value is 0.7252 per person and PEHE is 0.2347. Real records do not reveal both potential outcomes, so individual-effect error and PEHE cannot be calculated directly from ordinary real-world outcomes. For real-world evaluation, MetricsReport("uplift", ...) and uplift_threshold(...) provide the policy table and decile breakdown directly.

Next: the worked example also uses a simulation with a known effect, to check numerical effect recovery, which real Hillstrom outcomes cannot provide.

items.title: 5. Worked example: recovering a known treatment effect
items.text:
Use simulation to check numerical effect recovery. The Hillstrom sections above show how to evaluate a real randomized policy when individual effects are unknown.

Standard machine learning models optimize predictive accuracy: \(\hat{Y} = E[Y | X]\). In decision sciences, personalized medicine, and targeted marketing, the central quantity is not outcome prediction but intervention effect: $\(\tau(x) = E[Y | X=x, W=1] - E[Y | X=x, W=0]\)$

ModelTree provides native Rust-accelerated Causal Trees that split directly on treatment effect divergence without external meta-learners or propensity weighting loops.

Script: - benchmarks/suites/causal_benchmark.py (python3 benchmarks/suites/causal_benchmark.py)
