items.title: correlation_filter
items.text:
correlation_filter(result: 'Mapping[str, Any]', cutoff: 'float' = 0.9) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Greedy caret findCorrelation rule on a :func:correlation_matrix result.

Repeatedly takes the pair with the largest absolute correlation above cutoff and drops the column with the larger mean absolute correlation to the remaining columns (ties drop the later column in input order). Stops when no remaining pair exceeds the cutoff. None entries are ignored.

Args: result: dict with names and a square matrix (as returned by :func:correlation_matrix). cutoff: absolute correlation above which a pair is considered redundant.

Returns: dict with keys: drop: dropped names, in the order they were dropped. kept: remaining names, in input order. pairs: one dict per decision, {"a", "b", "corr"} with the two names in input order and the signed correlation of that pair.

Example: >>> res = {"names": ["a", "b"], "matrix": [[1.0, 0.95], [0.95, 1.0]]} >>> correlation_filter(res, cutoff=0.9)["drop"] ['b']

items.title: correlation_matrix
items.text:
correlation_matrix(columns: 'Any', method: 'str' = 'pearson') -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Pairwise correlation between numeric columns on pairwise-complete rows.

A row counts for a pair only when both values are finite numbers. Spearman is Pearson on average ranks, with the ranks taken over the pair's rows.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to values (or a table accepted by the data helpers). method: "pearson" or "spearman".

Returns: dict with keys: names: numeric column names, in input order. matrix: symmetric list of lists of float or None. Correlation is None when the pair has fewer than 3 rows or a zero variance. The diagonal is 1.0 when the column has at least 2 observed values and non-zero variance. n_pairs: symmetric list of lists of int, rows used per pair (diagonal: observed count of the column). skipped: non-numeric column names (strings or booleans), in input order. method: the method used.

Raises: ValueError: if method is not supported or columns differ in length.

Example: >>> r = correlation_matrix({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [2, 4, 6, 8]}) >>> round(r["matrix"][0][1], 6), r["n_pairs"][0][1] (1.0, 4)

items.title: cramers_v_matrix
items.text:
cramers_v_matrix(columns: 'Any', bias_corrected: 'bool' = True, n_category: 'int' = 20) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Cramer's V and chi-square p-values between categorical columns.

Only categorical columns (strings or booleans, or integer codes with at most n_category distinct values) take part. Each pair uses the rows where both values are observed; the rest are excluded and counted in n_pairs. Bias correction follows Bergsma (2013). The chi-square p-value is the uncorrected test of independence.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to values (or a table accepted by the data helpers). bias_corrected: apply the Bergsma bias correction to V. n_category: maximum distinct integer values for a numeric column to count as categorical.

Returns: dict with keys: names: categorical column names, in input order. matrix: symmetric list of lists of float or None. Diagonal is 1.0 when the column has at least 2 levels and 2 rows. None when a table has fewer than 2 levels or fewer than 2 rows, or when the bias-corrected denominator is zero. p_values: symmetric list of lists of float or None (same None rules). n_pairs: symmetric list of lists of int, rows used per pair. skipped: columns that are not categorical, in input order.

Example: >>> out = cramers_v_matrix({"x": ["a", "a", "b", "b"], "y": ["u", "u", "v", "v"]}, ... bias_corrected=False) >>> out["matrix"][0][1], round(out["p_values"][0][1], 6) (1.0, 0.0455)

items.title: describe
items.text:
describe(columns: 'Any', n_category: 'int' = 20, kinds: 'Mapping[str, str] | None' = None, trim: 'float' = 0.1, percentiles: 'Sequence[float]' = (0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95), inf_as_missing: 'bool' = False) -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Describe each column: kind, missingness, distinct count, and statistics.

Statistics are computed on the finite observed values. Numeric statistics are computed for every column whose observed values are all ints or floats (bools excluded), whatever its kind, so a 0/1 flag or a 1 to 5 rating gets a mean. Categorical statistics (mode and top, up to 10 (level, count) pairs ordered by count descending then str(level)) are computed for every column; infinities are excluded from them. Numeric keys are None when the column is not numeric-valued or the value is not computable.

The kind is a hint, never enforced:

  • 'categorical': any value that is not an int or float (bool included).
  • 'ordinal_candidate': all values integer-valued with fewer than 6 distinct values (likely a category code or an ordered rating such as 1 to 5; the user decides, and ordered levels suit monotone constraints).
  • 'numeric': all numbers that are not all integer-valued, or with more than n_category distinct values.
  • otherwise 'categorical' (integer-valued with 6 to n_category distinct values).

kinds overrides the hint per column with 'numeric', 'categorical' or 'ordinal' ('ordinal' is accepted only here). The override is echoed as kind without checking it against the data; kind_source is then 'user' instead of 'inferred'.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. n_category: Integer-valued columns with more distinct values than this are numeric; see the kind rule above. kinds: Optional {column: 'numeric' | 'categorical' | 'ordinal'}. trim: Fraction removed from each end before the trimmed mean and standard deviation, in [0, 0.5). floor(n * trim) values are removed from each end; trim=0 gives the plain mean and std. percentiles: Quantiles in [0, 1], whole percents only (e.g. 0.05). Each gives a key p05, p25, ... (p plus two digits). inf_as_missing: If True, infinities are also counted in n_missing and pct_missing. Statistics ignore infinities either way.

Returns: One dict per column, in input order, with keys:

- ``name``, ``kind``, ``kind_source`` (``'inferred'`` or ``'user'``).
- ``n`` (rows), ``n_missing``, ``pct_missing`` (0-100), ``n_inf``,
  ``n_distinct`` (distinct observed values, infinities included).
- ``mean``, ``std`` (sample), ``min``, ``q1``, ``median``, ``q3``,
  ``max``, ``skew`` and ``kurtosis`` (excess).
- One ``pNN`` key per requested percentile (default ``p05``, ``p25``,
  ``p50``, ``p75``, ``p95``).
- ``iqr`` (q3 - q1), ``mad`` (median absolute deviation from the median,
  unscaled), ``cv`` (std / mean; ``None`` when the mean is 0).
- ``trimmed_mean`` and ``trimmed_std`` after trimming (see ``trim``).
- ``n_outliers_iqr`` and ``pct_outliers_iqr`` (percent of finite values)
  outside the Tukey fences ``q1 - 1.5*iqr`` and ``q3 + 1.5*iqr``.
- ``n_zero``, ``n_negative``, ``n_positive`` (finite values).
- ``mode`` and ``top``.

Every column has the same keys; keys that do not apply are ``None``.

Raises: ValueError: For an invalid trim, a bad percentile, or a kinds entry naming an unknown column or kind.

Example: >>> rows = describe({"x": [1.5, None, 2.5, 3.5]}) >>> rows[0]["kind"], rows[0]["n_missing"], rows[0]["mean"] ('numeric', 1, 2.5) >>> describe({"flag": [0, 1, 1, None]})[0]["kind"] 'ordinal_candidate'

items.title: duplicate_columns
items.text:
duplicate_columns(columns: 'Any') -> 'list[list[str]]'

Groups of columns with identical values row by row.

Compared under the same rule as :func:duplicate_rows.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table.

Returns: List of name lists (input order within a group), ordered by each group's first column. Only groups of two or more columns are returned.

Example: >>> duplicate_columns({"a": [1, 2], "b": [1.0, 2.0], "c": [2, 1]}) [['a', 'b']]

items.text:
duplicate_rows(columns: 'Any') -> 'list[list[int]]'

Groups of identical rows, as ascending row indices.

Missing equals missing (None and NaN are the same marker), and 1 equals 1.0. Only groups of two or more rows are returned.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table.

Returns: List of index lists, ordered by each group's first index.

Example: >>> duplicate_rows({"a": [1, 2, 1, None], "b": ["x", "y", "x", None]}) [[0, 2]]

items.title: infer_types
items.text:
infer_types(columns: 'Any', n_category: 'int' = 20, kinds: 'Mapping[str, str] | None' = None) -> 'dict[str, dict[str, Any]]'

Kind and number of distinct observed levels per column.

Uses the same kind rule as :func:describe, including the kinds override (see there for its values).

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. n_category: Threshold for integer-valued columns (see :func:describe). kinds: Optional {column: 'numeric' | 'categorical' | 'ordinal'}.

Returns: {name: {'kind', 'n_levels', 'ordinal_candidate'}}. kind is the override if given, else the hint ('numeric', 'categorical' or 'ordinal_candidate'). n_levels is the number of distinct observed non-missing values. ordinal_candidate is True when the data-based hint is 'ordinal_candidate', whatever the override.

Raises: ValueError: For a kinds entry naming an unknown column or kind.

Example: >>> infer_types({"c": ["a", "b", None], "n": [1.5, 2.0, 3.0]})["c"]

items.title: information_value_table
items.text:
information_value_table(columns: 'Any', y: 'Sequence[Any]', n_bins: 'int' = 10, method: 'str' = 'quantile', monotone: 'str | None' = None, max_bins: 'int | None' = None, min_bin_frac: 'float' = 0.05, smoothing: 'float' = 0.5, min_level_frac: 'float' = 0.0) -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

IV for every column: iv_bins for numeric, iv_levels for categorical.

A column is numeric when every non-missing value is an int or float (bool excluded). Strength follows the usual rule of thumb: below 0.02 useless, below 0.1 weak, below 0.3 medium, below 0.5 strong, otherwise suspicious.

Args: columns: Dict of columns, or a table as_columns accepts. y: Binary target, same length as each column. n_bins, method, monotone, max_bins, min_bin_frac, smoothing: Passed to iv_bins for numeric columns. min_level_frac: Passed to iv_levels for categorical columns.

Returns: List of dicts with name, iv, kind ("numeric" or "categorical"), n_bins (ordered or level bins, missing excluded), and strength. Sorted by IV descending, then name.

Example: >>> t = information_value_table({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4]}, [0, 0, 1, 1], n_bins=2) >>> t[0]["name"], t[0]["kind"], t[0]["n_bins"] ('x', 'numeric', 2)

items.title: iv_bins
items.text:
iv_bins(values: 'Sequence[Any]', y: 'Sequence[Any]', n_bins: 'int' = 10, method: 'str' = 'quantile', monotone: 'str | None' = None, max_bins: 'int | None' = None, min_bin_frac: 'float' = 0.05, smoothing: 'float' = 0.5, edges: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, optimize: 'str' = 'greedy', n_prebins: 'int' = 50, trend: 'str | None' = None, special_values: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Information value of a numeric feature against a binary target.

Usable rows are those with a present target. Rows with a missing target are excluded and counted in n_y_missing. Missing feature values form missing_bin, which is never merged or dropped. Infinite feature values fall into the end bins. The events are the larger of the two target values (True or 1 for a 0/1 target).

optimize="greedy" (default, unchanged): bin (edges, or bin_edges on the usable rows); merge empty bins; enforce a monotone event rate by PAV if requested; merge bins smaller than min_bin_frac of the usable rows, smallest first; then merge the adjacent pair losing the least IV until at most max_bins ordered bins remain.

optimize="dp": exact optimal binning. Fine pre-bins are built first (n_prebins quantile, or width, cuts on the observed values, or the given edges; empty pre-bins are merged away, so ties may give fewer). Then the partition of the ordered pre-bins into contiguous bins is chosen to maximise objective subject to:

  • between 2 and max_bins ordered bins (max_bins defaults to n_bins);
  • each ordered bin holds at least min_bin_frac of the feature-present usable rows, and at least one event and one non-event;
  • the event rate across ordered bins follows trend: None (free), "increasing", "decreasing", "peak" (non-decreasing, then non-increasing), "valley" (non-increasing, then non-decreasing), or "auto" (the better of increasing and decreasing). Equal rates are allowed everywhere.

If no partition meets the presence and size rules, they are relaxed in that order, and finally the bin count may drop to one (always feasible). constraint_relaxed is True whenever that happens, or when fewer than two pre-bins exist. The trend itself is relaxed only by that last step. Ties in objective (within 1e-12) prefer fewer bins, then the earliest cuts.

DP objective (additive over ordered bins, with the fixed prior s and the totals E, N of events and non-events over the feature-present usable rows, special-value rows included, missing feature values excluded)::

contribution(bin) = (e/E - ne/N) * ln(((e+s)/(E+s)) / ((ne+s)/(N+s)))

objective is the sum over ordered bins of this term, for both optimisers, so the two can be compared directly. iv is the standard IV with the per-cell smoothing of this module (missing and special cells included).

Complexity (dp): contributions for all pre-bin ranges come from prefix sums in O(P^2). The DP has state (bins used, last bin start, last bin end, trend phase) and runs in O(max_bins * P^3) time for P = n_prebins, with the phase factor 2 for peak and valley. A 20 000-row feature with P = 50, max_bins = 8 and trend="auto" takes well under a second.

Special values. Each value in special_values that occurs in the feature forms its own bin, reported with "special": True and lo == hi == value. Special rows are counted, never dropped, and sit outside the ordered bins: they do not take part in the trend, the PAV or the greedy merges, and they are not subject to min_bin_frac.

Relation to optbinning. This solves the same problem class as the optbinning package (ordered numeric bins for a binary target, with a trend constraint, bounds on bin count and bin size, and special codes kept in their own bins). Here the optimum is exact for the chosen pre-bins by dynamic programming, with no solver library. Not supported: continuous or multiclass targets, categorical optimal grouping, and concave or convex trends (only the four shapes above).

Args: values: Numeric feature values. y: Binary target; exactly two distinct values, or one (no contrast). n_bins: Target number of quantile or width bins (greedy); also the default max_bins for dp. method: "quantile" or "width" for the initial bins. monotone: Alias of trend for None, "increasing", "decreasing", "auto". Conflicts with a different trend raise ValueError. max_bins: Upper bound on ordered (non-missing, non-special) bins. None means no cap for greedy, and n_bins for dp. dp needs at least 2. min_bin_frac: Minimum share of feature-present usable rows per ordered bin, in [0, 1]. For greedy, the share of all usable rows. smoothing: Positive prior count added to each cell. edges: Greedy: cut points used as given. Dp: the pre-bins, used as given. optimize: "greedy" (default) or "dp". n_prebins: dp only: number of quantile pre-bins to start from (at most). trend: None, "increasing", "decreasing", "peak", "valley" or "auto". greedy supports the first three and "auto". special_values: Finite numbers that get their own bins (e.g. [-999, 0]).

Returns: Dict with keys: iv (float): total IV, including the missing and special bins. bins (list[dict]): ordered bins first, then special bins. Each has lo, hi (floats, +-inf at the ends; equal for specials), special (bool), n, events, non_events, event_rate, woe, iv. missing_bin (dict): n, events, non_events, event_rate, woe, iv. When empty, n is 0, woe and event_rate are None and iv is 0.0. n_rows (int): len(values). n_used (int): rows with a present target. n_y_missing (int): rows with a missing target. trend (str | None): "increasing", "decreasing", "peak" and "valley" (dp only), "none" (constant or other shape), or None with fewer than two ordered bins. optimize (str): the optimiser used. objective (float): sum of the DP contribution over ordered bins. constraint_relaxed (bool): dp: True when a rule was relaxed (see above). greedy: always False, since its rules are not the DP ones.

Raises: ValueError: For a non-binary target, invalid options, conflicting monotone/trend, peak/valley with greedy, dp with max_bins below 2, non-numeric values, or mismatched lengths.

Example: >>> r = iv_bins([1, 2, 3, 4], [0, 0, 1, 1], edges=[2.5], min_bin_frac=0) >>> round(r["iv"], 6), r["trend"] (2.145917, 'increasing') >>> d = iv_bins([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1], optimize="dp", ... n_prebins=6, max_bins=2, min_bin_frac=0) >>> [(b["lo"], b["hi"], b["n"], b["events"]) for b in d["bins"]] [(-inf, 3.5, 3, 1), (3.5, inf, 3, 2)]

items.title: iv_levels
items.text:
iv_levels(values: 'Sequence[Any]', y: 'Sequence[Any]', min_level_frac: 'float' = 0.0, smoothing: 'float' = 0.5) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Information value of a categorical feature against a binary target.

One bin per level, sorted by event rate ascending (ties by level name). Levels with fewer than min_level_frac of the usable rows are pooled into a level named "__other__". Missing values form missing_bin. Target handling, smoothing and the returned keys follow iv_bins, with level in place of lo/hi and trend always None.

Args: values: Categorical values (any hashable); None and NaN are missing. y: Binary target. min_level_frac: Pool levels rarer than this share of usable rows, in [0, 1]. smoothing: Positive prior count added to each cell.

Returns: Dict with keys iv, bins (dicts with level, n, events, non_events, event_rate, woe, iv), missing_bin, n_rows, n_used, n_y_missing, trend.

Example: >>> r = iv_levels(["a", "b", "a", "b"], [0, 0, 1, 1]) >>> [b["level"] for b in r["bins"]], round(r["iv"], 6) (['a', 'b'], 0.0)

items.title: kfold
items.text:
kfold(n: 'int', k: 'int' = 5, seed: 'int' = 0, stratify: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, groups: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, time_order: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None) -> 'list[tuple[list[int], list[int]]]'

Split n rows into k (train, test) folds.

Modes:

  • plain: seeded shuffle, then k consecutive blocks whose sizes differ by at most one.
  • stratify: each class is shuffled within itself, then dealt round-robin across folds. The round-robin pointer carries over between classes, so fold sizes also differ by at most one. A class smaller than k is spread as evenly as possible and does not raise.
  • groups: groups are taken in seeded-shuffle order and each goes to the currently smallest fold (ties to the lower fold index). No group appears in two folds. Requires at least k groups.
  • time_order: expanding window. Rows are sorted by (key, index) and cut into k+1 consecutive blocks. Fold i trains on blocks 0..i and tests on block i+1. Block 0 is never tested. Requires n >= k+1.

groups and stratify cannot be combined in kfold. Each test fold is disjoint from the others, and the test folds cover all rows (except block 0 in time mode).

Determinism: the result depends only on (n, arguments, seed). See the module docstring.

Args: n: Number of rows. k: Number of folds, at least 2 and at most n. seed: Integer seed. stratify: One label per row. None/NaN is its own level. groups: One group id per row. None/NaN is its own group. time_order: One sortable key per row. Missing keys sort last.

Returns: A list of k (train_idx, test_idx) tuples, each list sorted ascending.

Raises: ValueError: If k < 2, k > n, there are fewer than k groups, time mode has n < k+1, or groups and stratify are both given.

Example: >>> folds = kfold(6, k=3, seed=0) >>> sorted(i for _, test in folds for i in test) [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] >>> [len(test) for _, test in folds] [2, 2, 2]

items.title: leakage_hints
items.text:
leakage_hints(columns: 'Any', y: 'Sequence[Any]', threshold: 'float' = 0.95) -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Single-feature predictive score per column, flagged when at or above a threshold.

Scores by feature kind and target type: numeric feature, binary y: AUC by ranks, folded to max(auc, 1 - auc), metric "auc". numeric feature, numeric y: squared Pearson correlation, metric "r2". categorical feature, binary y: AUC of the in-sample level event rates, folded; metric "auc_level_rate". In-sample rates overstate the score for high-cardinality columns (no leave-one-out). categorical feature, numeric y: eta squared (between-group share of variance), metric "eta2".

Binary y means exactly two distinct observed values. Rows with a missing or non-finite feature or y are excluded and counted in n_used. Nothing is removed; this only flags.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to values (or a table accepted by the data helpers). y: Target values, one per row. threshold: score at or above which a column is flagged.

Returns: list of dicts, one per column in input order, with keys: name: column name. score: float, or None when it cannot be computed (constant y, no rows, one class among the used rows, or zero variance). metric: "auc", "auc_level_rate", "r2", "eta2", or None. flagged: True when score is not None and score >= threshold. n_used: rows used (feature and y both observed).

Raises: ValueError: if y has more than two distinct values and is not numeric, or its length differs from the columns.

Example: >>> hints = leakage_hints({"f": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]}, [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]) >>> hints[0]["score"], hints[0]["flagged"] (1.0, True)

items.title: log1p
items.text:
log1p(values: 'Iterable[Any]') -> 'list[Any]'

Return log(1 + x) per row (x > -1 for observed values; missing passes through).

Example: >>> log1p([0.0, None]) [0.0, None]

items.title: missing_profile
items.text:
missing_profile(columns: 'Any', inf_as_missing: 'bool' = False) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Missingness per column, per row, by pattern, and as a co-missing matrix.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. inf_as_missing: If True, infinities count as missing in every count, pattern and per-row total below.

Returns: Dict with keys n_rows, n_cols, per_column ({name: {'n_missing', 'pct_missing'}}), per_row (missing count per row), n_complete_rows, patterns (list of {'columns': tuple of names missing together, 'count': int}, sorted by count descending then columns; the all-observed pattern is columns=()) and co_missing ({'names': [...], 'matrix': [[int]]}, the count of rows where both columns are missing; the diagonal is each column's missing count).

Example: >>> p = missing_profile({"a": [1, None], "b": [None, None]}) >>> p["n_complete_rows"], p["co_missing"]["matrix"] (0, [[1, 1], [1, 2]])

items.title: missing_vs_target
items.text:
missing_vs_target(columns: 'Any', y: 'Sequence[Any]', inf_as_missing: 'bool' = False) -> 'dict[str, dict[str, Any]]'

Target mean when each column is missing versus observed.

Rows whose target is missing or infinite are left out of every count and mean; their number is reported as n_y_missing_excluded. The counts n_missing and n_observed cover only the rows used for the means.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. y: Numeric target (0/1 or continuous), one value per row. inf_as_missing: If True, a column's infinite values count as missing (they are not missing by default).

Returns: {name: {'n_missing', 'n_observed', 'y_mean_when_missing', 'y_mean_when_observed', 'n_y_missing_excluded'}}. Means are None when there are no rows in that group.

Raises: ValueError: If y and the columns differ in length. TypeError: If y holds a non-numeric value.

Example: >>> r = missing_vs_target({"x": [1, None, 3, 4]}, [1, 0, 0, None]) >>> r["x"]["n_missing"], r["x"]["y_mean_when_missing"], r["x"]["n_y_missing_excluded"] (1, 0.0, 1)

items.title: near_zero_variance
items.text:
near_zero_variance(columns: 'Any', freq_cut: 'float' = 19.0, unique_cut: 'float' = 10.0) -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Columns flagged by the caret near-zero-variance rule.

Computed on observed values. freq_ratio is the count of the most common value divided by the count of the second most common; it is inf when there are fewer than two distinct values. pct_unique is 100 times the distinct count over the observed count (0.0 when nothing is observed). A column is flagged when it has at most one distinct value, or when freq_ratio > freq_cut and pct_unique < unique_cut.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. freq_cut: Frequency ratio cutoff. unique_cut: Percent-unique cutoff.

Returns: Flagged columns only, in input order, as dicts with keys name, freq_ratio, pct_unique and zero_var.

Example: >>> near_zero_variance({"a": [1, 1, 1, 1], "b": [1, 2, 3, 4]}) [{'name': 'a', 'freq_ratio': inf, 'pct_unique': 25.0, 'zero_var': True}]

items.title: outlier_flags
items.text:
outlier_flags(values: 'Sequence[Any]', method: 'str' = 'iqr', k: 'float | None' = None) -> 'list[bool | None]'

Flag outliers in one numeric column. Flags only; nothing is removed.

Methods: "iqr" (default k=1.5): flag values outside [q1 - k*iqr, q3 + k*iqr]. "mad" (default k=3.5): flag when the modified z-score 0.6745 * |x - median| / MAD exceeds k. When MAD is zero nothing is flagged.

Quartiles, median and MAD use the finite observed values.

Args: values: One numeric column. method: "iqr" or "mad". k: Threshold multiplier, or None for the method default.

Returns: One entry per value: None for missing, True for infinite, otherwise True or False.

Raises: ValueError: If method is unknown. TypeError: If a value is neither missing, infinite nor a number.

Example: >>> outlier_flags([1, 2, 3, 4, 100, None]) [False, False, False, False, True, None]

items.title: repeated_kfold
items.text:
repeated_kfold(n: 'int', k: 'int' = 5, repeats: 'int' = 3, seed: 'int' = 0, stratify: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, groups: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None) -> 'list[list[tuple[list[int], list[int]]]]'

Run :func:kfold repeats times, with repeat r using seed seed + r.

Args: n: Number of rows. k: Folds per repeat, as in :func:kfold. repeats: Number of repeats, at least 1. seed: Base seed. Repeat r uses seed + r. stratify: As in :func:kfold. groups: As in :func:kfold. time_order is not offered here.

Returns: A list of length repeats. Each item is the :func:kfold result for that repeat.

Raises: ValueError: If repeats < 1 or any :func:kfold argument is invalid.

Example: >>> runs = repeated_kfold(6, k=3, repeats=2, seed=0) >>> len(runs), len(runs[0]) (2, 3)

items.title: schema_capture
items.text:
schema_capture(columns: 'Any') -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Capture a schema (kind, missing count, range or levels) for later validation.

Each column records its inferred kind (kind_source is always 'inferred' here, as this function takes no kinds override). A 'numeric' column records the finite min and max, with levels None. Any other kind ('categorical' or 'ordinal_candidate') records the sorted observed levels, at most 200; beyond that the entry gets 'levels_truncated': True, and min and max are None.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table.

Returns: {'columns': {name: {'kind', 'kind_source', 'n_missing', 'min', 'max', 'levels'}}, 'n_rows': int}.

Example: >>> s = schema_capture({"x": [1.5, 3.5, None], "c": ["b", "a", "b"]}) >>> s["columns"]["x"]["max"], s["columns"]["c"]["levels"] (3.5, ['a', 'b'])

items.title: schema_validate
items.text:
schema_validate(columns: 'Any', schema: 'Mapping[str, Any]', allow_missing: 'bool' = True) -> 'list[dict[str, str]]'

Check columns against a schema from :func:schema_capture.

Problems reported:

  • missing_column: in the schema, absent from the data.
  • extra_column: in the data, absent from the schema.
  • kind_mismatch: the data breaks the stored kind. For an inferred kind this means only a change of value type (numbers against non-numbers); a change between numeric, ordinal_candidate and categorical is not a violation. A user-declared kind must match the data hint exactly. All-missing columns fit any kind.
  • out_of_range: finite numeric values outside the captured min and max (numeric columns only). Infinite values are not range-checked, matching how statistics ignore them.
  • unknown_level: observed values not among the captured levels (columns with levels). Skipped when the captured levels were truncated.
  • unexpected_missing: missing values when allow_missing is False.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to list, or a table. schema: The dict returned by :func:schema_capture. allow_missing: Whether missing values are acceptable.

Returns: List of {'column', 'problem', 'detail'} dicts. An empty list means the data is valid. Schema columns come first, in schema order, then extra columns in data order.

Example: >>> s = schema_capture({"x": [1.5, 2.5]}) >>> schema_validate({"x": [5.5, None]}, s)[0]["problem"] 'out_of_range'

items.title: select_rows
items.text:
select_rows(result: 'Mapping[str, Any]', indices: 'Iterable[int]') -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Subset the row-aligned fields of an xy/survival_xy/uplift_xy result.

x, y, time, event, treatment and outcome are subset by indices (negative indices follow Python rules; out-of-range raises IndexError). names and dtypes are copied unchanged. The n_*_missing counts are recomputed for the selected rows, so they always match the returned vectors. Rows are new lists.

Args: result: A dict returned by one of the accessors in this module. indices: Row positions to keep, in the order wanted; repeats allowed.

Returns: A new dict with the same keys as result.

Example: >>> res = xy({"a": [1, 2, 3], "y": [0, None, 1]}, "y") >>> sub = select_rows(res, [2, 0]) >>> sub["x"], sub["y"], sub["n_y_missing"] ([[3], [1]], [1, 0], 0)

items.title: survival_xy
items.text:
survival_xy(columns: 'Any', time: 'str', event: 'str', features: 'Iterable[str] | None' = None, exclude: 'Iterable[str]' = ()) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Build survival inputs: x rows, time and event vectors.

time and event are left out of the default features. The event column is passed through unchanged; coding differs between datasets (1 or 2 for death, or three outcomes in one trial), so map it to the model's convention yourself. Rows with a missing time or event are kept and counted.

Args: columns: A dict of column name to list, or a load_dataset result. time: Name of the follow-up time column. event: Name of the event column. features: Optional explicit feature names, in the order wanted. exclude: Column names to leave out of the features.

Returns: A dict with keys x, time, event, names, dtypes, n_time_missing and n_event_missing.

Raises: KeyError, ValueError: As for xy.

Example: >>> cols = {"t": [5.0, None, 9.0], "died": [1, 2, 0], "age": [60, 70, 50]} >>> out = survival_xy(cols, "t", "died") >>> out["event"], out["n_time_missing"] ([1, 2, 0], 1)

items.title: take
items.text:
take(columns: 'Any', indices: 'Sequence[int]') -> 'Any'

Subset rows of a dict of columns (or of a list) by index, keeping indices order.

Values are copied by reference and never transformed, so missing values stay missing. The input is not modified.

Args: columns: A dict mapping column name to a sequence of values, or a list or tuple of values. indices: Row positions to keep. Repeats are allowed. Order is preserved.

Returns: A dict with the same keys (dict input) or a list or tuple of the same kind (sequence input), each holding the selected rows.

Raises: IndexError: If an index is negative or at least the length of a column. The message names the bad index. TypeError: If an index is not an integer, or columns is not a dict, list or tuple.

Example: >>> take({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]}, [2, 0]) {'a': [3, 1], 'b': ['z', 'x']} >>> take([10, 20, 30], [1]) [20]

items.title: train_test_split
items.text:
train_test_split(n: 'int', test_size: 'float' = 0.2, seed: 'int' = 0, stratify: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, groups: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, time_order: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None) -> 'tuple[list[int], list[int]]'

Split n rows into train and test index lists.

Modes (at most one of stratify, groups, time_order; groups may be combined with stratify):

  • plain: a seeded shuffle, the first test rows go to test.
  • stratify: each label's rows are split proportionally (largest remainder), so class counts match their exact share within one row. A class of one row goes to train.
  • groups: whole groups go to test in seeded-shuffle order until the test count reaches the target. No group is split across the two sides.
  • groups with stratify: a group's label is its majority label. Groups are taken from the label furthest below its target share. This is approximate.
  • time_order: rows sorted by (key, index); the last test rows are test. No shuffling.

Determinism: the result depends only on (n, arguments, seed). See the module docstring.

Args: n: Number of rows. Must be at least 2. test_size: Float in (0, 1) for a fraction, rounded half up, then clamped to [1, n-1]. Or an int >= 1 for an absolute count, which must be at most n-1. seed: Integer seed for the shuffle. stratify: One label per row. None/NaN is its own level. groups: One group id per row. None/NaN is its own group. time_order: One sortable key per row. Missing keys sort last.

Returns: (train_idx, test_idx), both sorted ascending, both non-empty, and together they cover range(n) exactly once.

Raises: ValueError: For an invalid size, an invalid mode combination, a length mismatch, or a groups split that leaves one side empty.

Example: >>> train_test_split(10, test_size=0.2, seed=0) ([0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8], [4, 9])

items.title: train_val_test_split
items.text:
train_val_test_split(n: 'int', val_size: 'float' = 0.2, test_size: 'float' = 0.2, seed: 'int' = 0, stratify: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, groups: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, time_order: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None) -> 'tuple[list[int], list[int], list[int]]'

Split n rows into train, validation and test index lists.

The test split is made first with :func:train_test_split. The validation split is then made from the remaining rows with the same mode and seed. A float val_size is a fraction of the original n, not of the remainder.

Args: n: Number of rows. Must be at least 2. val_size: Fraction (float) of the original n, or an absolute count (int). test_size: As in :func:train_test_split. seed: Integer seed, used for both splits. stratify: As in :func:train_test_split. groups: As in :func:train_test_split. time_order: As in :func:train_test_split. The validation rows are the latest rows of the remainder.

Returns: (train_idx, val_idx, test_idx), each sorted ascending, together a partition of range(n).

Raises: ValueError: If the validation count leaves no training rows, or for any invalid argument covered by :func:train_test_split.

Example: >>> train_val_test_split(10, val_size=0.2, test_size=0.2, seed=0) ([1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8], [0, 3], [4, 9])

items.title: uplift_xy
items.text:
uplift_xy(columns: 'Any', treatment: 'str', outcome: 'str', features: 'Iterable[str] | None' = None, exclude: 'Iterable[str]' = ()) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Build uplift inputs: x rows, treatment and outcome vectors.

The treatment column is passed through unchanged (no recoding to 0/1). Rows with a missing treatment or outcome are kept and counted; this helper does not decide which rows to analyse.

Args: columns: A dict of column name to list, or a load_dataset result. treatment: Name of the treatment column. outcome: Name of the outcome column. features: Optional explicit feature names, in the order wanted. exclude: Column names to leave out of the features.

Returns: A dict with keys x, treatment, outcome, names, dtypes, n_treatment_missing and n_outcome_missing.

Raises: KeyError, ValueError: As for xy.

Example: >>> cols = {"treat": [1, 0, None], "conv": [0.0, 1.0, 1.0], "age": [30, 40, 50]} >>> out = uplift_xy(cols, "treat", "conv") >>> out["names"], out["n_treatment_missing"] (['age'], 1)

items.title: vif
items.text:
vif(columns: 'Any') -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Variance inflation factor of each numeric column on complete cases.

Rows with a missing or non-finite value in any numeric column are excluded (counted in n_excluded). VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R^2_j), where R^2_j comes from regressing column j on all the others with an intercept. A column that is an exact linear combination of the others gets inf. Constant columns get None (VIF undefined) and are named in warning. Regression is done on the centered correlation matrix with a Cholesky factor of the columns kept so far.

Args: columns: Dict of column name to values (or a table accepted by the data helpers).

Returns: dict with keys: vif: {name: float, inf or None} for each numeric column. n_used: complete rows used. n_excluded: rows left out because a numeric column was missing or non-finite. names: numeric column names, in input order. skipped: non-numeric column names, in input order. warning: None, or a message when VIF could not be computed (too few complete rows, or constant columns).

Example: >>> out = vif({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [1, 2, 3, 5]}) >>> out["n_used"], round(out["vif"]["x"], 6) > 1 (4, True)

items.title: xy
items.text:
xy(columns: 'Any', target: 'str', features: 'Iterable[str] | None' = None, exclude: 'Iterable[str]' = ()) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Build model inputs x (rows), y and feature metadata from columns.

Features default to every column except the target and exclude, in input order. features sets an explicit list and order instead; names in exclude are removed from it. Rows with a missing target are kept; the count is reported in n_y_missing.

Args: columns: A dict of column name to list, or a load_dataset result. For a load_dataset result its dtypes are used; otherwise dtypes are inferred (any str or bool observed value means categorical). target: Name of the target column. features: Optional explicit feature names, in the order wanted. exclude: Column names to leave out of the features.

Returns: A dict with keys x (one new list per row), y (list), names (feature names), dtypes ("numeric" or "categorical" per feature) and n_y_missing (int).

Raises: KeyError: If the target, a feature or an excluded name is not a column. ValueError: If columns have different lengths, a feature is repeated, or the target is also listed as a feature.

Example: >>> cols = {"a": [1, 2, None], "b": ["u", "v", "u"], "y": [0.5, None, 1.5]} >>> out = xy(cols, "y") >>> out["x"] [[1, 'u'], [2, 'v'], [None, 'u']] >>> out["dtypes"], out["n_y_missing"] (['numeric', 'categorical'], 1)

items.title: yeojohnson_lambda
items.text:
yeojohnson_lambda(values: 'Iterable[Any]') -> 'float'

Yeo-Johnson lambda maximising the profile log-likelihood on observed values.

Returns NaN when there are no observed values and 1.0 when fewer than two distinct values.

Example: >>> yeojohnson_lambda([2.0, 2.0]) 1.0

items.title: DatasetBuilder
items.text:
class DatasetBuilder(n_category=None, na_policy='allow', digits=None, add_intercept=False)

Ingest any data into the typed dataset.

Owns the ingestion semantics: n_category category inference, explicit NA policy, digit rounding and an optional intercept column. Missing is None or NaN — both are counted in na_counts, and filling is opt-in only.

Args (constructor): n_category: integral numeric columns with at most this many distinct levels become categorical; values < 1 mean a fraction of rows (None = no inference). na_policy: "allow" (keep missing), "drop" (drop rows containing any missing) or "impute" (numeric mean, categorical mode). digits: round floats to this many decimal places (None = no rounding). add_intercept: append a constant 1.0 column named intercept.

items.title: DatasetBuilder.add_categorical
items.text:
add_categorical(self, /, name, values)

Add a categorical column from strings; the vocabulary is first-seen order. None = missing.

Args: name: column name. values: one level per row (None = missing).

items.title: DatasetBuilder.add_numeric
items.text:
add_numeric(self, /, name, values)

Add a numeric column. NaN is treated as missing.

Args: name: column name. values: one value per row (None/NaN = missing).

items.title: DatasetBuilder.build
items.text:
build(self, /)

Build the typed dataset with the configured policies applied.

Returns: dict with columns (name -> values), dtypes ("numeric" or "categorical"), na_counts (missing per column), n_rows, n_cols.

Raises: ValueError: inconsistent column lengths, duplicate names, invalid policy usage (e.g. "drop" removing every row).

items.title: Dataset
items.text:
class Dataset(columns: 'Any', target: 'str | None' = None, *, features: 'Sequence[str] | str | None' = None, exclude: 'Sequence[str] | str' = (), event: 'str | None' = None, time: 'str | None' = None, treatment: 'str | None' = None, outcome: 'str | None' = None, groups: 'str | None' = None, weights: 'str | None' = None, name: 'str | None' = None) -> 'None'

Columns plus their roles, with the data helpers as methods.

Args: columns: A dict of column name to list, a load_dataset result, or any table mltreelib.data._common.as_columns accepts (for example a data frame). target: Name of the target column for supervised tasks. features: Explicit feature names, in the order wanted. Role columns cannot be features. exclude: Column names to leave out of the default features. event: Survival event column. time: Survival follow-up time column. treatment: Uplift treatment column. outcome: Uplift outcome column. It is the target, so it cannot be combined with a different target. groups: Column of group ids, for example for grouped splits. weights: Column of per-row sample weights. name: Optional label. A load_dataset result supplies its own name.

Raises: KeyError: If a role or exclude names a column that does not exist. The message names the column. ValueError: If a feature is also a role, one column is used for two roles, target and outcome differ, or the columns have different lengths.

Example: >>> ds = Dataset({"age": [30, 40], "t": [5.0, 9.0], "died": [1, 0]}, ... time="t", event="died") >>> ds.names ['age']

items.title: Dataset.associations
items.text:
associations(self) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Association checks on the features (plus leakage hints when there is a target).

Returns: A dict with correlation_matrix, cramers_v_matrix, vif and leakage_hints (None without a target).

items.title: Dataset.checks
items.text:
checks(self) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Feature-level checks, computed on the features only.

Returns: A dict with constant_columns, near_zero_variance, duplicate_rows (n_groups, n_extra_rows = rows that repeat an earlier row, and groups of row indices) and class_balance (None unless the target is categorical or has exactly two values).

items.title: Dataset.describe
items.text:
describe(self, **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Per-column statistics: profile.describe on every column.

items.title: Dataset.fit_args
items.text:
fit_args(self) -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Keyword arguments for ModelTree.fit: model.fit(**ds.fit_args()).

y is the time column when a time role is set (survival; event= is then passed too), otherwise the target. treatment= and sample_weight= are passed when those roles are set. Feature rows, col_names and dtypes always are.

Raises: ValueError: If there is neither a target nor a time role.

items.title: Dataset.iv
items.text:
iv(self, **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Information value per feature. The target must be binary.

The event level is the larger of the two target values, as in binning._event_flags (for strings, the alphabetically larger one).

Split into train and test, or train, validation and test.

Args: test_size: Fraction in (0, 1), or an int count of test rows. seed: Seed for the shuffle. The same seed gives the same split. stratify: True stratifies on the first of these roles that is set: treatment (uplift), then event (survival), then target. A column name, or a list of names, stratifies on those columns. True raises if the chosen column is numeric with more than 20 distinct values, since every value would be a class of one. groups: A column name, or a list of names, whose groups never split. Not taken from the groups role automatically. time: A column name (rows ordered by it, latest rows go to test) or True (row order). No shuffling. Cannot combine with stratify or groups. val_size: If given, a validation set is also cut from the rows left after the test split (a fraction of all rows).

Returns: (train, test), or (train, val, test) when val_size is given. Rows are never dropped or changed; missing values stay missing.

Raises: ValueError: For an invalid mode (see the helpers), a continuous column under stratify=True, or no role to stratify on. KeyError: If a named column does not exist.

items.title: FeatureTransformer
items.text:
class FeatureTransformer(kind: 'str', **params: 'float | None') -> 'None'

Fit-then-apply transform for one column.

Args: kind: One of 'log1p', 'power', 'mean_diff', 'median_diff', 'boxcox' or 'yeojohnson'. **params: p for 'power' (default 2.0, nonzero). lmbda for 'boxcox' and 'yeojohnson' fixes lambda instead of fitting it.

Attributes set by fit: params_ (dict): {} for log1p; {'p': p} for power; {'mean': m}; {'median': m}; {'lambda': lam} for boxcox and yeojohnson. NaN when there are no observed values to fit. n_fit_ (int): observed finite values used for fitting. n_missing_ (int): None and NaN rows (not used, kept in the output). n_inf_ (int): infinite rows (not used, kept in the output).

Rules: Missing and infinite rows come back unchanged. A value outside a transform's domain raises ValueError naming the first offending index.

Domains and formulas:
- ``log1p``: x > -1; y = log(1 + x); inverse x = expm1(y).
- ``power``: p is finite and nonzero. y = x**p, where a negative x is
  allowed only when p is an odd integer (then the inverse is the
  sign-preserving real root). Otherwise x >= 0, and x > 0 when p < 0.
  The inverse is y**(1/p) and needs y >= 0 (y > 0 when p < 0). Even
  integer p is rejected for negative x because it is not invertible there.
- ``mean_diff`` / ``median_diff``: y = x - centre; inverse adds it back.
- ``boxcox``: x > 0; y = (x**l - 1) / l, or log(x) when |l| < 1e-12.
  The inverse is x = (l*y + 1)**(1/l), or exp(y) when |l| < 1e-12.
- ``yeojohnson``: any real x; y = ((x+1)**l - 1) / l for x >= 0 and
  -((1-x)**(2-l) - 1) / (2-l) for x < 0, with log forms at l = 0 and l = 2.
  The inverse is exact for every lambda, including l = 0 and l = 2.

Lambda is fitted by golden-section search on [-5, 5] to tolerance 1e-8 of the profile log-likelihood. The search assumes a unimodal likelihood; a maximum at the boundary means the data wants lambda outside the range.

Example: >>> t = FeatureTransformer("mean_diff").fit([1, 2, 3, None]) >>> t.params_ {'mean': 2.0} >>> t.transform([4, None]) [2.0, None]

items.title: GroupedFeatureTransformer
items.text:
class GroupedFeatureTransformer(kind: 'str', *, fallback: 'str | None' = None, **params: 'float | None') -> 'None'

One FeatureTransformer per group label.

Args: kind: Transform kind, as for :class:FeatureTransformer. fallback: None (default) raises KeyError for a group unseen at fit time. 'global' uses a transformer fitted on all rows for unseen groups. **params: Passed to each per-group FeatureTransformer.

Domain errors name the offending input row. Groups are checked in order of first appearance, so the reported row is the first bad row in the first bad group.

Attributes set by fit: transformers_ (dict): group label to fitted FeatureTransformer, in first-appearance order. global_ (FeatureTransformer | None): fallback transformer when fallback='global'.

Example: >>> g = GroupedFeatureTransformer("mean_diff").fit([1, 3, 10, 20], ["a", "a", "b", "b"]) >>> g.transform([1, 3, 10, 20], ["a", "a", "b", "b"]) [-1.0, 1.0, -5.0, 5.0]

items.title: VariableScaler
items.text:
class VariableScaler()

Per-column distributional scaling — each variable transformed independently (legacy VariableTransformation semantics).

Same strategy names as GroupedScaler, applied per column, with exact inverse_transform. None/NaN are missing and pass through as missing; degenerate scales give missing, never inf.

items.title: VariableScaler.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, columns, strategy)

Fit all columns at once under the given strategy.

Args: columns: {name: values} for every column to scale (None/NaN = missing; counted in each column's n_missing). strategy: strategy name (see GroupedScaler).

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy.

items.title: VariableScaler.inverse_transform
items.text:

Exact inverse of transform under the fitted statistics.

Args: name: fitted column name. values: previously transformed values.

Returns: original-scale values (up to floating-point error).

items.title: VariableScaler.transform
items.text:

Scale one fitted column's values.

Args: name: fitted column name. values: numeric values (None/NaN = missing).

Returns: scaled values; None for missing inputs and degenerate scales.

items.title: GroupedScaler
items.text:
class GroupedScaler()

Fit/transform group distributional scaling with exact inverse (sklearn-shaped: fit once, then transform / inverse_transform).

Strategies: centered family — "zscore", "min-max", "median-iqr", "mean-iqr", "median-qd", "median-std", "median-range", "mean-range", "min-qd", "min-iqr"; ratio family — "min", "max", "mean", "median", "iqr", "qd", "std", "range". Missing in -> missing out; degenerate (zero) scales give missing, never inf.

items.title: GroupedScaler.fit
items.text:

Fit group statistics of values under the given strategy.

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing; counted in each group's n_missing). strategy: strategy name (see the class docstring).

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy or mismatched lengths.

items.text:

Args: keys: group label per row. values: numeric value per row.

items.title: BaseNEncoder
items.text:
class BaseNEncoder(base)

Base-N / binary encoding: each level becomes its base-base digits as indicator columns (base = 2 is the classic Binary encoder). Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen and missing rows are all-zero.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder
items.text:
class CatBoostEncoder(prior, permutations, seed)

CatBoost-style ordered target statistics — the leakage-safe flavour.

fit_transform gives each row the running statistic of its level using only rows earlier in a shuffled order: (sum_y_prefix + prior * global) / (n_prefix + 1), averaged over permutations seeded passes. The same level gets different values in different rows — that row-dependence is the anti-leakage mechanism. transform (new data) uses prior-smoothed fitted level means.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit prior-smoothed level means (used by transform on new data).

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.fit_transform
items.text:
fit_transform(self, /, values, y)

Leakage-safe ordered encodings of the training rows themselves.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Encode new rows from the fitted level means; unseen -> global mean, missing -> None.

class CountEncoder(normalize)

Count / frequency encoding: occurrence count per category (normalize gives the share of rows). Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen levels give 0.0; missing stays missing.

items.title: CountEncoder.transform

items.title: EmbeddingEncoder
items.text:
class EmbeddingEncoder(dim, lr, epochs, seed, task)

NN-style learned embeddings per category: a small embedding table and a linear head trained by SGD, one table per categorical feature. Task: both — softmax head for classification; for regression a ReLU output when all fitted targets are non-negative, linear otherwise. transform returns the embeddings, predict the trained head. Unseen levels give zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: JamesSteinEncoder
items.text:
class JamesSteinEncoder()

James-Stein encoding: level means shrunk toward the grand mean with B = max(0, 1 - ((L - 3) * sigma2) / sum((mean_i - global)^2)); fewer than three levels collapse to the grand mean. Task: both. Unseen -> global; missing -> None.

Fit shrunk means on (values, y).

items.title: JamesSteinEncoder.transform
items.text:

Shrunk mean per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder
items.text:
class LeaveOneOutEncoder()

Leave-one-out encoding: fit_transform gives each row its level's mean target without that row (leakage-aware); transform on new data uses the full fitted level mean. Task: both. Unseen -> global mean; missing -> None.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.fit

Fit level means on (values, y).

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.fit_transform
items.text:
fit_transform(self, /, values, y)

Row-level means excluding each row's own target.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.transform
items.text:

Full fitted level means for new rows.

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder
items.text:
class MEstimatorEncoder(m)

M-estimate encoding: (sum_y + m * global) / (n_level + m) — target smoothing with fixed strength m. Task: both (leaky on training data; prefer CatBoostEncoder or LeaveOneOutEncoder there). Unseen -> global; missing -> None.

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit smoothed level means on (values, y).

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Smoothed mean per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: OneHotEncoder
items.text:
class OneHotEncoder()

One-hot expansion: one indicator column per fitted level (first-seen order). Missing values and levels unseen at fit produce an all-zero row.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Learn the levels (first-seen order). Re-fitting resets them.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.levels
items.text:
levels(self, /)

Fitted levels, in column order.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Returns {level: indicator list}; unseen/missing rows are all-zero.

items.title: QuantileEncoder
items.text:
class QuantileEncoder(q, smoothing)

Quantile encoding: each level becomes its smoothed target quantile (default median), w * level_quantile + (1 - w) * global_quantile with w = n / (n + smoothing). Task: regression. Unseen -> global quantile; missing -> None.

items.title: QuantileEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit quantiles on (values, y).

items.title: QuantileEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Smoothed quantile per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: SumEncoder
items.text:
class SumEncoder()

Sum contrast coding: k-1 columns; level i < k-1 gets +1 in column i, the last level gets -1 across all columns. Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen rows give zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: SumEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Fit the level vocabulary on values.

items.title: SumEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Contrast row per row (None = missing).

items.title: TargetEncoder
items.text:
class TargetEncoder(smoothing)

Smoothed target encoding (fitted-mean flavour).

w * level_mean + (1 - w) * global_mean with w = n / (n + smoothing). Leaky on training data (the row's own target is in its level mean) — prefer CatBoostEncoder.fit_transform for training features. Unseen levels fall back to the global mean; missing stays missing.

items.title: TargetEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit level means on (values, y).

items.title: TargetEncoder.prior
items.text:
prior(self, /)

The global mean used as the unseen-level fallback.

items.title: TargetEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Encode values; unseen -> global mean, missing -> None.

items.title: TfidfEncoder
items.text:
class TfidfEncoder(normalize)

Class-level TF-IDF: each category becomes a vector over the target classes — tf(v,j) = count(v,j)/count(v) times idf(j) = ln(1 + n/(1 + count(j))) + 1; normalize scales each level vector to unit L2 norm. Task: classification. Unseen levels fall back to the global class shares; missing stays missing.

items.title: TfidfEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y, n_classes)

Fit class counts on (values, y, n_classes).

items.title: TfidfEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

One class-space vector per row (None = missing).

items.title: WoEEncoder
items.text:
class WoEEncoder(prior)

Weight of Evidence (credit-risk classic): one-vs-rest ln(distr_j(v) / distr_not_j(v)) per category, smoothed with additive prior. Task: classification. Positive = over-representation of the class in that level. Unseen levels give neutral zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: WoEEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y, n_classes)

Fit class counts on (values, y, n_classes).

items.title: WoEEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

One WoE vector per row (None = missing).

items.title: API reference — Feature functions
items.text: Grouped/trended/windowed transforms, lags and calendar parts. Guide: Data processing.

items.title: grouped_scale
items.text:
grouped_scale(keys, values, strategy='zscore')

One-shot group scaling: fit on (keys, values) and transform the same rows.

Each row's value is scaled by its group's summary under strategy (centered family like "zscore" or ratio family like "mean"; see GroupedScaler for the full list and the exact inverse).

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing). strategy: one of "zscore", "min-max", "median-iqr", "mean-iqr", "median-qd", "median-std", "median-range", "mean-range", "min-qd", "min-iqr", "min", "max", "mean", "median", "iqr", "qd", "std", "range".

Returns: scaled values; rows with a missing key/value, an unseen group or a degenerate (zero) scale give None — missing in, missing out.

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy or mismatched lengths.

items.title: grouped_transform
items.text:
grouped_transform(keys, values, kind='mean')

Per-row group summary of values within groups defined by keys.

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing; excluded from the group statistics but counted in each group's n_missing). kind: "mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1" or "q3".

Returns: the summary of each row's group; rows with a missing key/value or an unseen group give None.

Raises: ValueError: unknown kind or mismatched lengths.

items.title: trended_transform
items.text:
trended_transform(keys, dates, values, granularity='year_month', kind='mean', hemisphere='north')

Grouped summary trended at a time granularity.

Each row gets the summary of its (key x time-bucket) cell — e.g. with granularity "year_month" and kind "mean", the row's key-and-month mean. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). granularity: bucket spec joined by "_" from {year, halfyear, season, quarter, month, week, weekday, day} — e.g. "year_month", "year_week", "month_weekday". kind: summary kind ("mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1", "q3"). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (affects the season component).

Returns: per-row cell summaries; incomplete rows give None.

Raises: ValueError: unknown granularity/kind/hemisphere, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: windowed_transform
items.text:
windowed_transform(keys, dates, values, window_days=7, kind='mean', include_current=True)

Trailing-window aggregation per key over day windows.

Each row summarizes the observed values of its key in a window of window_days days; incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). window_days: window length in days (>= 1); covering the window_days days ending at the row's date, or strictly earlier days when include_current is false. kind: summary kind ("mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1", "q3"). include_current: include the row's own date in the window.

Returns: per-row window summaries; None for incomplete rows and for empty/all-missing windows.

Raises: ValueError: window_days == 0, unknown kind, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: lag_by_days
items.text:
lag_by_days(keys, dates, values, lag_days)

Lag values by whole days within each key (day granularity).

Each row receives the value of its key at date - lag_days; duplicate (key, date) rows keep the last occurrence. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). lag_days: lag in whole days (0 returns the row's own value).

Returns: lagged values; None where no source row exists.

Raises: ValueError: unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: decomposed_transform
items.text:
decomposed_transform(keys, dates, values, season_granularity='month', trend_window=3, hemisphere='north')

Additive decomposition, following the statsmodels seasonal_decompose (additive) convention.

The trend is a centered moving average over each key's rows ordered by date; the seasonal component is the mean of (series - trend) per (key, season bucket), estimated from rows with a complete trend window. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). season_granularity: bucket spec for the seasonal component (e.g. "month", "weekday" — same vocabulary as trended_transform). trend_window: centered moving-average window in rows (>= 1). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (affects the season component).

Returns: dict with detrended (series - trend), deseasonalized (series - seasonal) and residual (series - trend - seasonal); incomplete rows give None.

Raises: ValueError: trend_window == 0, unknown granularity/hemisphere, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: calendar_features
items.text:
calendar_features(dates, hemisphere='north')

Calendar features for ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD or timestamp prefix).

Produces year, halfyear, quarter, month, week (ISO), iso_year, weekday (0 = Monday), day, day_of_year, season and weekend as numeric parts, ready for tree learners.

Args: dates: ISO date strings or timestamps (None = missing). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (southern shifts the season by six months).

Returns: dict of 11 feature lists aligned with dates; rows with a missing date give None features.

Raises: ValueError: unparseable date or unknown hemisphere.

items.title: API reference — Metrics
items.text: Complete evaluation reports at once. Guides: Metrics, Evaluation reports.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
class Metrics()

One metrics class computing complete reports at once — the yardstick every learner is measured with. Task: both. Pairs with a missing/NaN side are dropped from the math and reported in n_missing, never hidden.

items.title: Metrics.brier_score
items.text:
brier_score(self, /, y_true, probs)

Calibration (reliability) bins: mean predicted score vs observed frequency per bin. Task: classification.

classification(self, /, y_true, y_pred, probabilities=None)

Complete classification report: accuracy, macro averages, per-class precision/recall/f1/support, confusion matrix — and with probabilities (P(class 1)) also logloss, brier and ROC-AUC.

Args: y_true: integer class labels (None/NaN = missing). y_pred: predicted labels (None/NaN = missing). probabilities: P(class 1) per row; enables the probabilistic metrics.

Returns: the full report as a dict.

Single-label classification scorecard (binary or multiclass). Task: classification.

Complete competing risks report for multi-cause survival endpoints: cause-specific Harrell's C, Uno's IPCW C, cause-specific IBS and time-dependent Brier scores over specified or sample decile evaluation horizons.

Args: durations: observed follow-up times. events: event indicators (0 = censored, 1..J = mutually exclusive causes). cif_curves: optional CIF curves mapping {cause: (N, T)} or 3D list (N, n_causes, T). risk_scores: optional risk scores mapping {cause: (N,)} or 2D list (N, n_causes). times: optional evaluation horizon times grid.

items.text:
fit(self, /, x, y=None, w=None, dtypes=None, control=None, id_col=None, group_col=None, col_names=None, event=None, treatment=None, n_classes=None, sample_weight=None, row_weights=None, col_weights=None, feature_weights=None, train_groups=None, train_ids=None, fairness_penalty=None, protected_col=None, protected_attribute=None, fairness_metric=None, sporf_d=None, sporf_projections=None, extratrees=None, ebm_fast=None)

Fit the tree on row-major data using the selected leaf family.

Args: x: rows of predictors; None entries are missing (NA rows train). y: targets; None/NaN drops that row for binomial/Poisson. Gaussian NaN handling follows the historical Gaussian path. Binomial targets are 0 or 1; Poisson targets are finite nonnegative counts or rates (including fractional values). Gaussian targets retain ordinary regression. w: optional per-row sample weights (row weightage); zero-weight rows are ignored. dtypes: optional per-column types — "numeric" (default) or "categorical" (values are level codes; the split search partitions levels, no encoding).

Returns: nothing; the fitted tree replaces the inner model.

items.title: API reference — Rust generic seam

The Rust core owns the shared optimization seam. Python callers reach it through mltreelib.solvers.optimize. Guide: Generic optimizer.

The short names Bounds, Budget, Constraint, ConstraintKind, Objective, ObjectiveError, OptimizationRequest, OptimizationResult, OptimizerKind, SmoothObjective, and SolveStatus are re-exported from mltreelib_core::solver.

items.text: Standalone weighted fitting and the generic bounded optimizer. Guide: Generic optimizer.

items.title: fit
items.text:
fit(X, y, *, family='gaussian', solver='auto', l1=0.0, l2=0.0, sample_weight=None, monotone=None, max_iter=250, tol=1e-09, seed=42, tweedie_p=None, tobit_threshold=None)

Fits a weighted Gaussian or generalized linear model without growing a tree.

Pass one numeric design matrix and one response per row. Use nonnegative case weights with a positive total weight. The solver picks the exact Gaussian path when it fits the family and the requested penalties.

items.title: optimize
items.text:
optimize(objective, bounds, *, method='random_search', start=None, max_evaluations=None, max_iterations=None, tol=1e-06, seed=0, gradient=None, samples=None, initial_population=None, constraints=None, constraint_kind='inequality', local_method=None)

Minimizes a callable scalar objective inside bounds.

The objective receives one list of parameter values and returns one finite scalar. The optional gradient callable receives the same list and returns one value per parameter. Smooth methods use a central-difference fallback when no gradient is supplied. For COBYLA, constraints returns a fixed-length sequence of finite inequality residuals. Nonnegative residuals are feasible. For basin hopping, local_method selects the inner optimizer.
